title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.1 What it is
An attribute inference attack uses a trained model to recover a sensitive field of a person’s record, such as smoking status, from the fields the attacker knows. For example, an insurer who knows your age and diagnosis could query a hospital’s model of the disease from age and smoking, and guess if you smoke. But a published study on smoking allows the same guess, so success alone is not a privacy failure. What matters is whether the model reveals more about you because it trained on your record.
Yeom et al. (2018) turned this question into a game (Threat models and privacy games). A fair coin decides whether the target is a training record, a member, or a fresh draw from the same population. The attacker knows the target’s public features and label, queries the model and guesses the sensitive value. Its score is the attribute advantage, \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attr}} = \Pr[\text{guess right} \mid \text{member}] - \Pr[\text{guess right} \mid \text{non-member}]. \tag{11.1}\] A guess from the whole population alone, called population inference, helps members and non-members equally, because both come from that population. So it cancels in the difference, and what is left is the leak about individuals.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.2 When you meet it
You meet it when someone claims that “the model reveals” a sensitive field, or asks if a model is safe without a column. Only the extra success on members is then a privacy leak. Success up to what the population allows exists without the person’s record, so it is a question for policy and fairness.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.3 How to use it
Start with the imputation baseline, the success of the best guess of the sensitive value from the public features and label, without the model. Many published attacks do no better (Jayaraman & Evans 2022), so it is the number to beat. To estimate it, fit a classifier for the sensitive field on population records the model never saw.
Then run the attack. Model inversion (Fredrikson et al. 2014) scores each candidate value \(s\) of the sensitive field by two numbers. The first is the probability \(p(s \mid x)\) that a person with the target’s public features \(x\) has that value, estimated from population data. The second is \(f_y(x, s)\), the model’s confidence in the known label \(y\) on input \(x\) with the candidate. The attack guesses the value that maximizes their product, \[\hat s = \arg\max_s\; p(s \mid x)\, f_y(x, s). \tag{11.2}\]
Give the attacker every column it could hold, because a near-copy of the sensitive field, such as relationship next to marital status, moves the baseline most. Run the attack on training members and on as many held-out non-members. Report the baseline and the two success rates with confidence intervals. Also put an interval on the advantage, because Pre-release privacy risk assessment blocks a release when that interval lies above zero.
The script practitioner_attribute.py, run with uv run python code/part02-attacks/practitioner_attribute.py, applies the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox (ART) to Adult, the census records of 45,222 people. A random forest predicts from every column if income exceeds $50K, and sex is the sensitive field. The attacker holds 4,000 records of its own, and everyone’s other columns and income.
def label(rows: IntArray) -> Array:  # the label the model returns for each record, as a column
    return np.argmax(target.predict(x[rows]), axis=1).reshape(-1, 1).astype(np.float64)

np.random.seed(seed)  # ART builds its random forests unseeded, from NumPy's global generator
attack = AttributeInferenceBlackBox(target, attack_model_type="rf", attack_feature=SENSITIVE)
attack.fit(x[attacker])  # the attacker's own records, sensitive field included
baseline = AttributeInferenceBaselineTrueLabel(attack_model_type="rf", attack_feature=SENSITIVE)
baseline.fit(x[attacker], y[attacker])  # the same records and the true label, without the model
hits: dict[str, list[int]] = {}
for name, rows in (("members", members), ("non-members", others)):
    known = np.delete(x[rows], SENSITIVE, axis=1)  # everything but the sensitive field
    guess = attack.infer(known, pred=label(rows), values=[0.0, 1.0])
    imputed = baseline.infer(known, y=y[rows], values=[0.0, 1.0])
    hits[name] = [int(np.count_nonzero(np.equal(g.ravel(), female[rows]))) for g in (guess, imputed)]
ART black-box attack: right on members 0.8300 [0.8180, 0.8415]  on non-members 0.8423 [0.8306, 0.8534]
ART black-box attack: advantage -0.0123 [-0.0285, +0.0040]
imputation baseline: right on members 0.8307 [0.8188, 0.8423]  on non-members 0.8417 [0.8301, 0.8529]
The attack is right on 0.8300 of the members, and the baseline, which never queries the model, on 0.8307. So the success comes from the population, and the advantage’s interval contains zero, which passes the rule. On a synthetic population the full edition does find a small leak. There, inversion is right on 0.7832 of members and 0.7262 of non-members, an advantage of 0.0569.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.4 What goes wrong
The most common error is one success rate, such as that 0.7832 on members, without the baseline and the rate on non-members. That report overstates the leak. A rate on fresh records only understates it, because a model is surer of the true label on its own members (Membership inference).
A model without the sensitive column still allows population inference, because the column’s correlates remain. Confidence masking, which rounds the confidences or returns only the top label, puts no bound on the gap between members and non-members. The gap can even grow. In the full edition’s experiment, labels only raised the advantage from 0.0569 to 0.0650, because success fell more on non-members than on members. Less overfitting shrinks the gap, and differential privacy bounds it for every attacker and every output format.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.5 References

Fredrikson, Jha & Ristenpart, “Model Inversion Attacks that Exploit Confidence Information and Basic Countermeasures” (CCS 2015): inversion from confidences, and rounding as a countermeasure.
Jayaraman & Evans, “Are Attribute Inference Attacks Just Imputation?” (CCS 2022): the imputation baseline, and what it takes to beat it.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.1 What it is
A property is a fact about a training set as a whole, such as the share of a hospital’s patients who are over 65. Property inference recovers it from a trained model. In the property game (Threat models and privacy games), a fair coin picks one of two shares for a subgroup, and the owner trains on data with that share. The attacker knows the two shares and the training method, and guesses the share. So a random guess is right half the time.
A property can leak when no single record does. Write \(n\) for the number of training records and \(g\) for the gap between the two shares. A switch of shares changes about \(n g\) records at once, so it moves the model far more than one record can. So the leak grows with \(n\), while the risk to one record shrinks.
Even a release of only the exact count of subgroup records shows this gap. With 10,000 records, the best guess of whether one patient is in the data is right with probability 0.502. The best guess of whether the share was 0.45 or 0.55 is right with probability 1.0000.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.2 When you meet it
You meet it when you share or publish a model trained on your organization’s data. First decide if the property is a secret, that is, if it describes the data owner rather than the world. One hospital’s patient mix is a secret, but the fact that smokers get more lung cancer is the point of a medical study. If the property is not a secret, write that in the threat model of Pre-release privacy risk assessment and move on.
If the property is a secret, differential privacy (DP) does not protect it. DP protects one record at a time, and its guarantee for a group is the privacy level \(\varepsilon\) times the group’s size (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). For a hospital of 1,000 patients and shares a tenth apart, the group is the \(n g = 100\) patients that differ between the two datasets. So the property gets only \(100\varepsilon\), which promises nothing at any useful \(\varepsilon\).

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.3 How to use it
To measure the risk, run the shadow-model attack of Ateniese et al. (2015), which treats whole models as data points. Draw many datasets of your training set’s size at each share, from data of the same population. Train a shadow model on each with your architecture and training code, and record its outputs on a fixed set of probe inputs.
With the outputs recorded, fit a linear meta-classifier, such as scikit-learn’s LogisticRegression, to tell the two shares apart from those outputs. Its accuracy on held-out shadow models is the attack’s accuracy. If the property is a secret, block the release when the interval on that accuracy lies above one half (Pre-release privacy risk assessment).
Use probe outputs rather than raw weights. A new order of the hidden units, or a sign flip of tanh units, changes the weights but not the network’s function. So on the full edition’s small tanh networks, every raw weight averages to zero under the two shares. A linear meta-classifier scores 0.497 on raw weights, which is chance, and 1.000 on the probe outputs. Probes need only query access, so a model behind an application programming interface is exposed too.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.4 What goes wrong
The most common error is to assume that DP, or a passed membership audit, covers the property. A weak measured attack is not evidence of safety either, because a meta-classifier fitted to noisy shadow models finds a small shift badly.
No defence is cheap. A model without the group column still sees its correlates, and noise that hides \(n g\) records destroys the model’s use. So if the property is a secret, do not release a model trained on that mix. If you must release it, report the attack’s accuracy and say in the release notes that DP protects individuals only.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.5 References

Ganju, Wang, Yang, Gunter & Borisov, “Property Inference Attacks on Fully Connected Neural Networks using Permutation Invariant Representations” (CCS 2018): the practical attack on neural networks, and why raw weights fail.
Zhang, Tople & Ohrimenko, “Leakage of Dataset Properties in Multi-Party Machine Learning” (USENIX Security 2021): property inference through queries alone.

Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.1 Why this matters
A language model trained on scraped text or support tickets sees phone numbers, addresses, keys and private messages. Asked to continue “Anna Smith’s phone number is”, it may finish with the real number. This is training-data extraction. Membership inference needs the record in hand to ask whether it was used, while extraction hands the attacker the record itself.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.2 Which memorization to measure
The notions of memorization in Table 13.1 give rates that differ by orders of magnitude, so a report must say which one it measures. All use greedy decoding, which writes out the most likely next token at each step.



Table 13.1: The notions of memorization and when to use each. The first three are verbatim, needing an exact match, and each implies approximate. Discoverable implies extractable.










Definition
The string counts as memorized if
Use it for




Discoverable (Carlini et al. 2023)
The text before it in the training data makes greedy decoding produce it
Measuring memorization on a model you own


Extractable (Carlini et al. 2021)
Some prompt, any at all, makes greedy decoding produce it
The real risk, which attacks find but no test measures


\(k\)-eidetic
It is extractable and appears in at most \(k\) documents
Flagging the dangerous case, \(k = 1\)


Approximate (Ippolito et al. 2023)
Greedy decoding comes within a set edit distance of it
Near copies, such as a number with one digit changed






Discoverable memorization is the one you can measure, because you hold the training text it uses as the prompt. Treat any verbatim rate as a lower bound on the leak, because near copies leak too. A filter that blocks only verbatim training text is easy to bypass (Ippolito et al. 2023).
Deployed systems sample rather than decode greedily, so whether a string comes out depends on how many samples the attacker draws. A sample at temperature 1 writes out a string with probability \(p\), the model’s probability of that string after the prompt. Write \(\beta\) for the chance of failure the attacker accepts. Then a number \(m\) of independent samples suffices when \[m \ge \frac{\ln(1/\beta)}{p}. \tag{13.1}\] For a string of probability \(10^{-3}\) and \(\beta = 0.01\), that is about 4,600 samples. So report a sampling budget alongside the greedy rate, and measure with the decoding settings you deploy.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.3 What gets memorized, and the first defences
text:
13.3 What gets memorized, and the first defences
Memorization grows with the copies of a string. On open models, the largest reproduced at least 1% of its training data in the discoverable sense (Carlini et al. 2023). A sequence repeated ten times is generated about a thousand times more often than one seen once (Kandpal, Wallace & Raffel 2022).
So the cheapest defence is deduplication, which lowers the copies of every repeated string. Models trained on deduplicated data emit memorized text about ten times less often, at the same quality (Lee et al. 2022). Deduplicate before you plant the canaries of the next section, so that only they carry known copy counts.
The second defence removes personal data before training. A detector of personally identifiable information (PII), such as Microsoft’s Presidio, finds names, phone numbers and similar fields so that you can mask them. But it misses whatever its patterns do not cover. Neither defence helps a secret seen once in a large model, where one copy is enough. Only fine-tuning with differential privacy, which limits how much any one training sequence can change the model, gives a guarantee for such singletons.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.4 Auditing with canaries and exposure
Discoverable memorization is all or nothing, while an auditor wants a graded answer. Carlini et al. (2019) plant canaries, random secrets of a fixed format such as “my pin is” followed by five random digits. After training, you order all the values the secret could have taken from the most to the least likely under the model. The planted value’s rank in that order is the number of guesses an attacker needs if it tries them in turn.
Write \(\hat r\) for the planted value and \(|\mathcal R|\) for the number of values in the set \(\mathcal R\) it could have taken. The exposure is the number of bits of search the model saves an attacker, \[\mathrm{exposure}(\hat r) = \log_2|\mathcal R| - \log_2\operatorname{rank}(\hat r). \tag{13.2}\] Each bit halves the guesses the attacker needs. At rank 1 the exposure reaches its maximum, \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\), and the secret can be extracted. For five digits, \(10^5\) values, the maximum is 16.61 bits.
Exposure works as an audit because we know how it behaves when the model memorized nothing. The canary’s value is uniformly random, so a model that never saw it gives it a uniformly random rank. So for any threshold of \(t\) bits, \[\Pr\big[\mathrm{exposure}(\hat r) \ge t\big] \le 2^{-t}. \tag{13.3}\] So \(2^{-\text{exposure}}\) bounds the p-value, the chance that an uninserted canary would look at least this memorized. The same uniform rank gives an uninserted canary an average exposure of \(\log_2 e\), about 1.44 bits, which the controls should match.
To run the audit, draw canaries in the format of the secrets your data could contain. A format unlike your data measures only how the model treats unfamiliar text. Insert each canary a chosen number of times, from once to many, keep some never inserted as controls, and fine-tune as usual. Then score each canary’s value, and many random values of the same format, by the model’s log-probability after the prefix. The share of random values that score at least as high estimates the rank fraction, the rank divided by \(|\mathcal R|\). Minus its base-2 logarithm is the exposure.
Most audits go wrong at the scoring step. A candidate’s log-probability is the sum over its tokens, but the mean loss that Hugging Face models return divides that sum by the number of tokens. Values of different token lengths then get scores on different scales, and the ranking is wrong. So score every candidate by its summed log-probability, in a format where every candidate has the same number of tokens. For example, write a pin as “the pin of Alice is 8 6 5 2 3”, so that each digit is one token.
Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA runs this audit on Pythia-14m, a small language model, and shows the code and its output. It inserts three canaries at each copy count from 1 to 64 into 1,024 sequences of Tiny Shakespeare. It keeps three more as controls and ranks each value among 2,000 random candidates. Exposure rises with the copies, and the controls sit at 1.4 bits, as the 1.44 expected for them predicts. Greedy decoding extracts only the three canaries seen 64 times. Yet two of the canaries seen 4 times reach 6.9 and 8.2 bits, which no extraction test notices. So an audit measures exposure and not only extraction.
The 2,000 candidates set a cap on the measured exposure. A canary that beats all of them shows only that its rank fraction is below about 1 in 2,000. So its exposure stops at \(\log_2 2000 = 10.97\) bits. Past the cap, fit a skew-normal distribution to the candidates’ scores and read the canary’s rank off its tail, as Carlini et al. (2019) do. Ties also hide memorization, because when every candidate gets the same score, every exposure is 0.
A canary repeated 16 or more times is the positive control. If it does not reach a high exposure without privacy, the run is too short to tell you anything. In that run the canaries fill a quarter of the training set, which lets so small a model memorize them. Pre-release privacy risk assessment sets the exposure that blocks a release.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.5 Extraction without the prefix: generate, rank, verify
text:
13.5 Extraction without the prefix: generate, rank, verify
A real attacker has only the model. Carlini et al. (2021) extracted data from GPT-2 in three steps. They generated many samples, ranked them by how likely each was to be memorized, and checked the top ones. The ranking is the hard step, because a model finds a string likely either because it is ordinary text or because it memorized it. A reference model, trained on similar data but not on the target’s training set, stands in for ordinary text. Write \(p_\theta(x)\) for the target model’s probability of a string \(x\), and \(p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)\) for the reference’s. Rank by the log-likelihood ratio \[\Lambda(x) = \ln p_\theta(x) - \ln p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x). \tag{13.4}\]
The ratio cancels the strings that any model finds likely, such as software licences and boilerplate. Raw likelihood would put these first, and they reveal nothing. A crude reference, such as a smaller model of the same family, works. To audit your own fine-tuned model, use the base model as the reference.
Without the prefix, an attacker extracts less than the discoverable rate suggests, but aligned production models are not safe. Nasr et al. (2023) asked ChatGPT to repeat one word forever, until it left its aligned behaviour and wrote memorized text. For about 200 US dollars of queries, they extracted over 10,000 records.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.6 Cheat sheet



Table 13.2: The results of this chapter.









Question
Answer




Exposure of a canary
\(\log_2\lvert\mathcal R\rvert - \log_2\operatorname{rank}\), at most 16.61 bits for five digits; p-value at most \(2^{-\text{exposure}}\); controls average 1.44 bits


How to score a candidate
Summed log-probability, in a format where all candidates have the same token count


Ranking generations
\(\ln p_\theta(x) - \ln p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)\), never raw likelihood


Defences, in order
Deduplicate (deduplicate-text-datasets, datasketch), scrub PII, then differential privacy for singletons

A verbatim rate is a lower bound on the leak, not a measure of it.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.1 Why this matters
In federated learning (FL), a server sends the current model to each phone or other client. The client computes the gradient of the loss on its own few records and sends back only that gradient. The server averages the gradients and takes a training step. People often call this private because “the data stay on the device”.
Yet one client’s gradient can give back all of that client’s data, because many of its derivatives are simple functions of the input. An average over a batch protects much less than people expect (Section 14.6). So treat each client’s update as being as sensitive as the data it came from.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.2 The attacker and what it sees
text:
14.2 The attacker and what it sees
The attacker is the server, which knows every parameter because it sent the model out, and which also sees each client’s own update. So its access is the transcript of Threat models and privacy games, everything that training exposes. Assume first that the server is honest-but-curious, so that it only analyses what it receives. Each client holds a batch of \(B\) records and sends the average of their gradients. Write \(\ell_i\) for the loss on record \(i\), which depends on all the parameters \(\theta\). The client then sends \[g = \frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\nabla_\theta\ell_i. \tag{14.1}\]

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.3 Exact recovery from a fully connected layer
text:
14.3 Exact recovery from a fully connected layer
The most common first layer, a fully connected layer with a bias, gives its input back by one division. Write \(W_1\) and \(b_1\) for its weights and bias. Each unit \(j\) multiplies the input \(x\) by its row of weights and adds its bias. Its backward signal \(u_j\) is how fast the loss responds to the unit’s output. The chain rule turns this signal into the weight and bias gradients \[\nabla_{W_1}\ell = u\,x^\top, \qquad \nabla_{b_1}\ell = u. \tag{14.2}\] So row \(j\) of the weight gradient is the input scaled by \(u_j\), and the bias gradient of unit \(j\) is that same scale. For a single record, divide one by the other. This gives the input exactly, for every unit whose bias gradient is not zero: \[x = \frac{(\nabla_{W_1}\ell)_{j,:}}{(\nabla_{b_1}\ell)_j}. \tag{14.3}\]
Everything above the layer, including the network’s depth, the loss and the label, sits inside \(u_j\) and cancels. So the attack needs no optimization and no knowledge of the data. The snippet below plays one client with one image of scikit-learn’s digits in PyTorch. Its last line reads the label, as Section 14.4 explains.
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits

torch.manual_seed(0)
images, labels = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
x = torch.tensor(images[[7]] / 16, dtype=torch.float32)  # one client's image, pixels in [0, 1]
y = torch.tensor(labels[[7]])
first, last = torch.nn.Linear(64, 32), torch.nn.Linear(32, 10)
F.cross_entropy(last(torch.relu(first(x))), y).backward()  # the gradient the client sends
# Row j of the weight gradient is the input times the bias gradient of unit j: divide them.
j = int(first.bias.grad.abs().argmax())
recovered = first.weight.grad[j] / first.bias.grad[j]
print(f"image recovered: {torch.allclose(recovered, x[0], atol=1e-6)}")  # image recovered: True
# Only the true label's logit has a negative gradient (softmax minus one-hot).
print(f"recovered label {int(last.bias.grad.argmin())}, true label {int(y)}")  # recovered label 7, true label 7
The snippet divides at the unit whose bias gradient is largest, because a ReLU unit that is off has a zero gradient. One active unit is enough. But a convolutional first layer stops the division. It uses the same filter at every position of the image, so its gradient is a sum of one product per image patch. No division can separate them. The attacker then has to search (Section 14.5).

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.4 Label recovery from the last layer
text:
14.4 Label recovery from the last layer
The label is often the most sensitive part of an example, such as a diagnosis. The attacker can read it off the last layer without search (Zhao, Mopuri & Bilen 2020). The condition is that the layer has a bias and feeds the softmax and cross-entropy loss. Write \(p\) for the predicted probabilities and \(e_y\) for the vector with a 1 at the position of the label \(y\). The gradient of the last layer’s bias \(b_2\) is then \(p - e_y\). Every entry of \(p\) lies between 0 and 1, so only the entry at the true label is negative, and for a single record \[y = \arg\min_k(\nabla_{b_2}\ell)_k, \tag{14.4}\] which is the snippet’s argmin. It fails only for a very confident model. If the true label’s probability \(p_y\) rounds to 1, that entry becomes zero, and no entry is negative.
A batch hides which record has which label, but not how many records each class has. Each entry of the bias gradient is then the class’s average predicted probability minus its share of the batch. So a server that estimates the average prediction can read off each class’s count. In the full edition’s experiment, this gave every count exactly in all batches of 4, and in 52.5% of batches of 64.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.5 Deep Leakage from Gradients
When the division does not apply, the attacker searches. Deep Leakage from Gradients (DLG), from Zhu, Liu & Han (2019), guesses inputs and computes the gradient they would produce. It then moves the guesses until that gradient matches the observed gradient \(g\). Write \(x_i'\) for the guessed inputs, \(y_i\) for their labels, read first from the last layer, and \(\ell(\theta; x', y)\) for the loss of one guess. The attack minimizes the matching loss \(R\), the squared distance between the guesses’ average gradient and \(g\): \[\hat x_1, \dots, \hat x_B = \arg\min_{x_1', \dots, x_B'}R(x'), \qquad R(x') = \Big\|\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; x_i', y_i) - g\Big\|^2. \tag{14.5}\] In PyTorch, create_graph=True in torch.autograd.grad makes the guess’s gradient differentiable, so an optimizer such as Adam can follow the slope of \(R\) back to the input.
Two things decide whether the search works. First, the activation’s slope must vary, because the search differentiates a gradient. The ReLU’s slope is constant on each side of zero, so Zhu et al. used the sigmoid. Second, \(R\) is not convex, so the search can get stuck. Run it until \(R\) stops falling, and compare the final value with the squared size \(\|g\|^2\) of the observed gradient. In double precision, a successful run in the full edition ends near \(10^{-27}\) and a stuck one near \(10^{-5}\). Another input can also give a small \(R\), so restart from several random guesses, and trust an image only when the restarts agree on it.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.6 Batches and averaging
Clients usually send the average over a batch, or the change in their parameters after several training steps on the device (local steps). The average breaks the division and slows the search, but much of the structure survives. Each record adds one outer product to the gradient of the first layer, so every row of that gradient is a combination of the \(B\) inputs. So the server learns their span, the set of all such combinations, which contains every record.
The division still recovers a record exactly when some ReLU unit is on for that record only. The other records then add nothing to that unit’s row. Such a unit isolates the record. Isolation is far more common than a count of random units suggests. On images that resemble one another, a unit fires on many records or on few. In the full edition’s network with 1,024 hidden units, a naive count predicts that 1.6% of a batch of 16 is exposed. But 69.1% was, as Table 14.1 shows. The share falls with a larger batch and rises with a wider first layer. So measure at your own width and batch size, and treat any isolated record as a breach.



Table 14.1: Isolation attack on synthetic images, from the full edition.

Batches hurt DLG more: on the full edition’s sigmoid network, the median run on a batch of 4 gets stuck. The search is harder, but the information is still there, because the isolation attack recovered all four images of such a batch. Local steps do not protect a single record either. The gradient of the first layer at each step is an outer product with the same input, so the division still works on the total change. A malicious server that chooses the weights can do more. It plants units that fire only on rare inputs, so that each unit isolates one record. It then recovers most records of a batch of any size (Boenisch et al. 2023, Fowl et al. 2022).

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.7 What to do as a deployer
text:
14.7 What to do as a deployer
The risk of an FL deployment depends on who can see one client’s update, as Table 14.2 shows.



Table 14.2: Gradient leakage by FL setting, and the response.










Setting
What leaks to the server
What to do




One record per update, fully connected first layer with bias
The input exactly, and the label
Never deploy without protection


Batches of any size, or several local steps
Label counts, the span of the batch, isolated records, and the rest by search in small batches
Treat each update as raw data


Server not trusted to choose weights
Most records of any batch
Batch size is no defence; treat each update as raw data


Updates protected by differential privacy (DP)
Bounded per client by the DP guarantee
The only protection with a guarantee






Secure aggregation is a cryptographic protocol that lets the server see only the sum over many clients. It removes the view of single clients that every attack here uses. But a sum over very few clients is close to a single update. So set a minimum cohort size, and make sure that clients who drop out in a round cannot shrink a sum below it.
Secure aggregation alone is not enough. The sum is still a batch average that the attacks above can read, and a malicious server can still choose its weights. For a guarantee, add DP with the client as the unit of privacy. Clip each client’s update to a fixed maximum norm and add noise to the sum. That bounds what any one client’s data can change (User-level privacy). Flower and TensorFlow Federated offer both protections. Gradient pruning and similar defences make the search harder but give no guarantee.
To assess your deployment, first find out whether the server sees single updates or only sums, and with what minimum cohort. Then run the attacks on your own architecture, batch size and number of local steps. Geiping’s open-source breaching framework for PyTorch runs them. If the server can see one client’s update on its own, block the deployment until secure aggregation or client-level DP is in place. Record the verdict in the Pre-release privacy risk assessment.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.1 Why this matters
A hospital deletes the names from its discharge records and shares them with researchers. It keeps the postcode, the date of birth, the sex and the diagnosis. A voter roll lists names next to the same three columns. Anyone who has one can join the two tables and put a name back on most rows. This is a linkage attack, and putting a name back on a “de-identified” record is re-identification.
To judge whether a table can be linked, count its identifying information in bits. Each bit halves the candidates. So it takes \(\log_2 n\) bits to single out one person in a population of \(n\) people. For the United States of 1990, that is 27.9 bits. Almost everyone is unique once the attributes an adversary knows carry a few bits more than that, and a unique record can be linked.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.2 Quasi-identifiers and the linkage attack
Direct identifiers, like a name or an email address, name a person on their own. Sensitive attributes, such as a diagnosis, are what the release is about. Quasi-identifiers sit in between. None of them names anyone alone, but together they often single out one person, and they appear next to names in other datasets.
To score a release you hold, group its \(n\) records into equivalence classes. A class is a set of records with identical quasi-identifiers. Write \(J\) for the number of classes. Suppose an adversary knows the target’s quasi-identifiers and knows that the target is in the release. If the target’s class holds \(k\) records, the adversary names the right one with probability \(1/k\). The class holds \(k\) possible targets, so every class adds one win whatever its size. Over all \(n\) targets, the chance of naming the right record is therefore \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac{J}{n}, \tag{15.1}\] and no adversary that sees only the quasi-identifiers can do better. This is the prosecutor model, the worst case, because it assumes the adversary knows the target is in the data.
The script practitioner_table_risk.py shows how fast uniqueness grows on a real table. The table is Adult, the 48,842 people of the 1994 US Current Population Survey in the UCI repository. Adult has no ZIP code or birth date, so the script starts from age, sex and race and adds one quasi-identifier at a time. For each set it prints the share of unique records, the share in classes smaller than 5, the smallest class size and \(J/n\).
n = df.height
for qis in QI_SETS:
    # One row per equivalence class (records that agree on every quasi-identifier), with its size.
    sizes = df.group_by(qis).len()
    unique = sizes.filter(pl.col("len") == 1).height / n  # share of records alone in their class
    small = sizes.filter(pl.col("len") < 5)["len"].sum() / n  # share in classes smaller than 5
    min_k = sizes["len"].min()  # the table is k-anonymous for this k
    print(
        f"{' + '.join(qis)}: unique={unique:.2%}  in classes <5={small:.2%}  "
        f"min k={min_k}  J/n={sizes.height / n:.3f}"
    )
Run it with uv run python code/part02-attacks/practitioner_table_risk.py, which prints:
age + sex + race: unique=0.12%  in classes <5=0.75%  min k=1  J/n=0.012
age + sex + race + native-country: unique=3.07%  in classes <5=7.83%  min k=1  J/n=0.060
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status: unique=5.88%  in classes <5=11.99%  min k=1  J/n=0.100
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status + education: unique=14.64%  in classes <5=26.83%  min k=1  J/n=0.227
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status + education + hours-per-week: unique=36.55%  in classes <5=57.05%  min k=1  J/n=0.480
Three columns that look harmless leave 0.12% of the records unique, and six leave 14.64%. The hours worked per week, which nobody would list as an identifier, then make 36.55% unique. So add every column an adversary could know to the test, one at a time. The column that breaks the table may be one that nobody suspected. A minimum class size of 5 is a common rule, yet every set here has classes of a single record.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.3 Pseudonyms and hashed identifiers
Many releases replace each identifier by a pseudonym, a code that stays the same across a person’s records. Such codes fail in two ways. First, an adversary can reverse a hash without a secret key, such as plain MD5, whenever the possible identifiers can be listed. It hashes every candidate and looks each pseudonym up. New York City hashed its taxi drivers’ licences this way in its 2013 trip release. There were only about 2 million possible licences, so in 2014 Vijay Pandurangan hashed them all in minutes and named each driver.
The second failure survives any key. The pseudonym ties a person’s records together, so a link to any one of them reveals all the others. In the taxi data, a passenger who knows the pickup minute and place can find one trip and its driver. The driver’s pseudonym, even a random one, then reveals every trip that driver made. For this reason the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) still counts pseudonymized data as personal data.
If you must keep a join key, make it with a keyed hash, a hash-based message authentication code (HMAC). Keep the key away from the data.
import hashlib
import hmac
import secrets

licence = "482913"  # a six-digit licence number, the identifier being pseudonymized
pseudonym = hashlib.md5(licence.encode()).hexdigest()  # what an unkeyed release prints

# Dictionary attack: hash all 10**6 possible licences once, then look the pseudonym up.
lookup = {hashlib.md5(f"{i:06d}".encode()).hexdigest(): f"{i:06d}" for i in range(10**6)}
print(lookup[pseudonym])  # 482913

# A keyed hash still gives one code per person, but without the key nobody can build the table.
key = secrets.token_bytes(32)  # store it apart from the data; draw a new one for each release
keyed = hmac.new(key, licence.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
print(keyed in lookup)  # False
The key stops the dictionary attack but not the second failure, because each person’s records still form an identifying history. The same key in two releases would join that history across them, so draw a new key for each release.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.4 How many people are unique?
When you design a release, there is no table to count yet, so estimate uniqueness by adding bits. An attribute with \(v\) equally likely values carries \(\log_2 v\) bits, and the bits of independent attributes add. Attributes that carry \(b\) bits in total split people into \(2^b\) cells. Suppose each person lands in a random cell, every cell equally likely. Then the expected share of the \(n\) people who are alone in their cell is about \[\frac{\text{unique people}}{n} \approx \exp\big(-2^{\log_2 n - b}\big). \tag{15.2}\] The share depends only on the bits beyond \(\log_2 n\), and it rises steeply with them. Half the people are unique at only 0.53 bits beyond \(\log_2 n\).
For example, ZIP code, birth date and sex carry 31.1 bits, a few more than the 27.9 bits that single out one American. The formula then predicts that 0.899 of Americans are unique, close to the 87% that Latanya Sweeney estimated from the 1990 census. Real attributes are skewed and correlated, which usually lowers uniqueness, so the estimate is cautious.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.5 Sparse data: the Netflix attack
Ratings, purchases and locations have no quasi-identifier columns, yet they identify people even better. In 2006 Netflix released about 100 million movie ratings, with random numbers in place of the subscribers’ names. Narayanan and Shmatikov (2008) matched its records to public reviews. Their score adds up the items on which a record agrees with what the adversary knows. It weights each item by its rarity, because an obscure film says more than a hit. Eight ratings with dates known to within 14 days identified 99% of the records, even when two of them were wrong.
The best score always points at some record, even when the target is not in the release. So the eccentricity test declares a match only if the best score beats the second best by a margin. It counts the margin in standard deviations of all the scores. Set that margin on people who are not in the data. On the full edition’s simulated ratings, the original attack’s margin also matched 26.3% of such outsiders. So report the attack’s success at a stated false positive rate (Hypothesis testing).

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.6 Does releasing a sample protect?
Agencies often release a sample, as Adult is, because a record unique in the sample may share its attributes with someone left out. This protects less than it seems. Suppose the release holds a share \(q\) of the population, the sampling rate, and the adversary finds exactly one record that matches a person. Write \(\lambda\) for the expected number of other people in the population who share the target’s cell. The record can be a look-alike’s only if the target was left out, which happens with probability \(1 - q\). So for a rare cell, the probability \(\kappa\) that the match is right is about \[\kappa \approx \frac{1}{1 + \lambda(1 - q)}. \tag{15.3}\]
For example, take a cell expected to hold \(\lambda = 0.1\) other people. Even in a 1% sample, a match is right with probability 0.910. The sample size enters only through \(1 - q\), which can never exceed 1. So the chance of a right match never falls below \(1/(1 + \lambda)\), and a smaller sample barely helps. A sample protects only people whose cells are crowded anyway.
So the Adult figures above are sample uniqueness, exact when the adversary knows the target is in the release. The population uniqueness behind them is lower, but not by much for rare cells. Estimate it with a model, and do not assume the risk away. ARX and sdcMicro offer such estimates, and Rocher, Hendrickx and de Montjoye (2019) model correlated attributes for it.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.7 A pre-release risk check
First list every column an adversary could find next to a name elsewhere, such as a date, a location or a rare event. No tool knows what other data exist, so no tool can make this list. To lower the risk, coarsen geography and dates first, because they carry the most bits. Then suppress the records that remain unique (Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks). If the analysis needs fine-grained or sparse data, release a differentially private output instead (Release statistics with a library). Pre-release privacy risk assessment runs this check with thresholds fixed before the counts are seen.

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.1 Why this matters
Linkage and re-identification showed that a table without names is not anonymous. Quasi-identifiers such as age, postcode and sex single out many people. The classic answer is to coarsen the table until every person hides in a crowd. The definitions of this answer are syntactic, because you check each one by reading the published table. You will meet them in audits, because statistics offices and tools such as ARX and sdcMicro still use them. But each one holds for one table and for an adversary whose knowledge is fixed in advance. One unexpected fact, or a second release of the same people, breaks it.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
section: 16.2 What the adversary believes about a class
text:
16.2 What the adversary believes about a class
To anonymize a table, the custodian, the organization that holds the data, applies a generalization. It turns an age into a range or a postcode into a prefix. Records with the same generalized quasi-identifiers form an equivalence class. An adversary who knows the target’s quasi-identifiers finds the target’s class \(E\) but cannot tell its records apart. So its belief about the target’s sensitive value, its posterior, is the share of the class with that value. Write \(\lvert E\rvert\) for the size of the class and \(n_E(v)\) for the number of its records with a sensitive value \(v\). Then the posterior that the target’s sensitive value, written \(S_{\text{target}}\), equals \(v\) is
\[\Pr[S_{\text{target}} = v \mid \text{release}] = \frac{n_E(v)}{\lvert E\rvert}. \tag{16.1}\] The adversary’s background knowledge about the target works by elimination. A fact that rules out a value crosses out its records, and the adversary computes the posterior again over the records that remain. Every attack in this chapter is this calculation.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.3 k-anonymity and what it costs
k-anonymity (Sweeney and Samarati, 1998) asks that every class hold at least \(k\) records, for a crowd size \(k\) that the custodian chooses. Generalization gets there, together with suppression, which deletes the records that still stand out. In the previous chapter, an adversary who knows the target is in the release links it with probability \(J/n\), the number of classes \(J\) over the number of records \(n\). So with at least \(k\) records per class, there are at most \(n/k\) classes, and \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac{J}{n} \le \frac1k. \tag{16.2}\] The guarantee covers names only, and only against an adversary who knows nothing beyond the quasi-identifiers. The choice of \(k\) is a policy, and 5 is a common minimum.
Anonymizers such as Mondrian search for a generalization that loses little, but you can also generalize by hand and check again. The script practitioner_table_risk.py takes the previous chapter’s Adult census extract and its six quasi-identifiers. It puts age into 10-year bands, native country into US or other, and education into four levels. Then it counts the records alone in their class, and the different occupations in each class, with occupation as the sensitive attribute. Both are Polars counts, because no maintained Python package computes k-anonymity or distinct \(\ell\).
general = df.with_columns(
    (pl.col("age") // 10 * 10).alias("age"),  # 10-year bands: 30 stands for 30-39
    pl.when(pl.col("native-country") == "United-States")
    .then(pl.lit("US"))
    .otherwise(pl.lit("other"))
    .alias("native-country"),
    # education-num runs from 1 (preschool) to 16 (doctorate); 9 is high-school graduate.
    pl.col("education-num")
    .cut([8, 9, 12], labels=["no diploma", "HS-grad", "some college", "bachelor+"])
    .alias("education"),
)
# Recheck, and count the occupations in each class (distinct l).
classes = general.group_by(QIS).agg(pl.len(), pl.col("occupation").n_unique().alias("l"))
unique = classes.filter(pl.col("len") == 1).height / general.height
one_job = classes.filter(pl.col("l") == 1)["len"].sum() / general.height
print(f"after generalizing: unique={unique:.2%}  in a class with one occupation={one_job:.2%}")
Run it with uv run python code/part02-attacks/practitioner_table_risk.py. Its first two output lines use the six generalized quasi-identifiers, and the third adds the raw hours worked per week.
after generalizing: unique=0.94%  in a class with one occupation=1.20%
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status + education: unique=0.94%  in classes <5=3.31%  min k=1  J/n=0.032
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status + education + hours-per-week: unique=10.09%  in classes <5=21.78%  min k=1  J/n=0.175
  records in classes of size >=5 with l=1: 0.03%
Generalization cut the unique share to 0.94%, from 14.64% before. Yet the smallest class still holds one record. So suppress the 3.31% of records in classes smaller than 5, or make the bands coarser. The result is fragile, because an adversary who also knows the hours worked finds 10.09% of the records unique again.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.4 Homogeneity, background knowledge and l-diversity
k-anonymity hides who a record belongs to, but not what it says (Machanavajjhala and colleagues, 2006). In the homogeneity attack, all three records of Alice’s class say heart disease. Her posterior is then 1, and nobody has to find her record. In the background knowledge attack, Bob’s class says cancer, cancer and flu. A neighbour who knows that Bob did not have flu crosses out that record and learns that Bob has cancer.
l-diversity asks each class to hold enough different sensitive values. The distinct version asks for at least \(\ell\) different values. It does not cap the most common value’s share, so a class can be 3-diverse with one value in most of its records. The recursive version adds that cap, with a constant \(c\) that the custodian picks. An adversary who rules out \(\ell - 2\) values then keeps a posterior below \(c/(1 + c)\). That cap is already one half at \(c = 1\), so even this version protects against certainty, not likelihood.
Suppression of the small classes also removes most homogeneous ones. On Adult, 1.20% of the generalized records sit in a class where everyone has the same occupation. Only 0.03% sit in such a class of 5 or more. On a synthetic hospital table of the full edition, distinct 3-diversity removed the certain disclosures at little cost. The recursive version forced some classes to grow to 641 patients.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.5 Measuring what a release teaches
Compare every posterior with the imputation baseline of Attribute inference and model inversion, the best guess of a sensitive value from the population alone. Only the success beyond it is about the individual. On the hospital table, a guess of each patient’s diagnosis from age alone is right for 53.6% of patients, and a 5-anonymous release raises that to 59.3%. Most of that gain is the link between age and diagnosis, which any useful study reports. Only the excess of 5.7 percentage points is a leak.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.6 Skewness, similarity and t-closeness
l-diversity misses two attacks (Li, Li and Venkatasubramanian, 2007). In the skewness attack, a class that is half HIV is 2-diverse, yet in a table where 1% have HIV it raises its members’ posterior fifty-fold. In the similarity attack, a class of three different stomach diseases is 3-diverse but still reveals a stomach disease.
t-closeness answers both. It asks that the distribution of values in every class \(E\) be within a distance \(t\) of the whole table’s. Write \(P_E(A)\) and \(P(A)\) for the chance that a value drawn from the class, or from the table, lands in a set \(A\) of values. With the total variation (TV) distance, no such chance, and so no belief, moves by more than \(t\), \[\lvert P_E(A) - P(A)\rvert \le t. \tag{16.3}\] The bound is a difference, not a ratio, so it protects rare values badly. At \(t = 0.15\), a value held by 1% of the table may rise to 16%. Against the similarity attack, Li and colleagues used the earth mover’s distance instead, which counts similar values as close.
t-closeness costs a lot. At \(t = 0.15\), a guess of diagnoses from the hospital release was right for only 22.2% of patients, below the 53.6% from age alone. So the release told less about the population than no release.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.7 The composition attack
Ganta, Kasiviswanathan and Smith (2008) asked what happens when two hospitals each publish a k-anonymous or l-diverse table. A patient treated at both sits in a class \(E_A\) of one release and a class \(E_B\) of the other. The adversary keeps only the diagnoses that appear in both classes, \[\{v : n_{E_A}(v) > 0\} \cap \{v : n_{E_B}(v) > 0\}. \tag{16.4}\] When one candidate is left, the diagnosis is pinned down.
In the full edition’s simulation, two hospitals share 6,649 patients. Together, their two 5-anonymous releases pin down the diagnosis of 9.9% of them, over three times what either pins alone. With distinct 3-diversity, neither release pins anyone, yet together they pin 18.
No definition for a single table can stop this, because the intersection of two tables is a table that neither custodian checked. A definition that survives must compose across releases and hold whatever the adversary knows. It must also bound the ratio of beliefs, so that it protects rare values. The definition of differential privacy meets these needs, and statistics offices such as the US Census Bureau have moved towards it (Reconstruction attacks).
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.8 Choosing and running an anonymization
Start from the quasi-identifiers of Linkage and re-identification, because a list that is too short is the most common failure. Use k-anonymity against linkage. Add distinct l-diversity when a class with one sensitive value is a disclosure. Use t-closeness, the costliest, only when the sensitive attribute is skewed or has similar values.
Then audit the anonymizer’s output yourself, in Polars as the excerpt does, or with pycanon, which reports \(k\), \(\ell\) and \(t\) for a pandas table. Pre-release privacy risk assessment turns these checks into a release decision. Move to differential privacy if other releases of the same people exist, if the sensitive attribute is rare, or if the data are sparse. For tables of counts and sums, Release statistics with a library does the job end to end.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

k-anonymity

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.1 What it is
A reconstruction attack rebuilds the records behind published aggregates, because every count is a linear equation in the secret values of the people counted. For example, each of \(n\) people has one secret bit, listed in \(d\). A subset-sum query asks how many people in a set have bit 1. So the attacker’s \(m\) queries form a matrix \(A\) of zeros and ones, one query per row. The curator who answers them publishes the true answers plus an error vector \(e\), \[a = Ad + e. \tag{17.1}\]
Least squares finds the real numbers with answers closest to the published ones, then rounds each to 0 or 1. Let each query include each person with probability one half. Let the noise be normal with standard deviation \(\sigma\). Then least squares recovers about a fraction \[\Phi\left(\frac{\sqrt{m - n}}{4\sigma}\right) \tag{17.2}\] of the bits, where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function. The baseline is the majority guess, which gives everyone the more common value, so it is right on one half of balanced bits. So with a few times more queries than people, noise well below \(\sqrt n\) reveals the data. If the curator answers all \(2^n\) subset sums, only error of order \(n\) stops reconstruction (Dinur and Nissim 2003).
These results are the Fundamental Law of Information Recovery: too many answers that are too accurate destroy privacy. But a release that stops reconstruction is not private for that reason. A curator that answers from a secret random half of the people stops it, yet gives that half away exactly. And a test of membership needs far fewer statistics (Lower bounds).

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.2 When you meet it
Every published count, cross-tabulation, dashboard cell or query answer is such an equation. The Census Bureau attacked its own 2010 publications and rebuilt a record for every person. About 46% of them matched a real person exactly on block, sex, age, race and ethnicity. With commercial data, they confirmed the identity of about 17% of the population, so the 2020 Census moved to differential privacy. Query systems fall too: the noise of Diffix did not grow with the number of queries, so Cohen and Nissim (2020) averaged it away.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.3 How to use it
To audit an aggregate release, first count the equations. If the cells or allowed queries outnumber the people, only the noise protects the people. Put your noise level and number of queries into Equation 17.2. If the prediction is far above the majority guess, run the attack. The snippet draws the noise from OpenDP’s Gaussian mechanism and runs least squares. OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so the snippet compares the share recovered with the prediction instead of printing it.
from statistics import NormalDist

import numpy as np
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, m = 500, 2000  # people with a secret bit each, and random subset-sum queries
sigma = 0.25 * np.sqrt(n)  # noise sd added to each answer
secret = rng.integers(0, 2, n)
queries = rng.integers(0, 2, (m, n))
space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False)), dp.l2_distance(T=float)
gaussian = dp.m.make_gaussian(*space, scale=sigma)  # OpenDP's Gaussian mechanism on all m answers
answers = np.array(gaussian((queries @ secret).astype(float).tolist()))
estimate = np.linalg.lstsq(queries, answers, rcond=None)[0]  # the textbook attack: least squares
recovered = np.mean(np.clip(estimate, 0, 1).round() == secret)
predicted = NormalDist().cdf(np.sqrt(m - n) / (4 * sigma))
print(f"predicted {predicted:.4f}")  # predicted 0.9584
print(f"recovered within 0.04 of it: {abs(recovered - predicted) < 0.04}")  # recovered within 0.04 of it: True
The number of queries matters as much as the noise. In the full edition’s simulation, with noise of twice \(\sqrt n\), four queries per person recovered only 0.5875 of the bits. But Equation 17.2 shows that at that noise, 106.1 queries per person recover 90%. So fixed noise falls to enough queries, and the noise must grow with the number of answers, as differential privacy makes it.
For queries that are not random, use the linear-programming decoder of Dinur and Nissim, which fits unknowns between 0 and 1 with scipy.optimize.linprog. For published tables, write each cell as a constraint on whole-number unknowns. Solve the constraints with scipy.optimize.milp. Then count the solutions, because a single solution rebuilds the records. The release fails if either decoder beats the majority guess.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.4 What goes wrong
Rounding, household swapping and small-cell suppression are not noise. Rounding hides nothing, because the attacker can round the answers of each candidate dataset too. Swapping leaves most constraints exact, and a suppressed cell even adds a constraint: the count is below the threshold. And sticky noise, the same answer to a repeated query, stops only repeats, which the attack never needs.
Test the union of all releases, not one table at a time. Do not trust least squares alone, because errors chosen against it hurt it more than random noise. Before you publish, reconstruct your own release with the two decoders. Record the result in Pre-release privacy risk assessment.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.5 References

Cohen & Nissim, “Linear Program Reconstruction in Practice” (Journal of Privacy and Confidentiality, 2020): the attack on Diffix.
Garfinkel, Abowd & Martindale, “Understanding Database Reconstruction Attacks on Public Data” (2019): a census block rebuilt with a solver.

Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 18  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
text:
18.1 Why this matters
Before a model or a table leaves your hands, someone has to decide whether it leaks too much about the people in it. This chapter makes that decision for three releases. They are a classifier behind a scoring API, a language model whose weights go to a partner, and a census extract. The attacks themselves run in earlier chapters, and this one reads their results against fixed thresholds and writes the verdict down.
The order matters as much as the attacks. Write down which results block the release before any attack runs, because a threshold that you choose after you see the numbers can bend to fit them. A failed attack shows only that this attack failed, so the assessment also reports how strong its attacks were.
The three scripts below produce every result on this page. The first two run in seconds on public data. The third comes from Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA and takes a few minutes on an idle CPU.

title: 18  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
text:
uv run python code/part02-attacks/practitioner_lira.py
uv run python code/part02-attacks/practitioner_table_risk.py
uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/practitioner_lora.py

title: 18  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
section: 18.2 Fix the threat model and the thresholds first
text:
18.2 Fix the threat model and the thresholds first
Fill in the worksheet of Threat models and privacy games once per artefact, because each release can expose the same data differently. By default the privacy unit is the person, and the adversary sees scores, the confidences a model returns, because many services return them.
Then write the blocking rules of Table 18.1 into the plan. The membership rule uses two rates. The true positive rate (TPR) is the share of members an attack flags, and the false positive rate (FPR) is the share of non-members it wrongly flags. At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), it blocks when the lower end of the TPR’s 95% confidence interval exceeds ten times the FPR. The rule reads the lower end, so a lucky run cannot trigger it. The factor of ten is a policy choice: an attack may beat chance, but not tenfold.
Several remedies use differential privacy (DP), Part 3’s guarantee that caps what any attack learns about one person by a privacy level \(\varepsilon\). One is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with each record’s gradient clipped and noise added, called DP-SGD.

In the last row, an audit with independent trials certifies a lower bound on a DP model’s \(\varepsilon\). A bound above the claim proves a bug (Auditing private training).

title: 18  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
text:
18.3 Classifier: the free check
Start with the check that costs nothing: compare the model’s accuracy on its training data and on held-out data. The classifier is a logistic regression on scikit-learn’s 1,797 images of handwritten digits, from Membership inference. There, the mean gap over 64 models is 0.0422. So even the rule “member if correctly classified” beats chance by 0.0422, which is a lower bound on the leak.
Do not clear a model on this check, because the gap is an average over records and does not say who is exposed. For example, the loss attack flags every record with a low loss. At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) its TPR is only 0.0009, so it flags no more members than non-members. A weak attack’s failure proves little. A large gap says regularize first, and a small one says only that you need the next step.

title: 18  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
text:
18.4 Classifier: LiRA with shadow models
The release decision rests on the likelihood ratio attack (LiRA) of Membership inference. It compares the target’s output on each record with the outputs of shadow models, copies trained like the target with and without that record. Fix its strength before the run, because a weaker attack can pass a model that a stronger one blocks. The defaults come from Running LiRA on your model. Use online LiRA, the strongest version, with 64 shadows when training is cheap. If you can afford only 16 or fewer, fit one variance for all records. Put each record in each model by a fair coin, and let each model take one turn as the target.
With these defaults, the digits give 57,704 member and 57,304 non-member pairs of a model and an image. Reading the result counts the attack’s hits on them. Online LiRA reaches a TPR of 0.0318 at an FPR of 0.00099. The lower end of its 95% interval is 0.0303, which is above 0.01, so the classifier fails Table 18.1. Offline LiRA would have passed it, and so would the shadow-model attack of the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox. So base the decision on the strongest attack you can afford.
Report the interval on the FPR as well. At \(10^{-3}\), the non-member pairs allow only about 57 false positives, so the FPR’s interval runs from 0.00075 to 0.00129. The script also sets thresholds and measures on the same pairs, which flatters the attack slightly. Inspect the ten records the script prints as most exposed, because such records are usually rare or mislabelled.

title: 18  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
section: 18.5 Fine-tuned language model: canaries and extraction
text:
18.5 Fine-tuned language model: canaries and extraction
A language model can repeat a secret word for word, and a membership test does not measure that. So the assessment plants canaries, random secrets of a fixed format, and checks how well the trained model knows them. Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA runs this audit, with the scoring of Memorization and training-data extraction. It adapts Pythia-14m to 1,024 sequences of Tiny Shakespeare, once without privacy and once with DP at \(\varepsilon = 8\) per sequence. Canaries with 1 to 64 copies and uninserted controls get two scores each. Exposure, in bits, ranks the secret by the sum of its tokens’ log-probabilities, not their mean. Extraction checks whether greedy decoding, with the partner’s settings, writes the secret out.
Read the exposure rule on the extrapolated column, not the measured one. The rank among 2,000 random candidates caps the measured exposure at 10.97 bits, while the whole space of secrets allows 16.61. So the measured column can never come within 3 bits of the maximum. First check the controls: a random rank is worth \(\log_2 e = 1.44\) bits on average, and the controls’ 1.4 bits match it, so the measurement is sound.
The non-private model fails Table 18.1. Its one-copy canaries stay far below the line, at 2.0 bits. But greedy decoding writes out all three 64-copy secrets, so the model must not be shared. The DP run extracts nothing. But its most repeated canaries still average about 4 bits, against 2.2 for its controls. The reason is that \(\varepsilon\) protects one sequence, and a repeated secret is many sequences. So deduplicate before training, whatever else you do.

title: 18  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
text:
18.6 Table: re-identification on quasi-identifiers
Quasi-identifiers are the columns an adversary can find elsewhere, such as age, sex and country in a register. Records that agree on all of them form an equivalence class, and a record alone in its class can be linked to a name. The table is Adult, a census extract of 48,842 records, and the agreed quasi-identifiers are six columns, from age to education.
Linkage and re-identification runs the uniqueness check. On the agreed six columns, 14.64% of the records are unique, so the table fails. Hours per week, a column that looks harmless, raises that to 36.55%. So list every column an adversary might hold, and when in doubt, test with the column added.
Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks then generalizes age, country and education and checks again. Generalization cuts the unique share to 0.94%, but the smallest class still has one record, so the table still fails. Suppression of the classes smaller than 5 removes 3.31% of the records. That fix works only for these columns, because raw hours per week makes 10.09% unique again. Also, 1.20% of the records sit in a class with a single occupation, a distinct \(\ell\) of 1 (Syntactic anonymity). Such a class reveals the occupation without a unique match.
These shares count uniqueness in the sample, which fits the prosecutor model, where the adversary knows the target is in the table. Otherwise, estimate population uniqueness (Linkage and re-identification). Also, a table that passes after suppression can still be intersected with a second release of the same people (Syntactic anonymity). So when a table cannot pass and stay useful, release statistics with DP, as Release statistics with a library does. Plain aggregates are no fallback, because many accurate counts let an attacker rebuild records (Reconstruction attacks).

title: 18  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
text:
18.7 Write the decision
The last step compares each result with its threshold and writes a release memo, Table 18.2. A reviewer who did not run the attacks must be able to check it, so it gives each estimated rate with its interval.

For a DP model the memo carries that guarantee and its evidence, which Release and governance puts into the release package.

title: Differential privacy foundations
text:
Part 2 showed that anonymization and access control do not stop a release from leaking. This part introduces differential privacy (DP), a property of the release process, not of a dataset. If the data of one person changes, the probability of each output changes by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), plus a small slack \(\delta\). Here \(\varepsilon\) is the privacy level. This one condition limits every attack of Part 2. So a DP claim must state \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\) and the unit of privacy, such as a record or a user.



Table 1: Notation used throughout Part 3.









Symbol
Meaning




\(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\)
Privacy level and slack


\(\Delta_1f\), \(\Delta_2f\)
Sensitivity, the most one record moves the answer


\(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\), \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\)
Laplace noise of scale \(b\), normal noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\)






The part teaches one workflow in three steps. First, fix the unit of privacy and the neighbouring relation (the definition of differential privacy). Then bound each person’s contribution and calibrate a mechanism to it (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). Last, account for every release, because only post-processing is free (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). Release statistics with a library does all three steps with OpenDP on the invoices of a real shop.
The full chapters between them cover common tasks. Selection picks the best of many options or a private median, and Query release publishes many counts at once. Use Trust models when nobody can hold the raw data, and Private mean estimation to find how many records a private mean needs. Of the four reference pages, Advanced composition and Beyond global sensitivity help when the simple rules are too loose. Read Discrete mechanisms before you sample noise yourself, and Lower bounds before you promise an accuracy.
Part 4 then replaces hand composition with accountants, and Part 5 uses all of it to train models. At the end of the part, you can release a count, a sum, a median or a table with error bars and a guarantee.

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
text:
19.1 Why this matters
Every attack in Threat models and attacks runs an algorithm on one of two datasets that differ in one person, and guesses from the output which dataset it saw. Differential privacy (DP) makes the two outputs look alike against every test, including tests that nobody has invented yet. It is a property of the algorithm, not of the data, so you can check it before anyone touches the data.
crumbs: 19  The definition of differential privacy

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
text:
19.2 Neighbouring datasets
The first question about a claim is what “differ in one record” means, and the neighbouring relation answers it. Under add/remove, two datasets are neighbours when one has a record that the other lacks, so the guarantee hides whether a person is in the data at all. Under replace, they have the same size and differ in the value of one record, so the guarantee hides only what the record says. A replacement is a removal and then an addition, and each step costs the privacy level \(\varepsilon\) of Section 19.3, so \[\varepsilon\text{-DP under add/remove} \implies 2\varepsilon\text{-DP under replace}. \tag{19.1}\] The reverse fails, because replace never compares datasets of different sizes.
You also choose the unit of privacy, what one record is. At the example level, it is one training record or one event, and at the user level, all the data of one person. A user who wrote 200 messages is then a group of 200 records under example-level DP, with protection only at \(200\varepsilon\) (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). So check that the claim protects the person. The guarantee must also hide every record that the data format allows, even a person aged 900, who could move an average a long way. So private algorithms clip each input to a fixed range before they add noise.
crumbs: 19  The definition of differential privacy

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
text:
19.3 The definition
A mechanism \(M\) is a randomized algorithm that takes a dataset and returns an output. Write \(D\) for a dataset and \(D'\) for one of its neighbours. The definition asks that no set of outputs becomes more than a factor \(e^\varepsilon\) more likely when one record changes, up to a small additive slack \(\delta\). Here \(\varepsilon\) is not negative. A mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differentially private if every pair of neighbours and every set \(S\) of outputs satisfy \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\,\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta. \tag{19.2}\] The probabilities come only from the randomness of the mechanism, and the data stay fixed.
When \(\delta = 0\), the guarantee is pure DP, and otherwise it is approximate DP. In both cases, a private mechanism must be random. A deterministic one that answers differently on two neighbours gives that answer probability 1 on one and 0 on the other, which no factor \(e^\varepsilon\) covers. So rounding, aggregation or the removal of small cells gives no guarantee by itself.
crumbs: 19  The definition of differential privacy

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
text:
19.4 The privacy loss and δ
For an output \(y\), write \(p_{M(D)}(y)\) for its probability, or its density, when the mechanism runs on \(D\). The privacy loss of \(y\) is the logarithm of how much more likely the output is on \(D\) than on \(D'\), \[L(y) = \ln\frac{p_{M(D)}(y)}{p_{M(D')}(y)}. \tag{19.3}\] Independent outputs multiply their likelihood ratios, so their losses add, and that is why the accountants of Part 4 work with the loss. Pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP holds exactly when every output has a loss between \(-\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon\). Laplace noise meets that condition, but the loss of Gaussian noise has no limit in the far tail (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms).
Under approximate DP, \(\delta\) pays for the outputs whose loss is more than \(\varepsilon\). It counts only the part of each one’s probability on \(D\) above \(e^\varepsilon\) times its probability on \(D'\). So \(\delta\) is not the chance that the loss is more than \(\varepsilon\), and the total is the hockey-stick divergence (Divergences). Each \(\varepsilon\) has its own smallest \(\delta\), and the function \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the privacy curve of the mechanism. The noise parameters fix the whole curve, so report them with the pair, and others can recompute it (Numerical accounting).
crumbs: 19  The definition of differential privacy

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
text:
19.5 Randomized response
In randomized response, a survey design, each person tells the truth with some probability \(t\) and lies otherwise, so a single answer proves nothing. A person who tosses a coin, answers truthfully on heads and answers by a second toss on tails tells the truth with probability \(\frac34\). So the true answer is three times as likely as the false one, which gives pure DP at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\). In general, randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\) tells the truth with probability \[t = \frac{e^\varepsilon}{1 + e^\varepsilon}. \tag{19.4}\]
With independent coins, the guarantee is \(\varepsilon\) per person for any number of people. But it holds only under replace, because under add/remove the number of reports shows who answered. Write \(\bar y\) for the share of “yes” reports among the \(n\) people. A correction with \(t\) for the lies gives the estimate of the true fraction \(\pi\) and its standard deviation, \[\hat\pi = \frac{\bar y - (1 - t)}{2t - 1}, \qquad \operatorname{sd}(\hat\pi) = \frac{e^{\varepsilon/2}}{(e^\varepsilon - 1)\sqrt n}. \tag{19.5}\] For 1,000 people, the two-coin scheme has a standard deviation of 0.0274. When the true fraction is 0.3, that is about twice the sampling error of 0.0145 that the survey already has. This doubling is the price of the local model, in which nobody sees a true answer (Local, shuffle and distributed trust models).
OpenDP builds the mechanism from its truth probability, 0.75 for the two coins, and map turns one changed answer into its \(\varepsilon\), \(\ln 3\). The contrib feature turns on mechanisms that are not yet formally vetted.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
rr = dp.m.make_randomized_response_bool(prob=0.75)
print(f"{rr.map(1):.4f}")  # 1.0986
crumbs: 19  The definition of differential privacy

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
section: 19.6 What ε means for an attacker
text:
19.6 What ε means for an attacker
A membership attacker looks at the output and decides whether to accuse the target of being in the data (Hypothesis testing). Its false positive rate (FPR) is how often it accuses a target who is out. Its true positive rate (TPR) is how often it accuses one who is in. The outputs on which it accuses form a set, which the definition bounds, so under add/remove every attack satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta. \tag{19.6}\]
Use this form, because Part 2 judged attacks by their TPR at a low FPR. Take \(\varepsilon = 1\) and the \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) that Section 19.7 gives for 10,000 people. At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), no attack gets a TPR above \(e \cdot 10^{-3} + 10^{-5} = 0.002728\). As the FPR goes to 0, so does the first term, and the guarantee then depends almost entirely on \(\delta\).
Read backwards, the cap turns a measured attack into a lower bound on \(\varepsilon\), \[\varepsilon \ge \ln\frac{\mathrm{TPR} - \delta}{\mathrm{FPR}}. \tag{19.7}\] Suppose that a model is claimed to be \((2, 10^{-5})\)-DP, and an attack gets a TPR of 0.05 at an FPR of 0.001. If those rates were exact, \(\varepsilon\) would be at least about \(\ln 50 = 3.91\), so the claim would be false. A real audit puts confidence bounds on the rates and plants a canary, a record that is as easy to detect as possible (Auditing).
Two summaries are easier to explain to a lawyer. The first, the membership advantage, is the TPR minus the FPR, how much better than a coin flip an attacker does. Under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, it is at most \[\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} \le \frac{e^\varepsilon - 1 + 2\delta}{e^\varepsilon + 1}. \tag{19.8}\]
The second, the posterior bound, is about beliefs. Under pure DP, one output can multiply the odds of an adversary between two neighbours by at most \(e^\varepsilon\). So a prior belief \(p\) that the data are \(D\) can rise at most to \[\Pr[D \mid y] \le \frac{e^\varepsilon p}{e^\varepsilon p + 1 - p}. \tag{19.9}\] Table 19.1 turns a claimed \(\varepsilon\) into both numbers.



Table 19.1: What a pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP guarantee promises against the strongest attacker.
