So an \(\varepsilon\) of at most 1 is strong for any mechanism, because a 1% prior rises to less than 3%. Between 1 and 10, a claim needs the privacy curve of the mechanism as its justification. Above 10, where the bounds promise almost nothing, it needs an audit as well (Choosing ε). For statistics, start from the error that you can accept and solve for \(\varepsilon\) (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). The table is for pure DP, so for an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) claim, quote the advantage bound and the cap on the TPR, which both include \(\delta\).
crumbs: 19  The definition of differential privacy

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
text:
19.7 How small δ must be
A small \(\delta\) almost does not change the advantage bound. But the advantage is an average, so it can hide total harm to a few people. Take a mechanism that publishes each record in full, independently with probability \(\delta\). It is \((0, \delta)\)-DP under add/remove, because a record changes the output only when its own coin publishes it. But over \(n\) records, it publishes at least one with probability \[1 - (1 - \delta)^n \approx 1 - e^{-n\delta}. \tag{19.10}\] With 10,000 records and \(\delta = 1/n\), that is \(1 - e^{-1} = 0.6321\).
So treat \(\delta\) as a budget per person for catastrophe, such as these total failures. The default of this book follows Ponomareva et al. (2023) and keeps \(n\delta\), the expected number of people exposed this way, well below 1. Let \(n\) count people, not records, and choose \[\delta \le \frac{1}{n^{1.1}}, \tag{19.11}\] rounded down to a power of ten. For 10,000 people, the rule gives \(10^{-5}\). The publishing mechanism then has \(n\delta = 0.1\), and it exposes someone with probability only 0.0952.
crumbs: 19  The definition of differential privacy

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
section: 19.8 What differential privacy does not protect
text:
19.8 What differential privacy does not protect
DP compares a world with your record and a world without it, so the guarantee does not cover what someone can learn in both worlds. A study that never used Alice’s record may show that smokers get cancer at a high rate. That changes what anyone believes about Alice, a smoker, yet the study is 0-DP with respect to her. So a harm is a DP violation only if the inference would be materially different without her record. Correlated records are a second gap, because a household of five that always answers alike is a group of five, unless the household is the unit of privacy. The third gap is the implementation (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms).
crumbs: 19  The definition of differential privacy

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
text:
19.9 Writing the guarantee down
A reviewer can check only what a claim writes down. So a guarantee names the unit of privacy with its neighbouring relation, and \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\) for the whole release, not per query. It also names the mechanism, the library version, the trust model and the data treated as public, which the guarantee does not protect. This example uses the central model, in which a trusted curator holds the raw data and adds the noise:

This release satisfies \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP for adding or removing one customer and all their invoice lines, at most 100 per customer, under the central model, with Gaussian noise from OpenDP 0.16.0. The market list was fixed in advance.

Release statistics with a library and Release and governance print such statements from the code that made the release.

title: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
20.1 Why this matters
A private mechanism is never the whole system. Its output is rounded or goes into a model, a person often owns many records, and an analyst seldom asks only one question. Three properties of differential privacy (DP) cover these cases, which are post-processing, group privacy and composition. With them you prove each building block once and keep a ledger of what you spend.
crumbs: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
20.2 Post-processing
Take a mechanism \(M\) that is DP with privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and slack \(\delta\). Apply to its output a function \(f\) that never reads the data, although it can use random numbers of its own. Then the processed release is just as private, \[f(M(D)) \text{ is } (\varepsilon, \delta)\text{-DP}. \tag{20.1}\]
So it costs nothing to round a noisy count, to clamp it at zero, or to make noisy subtotals agree with their noisy total. So a private system adds noise at one narrow point, such as counts or gradients, and treats everything after it as public. The rule also covers attackers, because a membership-inference attack is a function of the output. So the definition’s limit on the success of an attack holds even for attacks invented after the release.
The condition is that \(f\) never reads the data. “Take the noisy top category, then report its exact count” breaks it, because the second step is a new and non-private mechanism.
crumbs: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
20.3 Group privacy
The definition protects one record, but a customer of an online shop has dozens of invoice lines. For a person with \(k\) records, the guarantee must cover datasets that differ in \(k\) records. You can go from one such dataset to the other in \(k\) steps that each change one record and each cost \(\varepsilon\). So under pure DP, where \(\delta = 0\), \(\varepsilon\)-DP per record becomes \(k\varepsilon\)-DP for the group. But the slack grows much faster than \(k\). For a group of \(k\) records, an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism is \[\Big(k\varepsilon,\ \delta_k\Big)\text{-DP}, \qquad \delta_k = \delta\,\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1} \le k\,e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\delta. \tag{20.2}\]
The form on the right is simpler but looser. With \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) per record, a person with 10 records gets a slack of \(2.272\times10^{-3}\). That slack is too large, because the book chooses \(\delta\) far below one over the number of people (How small δ must be).
OpenDP calculates group guarantees from the mechanism itself. A measurement’s map(d_in=k) gives its guarantee when neighbouring datasets differ in \(k\) records, here for a Laplace count and a Gaussian count.
count = dp.t.make_count(dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int)), dp.symmetric_distance())
laplace = count >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=2.0)  # epsilon = 0.5 per record
print(f"Laplace count: epsilon {laplace.map(d_in=1):.1f} per record, {laplace.map(d_in=10):.1f} for 10")

def gaussian(scale: float) -> dp.Measurement:  # a Gaussian count, as a privacy curve
    return dp.c.make_zCDP_to_approxDP(count >> dp.m.then_gaussian(scale=scale))

def at_1e5(scale: float) -> dp.Measurement:
    return dp.c.make_fix_delta(gaussian(scale), delta=1e-5)

scale = dp.binary_search_param(at_1e5, d_in=1, d_out=(0.5, 1e-5))  # (0.5, 1e-5) per record
curve = gaussian(scale).map(d_in=10)  # the privacy curve for a group of 10 records
print(f"Gaussian count, group of 10: epsilon {curve.epsilon(1e-5):.2f} at delta 1e-5")
# delta_k is the slack that the group-privacy formula gives the group
print(f"Gaussian count, group of 10: epsilon {curve.epsilon(delta_k):.2f} at delta {delta_k:.3e}")
Laplace count: epsilon 0.5 per record, 5.0 for 10
Gaussian count, group of 10: epsilon 6.43 at delta 1e-5
Gaussian count, group of 10: epsilon 4.57 at delta 2.272e-03
For the Laplace count, map(d_in=10) gives \(k\varepsilon = 5.0\), the same as the formula. The Gaussian count, set to \((0.5, 10^{-5})\) per record, does better, because OpenDP gets the group’s guarantee from the whole privacy curve of the mechanism. At the formula’s slack of \(2.272\times10^{-3}\), the group gets \(\varepsilon = 4.57\), less than the formula’s 5.0. So take a group guarantee from the library’s map, and use the formula only for a mechanism that the library cannot map.
Better still, make the person the unit of privacy. Then neighbouring datasets differ in all of one person’s records. Bound the number of records that each person can contribute before you add noise, as Release statistics with a library does on real data. Use group privacy when you cannot do this, and for records of different people that reveal each other, such as a household with one address and one income.
crumbs: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
20.4 Sequential composition
An analyst asks several queries of the same data, each with fresh noise, and an adversary sees all the answers together. For \(k\) mechanisms, write \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\) for the budget of the \(i\)-th. Then the release of all their outputs is \[\Big(\sum_{i=1}^k\varepsilon_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\delta_i\Big)\text{-DP}. \tag{20.3}\] This is basic composition. It needs every mechanism to draw fresh noise and to use the same neighbouring relation, add/remove or replace.
The rule also covers adaptive composition, where the analyst chooses each query from the earlier answers, but only if each budget is fixed in advance. A budget chosen from the answers, as in “continue until the estimate looks good”, needs a privacy filter. That is a rule that decides when to stop (Adaptive composition).
For many releases, basic composition gives too much. Ten Gaussian counts at \((0.5, 10^{-5})\) each cost \((5, 10^{-4})\) by basic composition, but at that slack their exact \(\varepsilon\) is only 1.504. So for more than a few releases, use an accountant. It calculates the total from the mechanisms themselves (Advanced and optimal composition, Part 4).
crumbs: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
20.5 Parallel composition
Statistics per region use disjoint subsets of the data. When each person has one record, that record is in one region only. So each region can spend the full budget. To use this, fix in advance a public rule that puts every possible record in exactly one part. Then run a mechanism \(M_i\) with independent noise on the \(i\)-th part. If each \(M_i\) is \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\)-DP under add/remove, the whole release is \[\big(\max_i\varepsilon_i,\ \max_i\delta_i\big)\text{-DP under add/remove}. \tag{20.4}\]
So a histogram with Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) on every bin is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any number of bins. Under replace, a record can move from one bin to another, so two bins change and the cost doubles to \(2\varepsilon\). A person with records in several bins also breaks the rule. Then charge each bin as a separate query, or first bound the number of bins that a person can touch.
The condition that is easiest to break is the rule fixed in advance. A split into “the top 10% of earners and the rest” moves its boundary when one high earner is added, so both parts change. A split on the keys that appear in the data also fails, because a key that only one person’s record contains reveals that person. So use fixed bins or a public list of keys. When the keys are not public, release only the keys whose noisy count is above a threshold, a step called partition selection (Release statistics with a library).
crumbs: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
20.6 Keeping a budget
Fix a total budget for a dataset before the first release, and charge every release against it. In the Python library diffprivlib, a BudgetAccountant holds the total, and each function that you give it charges its own \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\). A call that would go above the total raises a BudgetError and gives no answer. The script practitioner_adult_statistics.py uses it on the Adult census data, 48,842 people with one row each. For these people, the default slack is \(10^{-6}\). It spends the budget on two queries and then asks for one more count.
age = adult["age"].to_numpy()
acc = BudgetAccountant(epsilon=1.0, delta=1e-6)  # the total, fixed in advance
mean_age = tools.mean(age, epsilon=0.5, bounds=(17, 90), accountant=acc, random_state=seed)
over_50 = tools.count_nonzero(age > 50, epsilon=0.5, accountant=acc, random_state=seed)
print(f"private mean age: {mean_age:.2f}  private count over 50: {over_50:,}")
print(f"spent: {acc.total()}")
try:
    tools.count_nonzero(age > 60, epsilon=0.1, accountant=acc, random_state=seed)
except BudgetError as err:
    print(f"refused: {err}")
Run it with uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/practitioner_adult_statistics.py. With random_state=0 it prints the following.
private mean age: 38.64  private count over 50: 9,813
spent: (epsilon=1.0, delta=0.0)
refused: Privacy spend of (0.1,0) not permissible; will exceed remaining privacy budget. Use BudgetAccountant.remaining() to check remaining budget.
The true values are 38.64 and 9,808. The two calls add Laplace noise, so they spend no \(\delta\), and the \(10^{-6}\) stays available for a Gaussian query. The ledger has two limits. First, it applies basic composition to every call, so it charges too much for calls on disjoint parts of the data. Second, it trusts the guarantee of each call, and diffprivlib’s mean divides by the exact number of rows as if that number were public. The number is public only when neighbours have the same size, so this ledger holds only under replace neighbours.
Most real failures break a condition of the three properties, and then the guarantee is usually lost completely (Table 20.1).

Shared noise is the clearest case of a broken condition. Suppose that you release the number of smokers and the number of smokers aged 40 or more, with the same Laplace draw of scale 1 on each. Each release alone is 1-DP, but their difference cancels the noise and gives the exact number of smokers under 40. So the pair is not DP at all. In code, the bug hides in a shared random seed, a cached noise value or noise that several shards use. A fixed seed such as random_state=0 above makes a book’s numbers repeatable, but in production it makes the noise known and so removable. The same noisy answer to a repeated identical query is safe, because it is post-processing of one release.

title: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
21.1 Why this matters
Suppose that a hospital wants to publish, with a differential privacy (DP) guarantee, how many of its patients have diabetes. Almost every such release, and every noisy gradient of private training, uses one of the two mechanisms of this chapter. Both calculate the exact answer of a query \(f\) on the dataset \(D\), add fresh random noise, written \(Z\), and publish \[M(D) = f(D) + Z. \tag{21.1}\] Three decisions fix such a mechanism. The noise must hide the sensitivity, which is how far one record can move the answer. The noise distribution sets the kind of guarantee, because Laplace noise gives pure DP and Gaussian noise needs a small slack \(\delta\). And a calibration formula sets the amount of noise for a target \(\varepsilon\), through the privacy loss of the definition of differential privacy.
crumbs: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
21.2 Sensitivity
The noise must cover the largest change that one record can make to the answer. A query often gives a vector of \(d\) numbers, such as the bins of a histogram, so the change needs a size. Laplace noise uses the \(\ell_1\) norm, the sum of the absolute changes. Gaussian noise uses the \(\ell_2\) norm, the square root of the sum of the squared changes. For a pair of neighbours \(D \sim D'\), the \(\ell_p\) sensitivity of the query is the largest change between their answers, \[\Delta_pf = \max_{D \sim D'}\big\|f(D) - f(D')\big\|_p, \qquad p \in \{1, 2\}. \tag{21.2}\] The two are equal when one record moves a single coordinate. When it moves all \(d\) of them, \(\Delta_1f\) can be \(\sqrt d\) times \(\Delta_2f\).
The sensitivity also depends on the neighbouring relation. Under add/remove, one dataset has one record more than the other. Under replace, one record changes into another, so the size \(n\) is public. With \(B\) for the largest value of a record after clipping, Table 21.1 gives the standard queries.

A replaced record leaves one histogram bin and goes into another, so it changes two bins. The threshold counts, the numbers of records at or above each of \(d\) values, are a dense query, in which one record can move every coordinate.
Calculate the sensitivity from the domain, before you look at the data. If you take it from the data, for example as the largest value, the noise leaks that value (Beyond global sensitivity). Unbounded data have infinite sensitivity, so first clip every value to a fixed range. With ages clipped to at most 100, the mean age of 1,000 patients has sensitivity \(B/n = 0.1\) under replace.
crumbs: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
21.3 The Laplace mechanism
The Laplace mechanism adds independent noise from the Laplace distribution, a two-sided exponential with its peak at 0, to each coordinate. We write \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) for this noise with scale \(b\), which sets its typical size. For an \(\varepsilon\)-DP guarantee, the scale is the sensitivity divided by \(\varepsilon\), \[b = \frac{\Delta_1f}{\varepsilon}. \tag{21.3}\]
The error of the mechanism is the noise itself. Each coordinate of the noise is \(b\) from zero on average, and goes past a distance \(t\) with probability \(e^{-t/b}\). Give all \(d\) coordinates together a small failure probability \(\beta\), so that each coordinate gets a share \(\beta/d\). Then the width that holds for all of them is \[\Pr\Big[\max_i|Z_i| > b\ln\frac d\beta\Big] \le \beta. \tag{21.4}\] Publish this width with the release. In reverse, the width gives an error budget, because for a single number you can fix a target width \(t\) and solve for the privacy level, \[\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta_1f\,\ln(1/\beta)}{t}. \tag{21.5}\] So a count that must be within 10 of the truth with probability 0.95 needs \(\varepsilon = \ln(20)/10 = 0.2996\). For \(d\) numbers, solve each with the failure probability \(\beta/d\), and add their values of \(\varepsilon\) by composition.
At the hospital, 1,234 of the 10,000 patients have diabetes. A count has sensitivity 1 under add/remove, so at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) the noise is \(\mathrm{Lap}(10)\). Its 95% error bar is \(10\ln 20 = 29.96\), or 2.43% of the count.
The scale does not depend on the size of the data, so the relative error of a count of size \(n\) is about \(1/(n\varepsilon)\). But the sensitivity must include every number that one record can move. If one record can change all of 10 released counts, noise for one count makes the release \(10\varepsilon\)-DP, not \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
crumbs: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
21.4 The Gaussian mechanism
The Gaussian mechanism adds independent normal noise with mean 0 and standard deviation \(\sigma\) to each coordinate. Its privacy loss has no upper limit in the far tail, so it always needs a \(\delta\). But its noise follows the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, which can be much smaller than the \(\ell_1\) one. Only the ratio of the sensitivity to the noise is important, so write \(\mu = \Delta_2f/\sigma\) for the number of noise standard deviations between the answers on two neighbours. Write \(\Phi\) for the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the standard normal distribution. Then the mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when \(\delta\) is at least \[\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big). \tag{21.6}\]
You calibrate with this formula. As \(\mu\) increases, the exact \(\delta\) increases from 0 to 1, so exactly one value \(\mu^*\) gives your target. The smallest noise that works is then \[\sigma^* = \frac{\Delta_2f}{\mu^*}, \qquad \text{where } \delta_{\mu^*}(\varepsilon) = \delta, \tag{21.7}\] and libraries solve for \(\mu^*\) (Section 21.7). For 10,000 patients, the book’s default slack is \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\), this analytic calibration then gives \(\sigma^* = 3.7306\,\Delta_2f\).
Many papers and libraries still use the classic calibration of Dwork and Roth (2014), which has a proof only for \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\) between 0 and 1, \[\sigma = \frac{\Delta_2f\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}. \tag{21.8}\] At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), it gives \(4.8448\,\Delta_2f\), 30% more noise than the analytic \(3.7306\,\Delta_2f\). Above \(\varepsilon = 8.42\), it gives too little noise for the guarantee it claims. So use the analytic calibration.
A Gaussian mechanism has a whole curve of guarantees, one \(\delta\) for each \(\varepsilon\), and the accountants of Part 4 compose whole curves. So report \(\sigma/\Delta_2f\) with every Gaussian release, together with the pair that you chose.
At the hospital, Gaussian noise for the diabetes count at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) gives a 95% error bar of 60.27, which is 1.96 standard deviations. Laplace noise gave 29.96 with no \(\delta\), so for a single count Laplace noise is better in error and in guarantee.
crumbs: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
21.5 Laplace or Gaussian?
The choice depends on how one record spreads its change across the coordinates. To see why, compare the root-mean-square error (RMSE) of each released number at the same \(\varepsilon\). Laplace noise of scale \(b = \Delta_1f/\varepsilon\) has standard deviation \(\sqrt2\,b\). With \(\sigma_1\) for the analytic Gaussian noise level at unit \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, the errors per coordinate are \[\text{Laplace: } \frac{\sqrt2\,\Delta_1f}{\varepsilon}, \qquad \text{Gaussian: } \Delta_2f\,\sigma_1. \tag{21.9}\]
In a sparse query, such as a histogram under add/remove, one record moves one coordinate, so the two sensitivities are equal. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and the default \(\delta\), \(\sigma_1 = 3.7306\). So Laplace noise is better at every \(d\), because \(\sqrt2 = 1.4142\) is smaller. In a dense query, such as the threshold counts, one record moves every coordinate. Then the Laplace error grows like \(d\) and the Gaussian error only like \(\sqrt d\). So Laplace noise is more accurate only while \[d < \frac{(\varepsilon\sigma_1)^2}2, \tag{21.10}\] so with \(\sigma_1 = 3.7306\), Gaussian noise is better for 7 or more threshold counts.
Gaussian noise is also better for many releases, because several Gaussian releases compose exactly into one Gaussian mechanism. Private training has dense queries and many releases, because one record’s gradient moves every coordinate of a model at every step. So it clips the \(\ell_2\) norm of each gradient and calibrates Gaussian noise to that clip.
crumbs: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
21.6 Calibrating a release
Every noisy release has five steps.

Fix the neighbouring relation and the unit of privacy, usually one person under add/remove.
Clip every value to a range fixed in advance. Then take the sensitivity from Table 21.1, or calculate it from the worst record.
Use Laplace noise for one number or a sparse vector, and Gaussian noise for a dense vector.
Set the scale with Equation 21.3 or Equation 21.6. Charge it to your budget (Post-processing, group privacy and composition).
Draw the noise with a library that experts have checked. Publish the error bar and the noise parameters with the result.

A mean under add/remove has no simple sensitivity, because its denominator also moves. So release a noisy sum and a noisy count, each with half of the budget. Then divide the sum by the count, which is post-processing and costs nothing. For the error bar of the mean, take the bar of each at 97.5%, so that both hold together 95% of the time. Then the mean is above the sum’s lower end divided by the count’s upper end. It is below the sum’s upper end divided by the count’s lower end, if both lower ends are positive.
OpenDP’s .dp.mean makes the same split, and summarize(alpha=0.025) gives the two bars at 97.5%. When you do not know the range for the clip, Private mean estimation finds it privately. Use plain numpy.random.laplace only for prototypes, because textbook floating-point samplers can leak through the low-order bits of their output (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms). For a whole release with clipping, grouping and one budget, follow Release statistics with a library.
crumbs: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
21.7 Code
The snippet checks the hospital’s numbers and the analytic \(\sigma^*\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\). In OpenDP, a mechanism’s map takes the sensitivity and gives the \(\varepsilon\) that it costs, and the accuracy helpers change a scale into a 95% error bar or back. For a count, with sensitivity 1, one over that scale is the \(\varepsilon\) of the error budget. IBM’s diffprivlib calibrates the analytic Gaussian.
import math

import opendp.prelude as dp
from diffprivlib.mechanisms import GaussianAnalytic

dp.enable_features("contrib")
laplace = dp.m.make_laplace(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False), dp.absolute_distance(T=float), scale=10.0)
print(laplace.map(1.0))  # 0.1
print(f"{dp.laplacian_scale_to_accuracy(10.0, alpha=0.05):.2f}")  # 29.96
print(f"{1 / dp.accuracy_to_laplacian_scale(10.0, alpha=0.05):.4f}")  # 0.2996
gauss = GaussianAnalytic(epsilon=1.0, delta=1e-5, sensitivity=1.0)
print(f"{math.sqrt(gauss.variance(0.0)):.4f}")  # 3.7306
To add the noise, call the mechanism on the value, as in laplace(1234.0).

title: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
21.8 Cheat sheet

Rules of thumb

Calibrate Laplace noise to \(\Delta_1f\) and Gaussian noise to \(\Delta_2f\), never the other way round.
When \(n\) is not public, never use \(B/n\) as the sensitivity of a mean.
crumbs: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
21.9 References

Dwork & Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy (2014), §3.3 and Appendix A: the Laplace mechanism and the classic Gaussian calibration.
Balle & Wang, “Improving the Gaussian Mechanism for Differential Privacy” (ICML 2018): the exact privacy curve and the bisection calibration.

Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.
crumbs: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 22  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
22.1 What it is
A dashboard refreshes a hundred counts, and a training run takes thousands of noisy steps, but you report one differential privacy (DP) guarantee for the whole run. Each step has its own privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and slack \(\delta\) (The definition of differential privacy). Basic composition adds them, so a run of \(k\) steps costs \(k\varepsilon\) and \(k\delta\) (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). That total is correct but too large, because each step’s privacy loss depends on the noise and is often negative. So the sum almost never reaches \(k\varepsilon\).
Advanced composition (Dwork, Rothblum & Vadhan 2010) uses these cancellations. With an extra slack \(\delta'\) that you pick for the whole run, the steps are together \((\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}, k\delta + \delta')\)-DP, with \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}} = \varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2). \tag{22.1}\] The first term is the spread of the total loss, which grows only like \(\sqrt k\). The second term, the drift, is its average.
Optimal composition (Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath 2015) gives the smallest total that is correct when you know each step only by its pair \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). For a hundred counts on 10,000 people, each at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) with no slack, basic composition gives a total of 10. Advanced and optimal composition spend a slack \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\), the book’s default for 10,000 people, and give 5.30 and 4.31.

title: 22  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
22.2 When you meet it
You meet these rules in papers, privacy reviews and libraries that give one total \(\varepsilon\) for many steps (Table 22.1).



Table 22.1: Which composition rule to use, at a slack of \(10^{-5}\) (none for basic composition).










What you know about the steps
Rule
Total \(\varepsilon\) for 100 steps at 0.1




Each step’s \(\varepsilon\), and \(\delta\) must stay 0
Basic composition
10


Each step’s \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), to plan by hand
Advanced composition
5.30


Each step’s \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), for the number you report
Optimal composition
4.31


The mechanism itself, such as Gaussian noise
An accountant (Part 4), which composes whole privacy curves
Often far smaller


Budgets chosen during the run
A privacy filter, which enforces a budget fixed in advance
—






Optimal composition is optimal only for steps that you know by one pair each. A real mechanism has a whole privacy curve, with one \(\delta\) for each \(\varepsilon\), and one pair loses the rest of it. For example, a thousand Gaussian steps with noise standard deviation 20 on a query of sensitivity 1 are exactly \((7.51, 10^{-5})\)-DP as curves. With the best single pair of each step, optimal composition gives 62.7, about eight times worse. So when you know the mechanism, compose its curve with an accountant (Privacy accounting).

title: 22  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
22.3 How to use it
To divide a total budget \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}\) among \(k\) steps, use advanced composition in reverse. When \(\varepsilon\sqrt k\) is small, the drift term of Equation 22.1 is very small, so each step can have about \[\varepsilon \approx \frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}}{\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}}. \tag{22.2}\] When \(\varepsilon\sqrt k\) comes near 1, the drift is no longer small, and this shortcut gives each step too much.
To report a run, give the accountant’s number at the run’s total \(\delta\) when you know the mechanism. Otherwise, give the optimal composition. The snippet below plans the hundred counts within a total of \((1, 10^{-5})\), with all of the slack in \(\delta'\). Then it reports the thousand Gaussian steps with two accountants of Google’s dp_accounting, one on the privacy loss distribution (PLD) and one on Rényi differential privacy (RDP).
import math

import dp_accounting

print(f"{1.0 / math.sqrt(2 * 100 * math.log(1e5)):.4f}")  # 0.0208
step = dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(noise_multiplier=20.0)
run = dp_accounting.SelfComposedDpEvent(step, 1000)
pld = dp_accounting.pld.PLDAccountant()
pld.compose(run)
print(f"{pld.get_epsilon(target_delta=1e-5):.2f}")  # 7.51
rdp = dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant()
rdp.compose(run)
print(f"{rdp.get_epsilon(target_delta=1e-5):.2f}")  # 8.08
Each count gets 0.0208, twice the \(1/100\) of basic composition. The PLD accountant gives the exact 7.51, and the RDP accountant a correct but larger 8.08 (Choosing an accountant).

title: 22  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
22.4 What goes wrong
For a few steps, advanced composition can give more than basic composition, so always take the smaller of the two. Every rule also adds the slacks of the steps, so count each \(\delta\).
All these rules hold when each query depends on earlier answers, but only if you fix the budget of each step before the run. If you choose the budgets from the answers, you need a privacy filter (Adaptive composition). Early stops also need care. A stop rule that reads only the noisy answers is post-processing, so the run costs no more than its planned length. But if a run stops when the true count of a group goes above a threshold, its length shows that count. Then each answer is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, but the whole run is not DP for any finite \(\varepsilon\).
So in a review, a total below optimal composition is a red flag, unless an accountant calculated it from the curve of the mechanism.
Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
23.1 Why this matters
Many questions ask you to pick something, such as the best model on a validation set, a median, or the first alarm among many statistics. If you publish the score of every candidate with Laplace noise, you pay the budget once per candidate, because the budgets of separate releases add. The mechanisms of this chapter release the position, not the values. One record can change the winner only a little, for any number of candidates. So under differential privacy (DP), a selection costs as much as a single query, and the number of candidates changes only the accuracy, through its logarithm.
crumbs: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
23.2 Which mechanism to use
Table 23.1 gives the mechanism for each common task. In each, the sensitivity \(\Delta u\) is the most that one person’s record can change the score of a candidate.



Table 23.1: Which selection mechanism to use.










Task
Mechanism
Privacy cost




Pick the best of a fixed list
Exponential mechanism or report-noisy-max
\(\varepsilon\)


Pick the top \(c\), such as the most frequent items
Gumbel noise, keep the \(c\) largest, or noisy max \(c\) times
\(c\varepsilon\)


Pick a number from a range, such as a quantile or a clipping norm
Exponential mechanism over the range
\(\varepsilon\)


Find the first query in a stream above a threshold
AboveThreshold
\(\varepsilon\), however long the stream
crumbs: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
23.3 The exponential mechanism
The candidates form a fixed set, written \(\mathcal R\). Each candidate \(r\) has a score on the dataset \(D\), written \(u(D, r)\), such as the number of validation records that a model gets right. The exponential mechanism of McSherry and Talwar (2007) picks each candidate with a probability proportional to an exponential of its score. With a privacy budget \(\varepsilon\), it outputs candidate \(r\) with probability \[\Pr[M_E(D) = r] = \frac{\exp\big(\varepsilon\,u(D, r)/(2\Delta u)\big)}{\sum_s\exp\big(\varepsilon\,u(D, s)/(2\Delta u)\big)}. \tag{23.1}\] It is \(\varepsilon\)-DP because one record changes each weight, and also their sum, by at most a factor \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\), which makes \(e^\varepsilon\) for their ratio.
Two conditions decide whether a use is correct. First, fix the list of candidates before you look at the data. A list made from the data reveals records by itself, such as a word that only one person used. Second, remove the 2 in the exponent only when the scores are monotone, which means that one record pushes all of them the same way. Counts under add/remove neighbours are monotone. A histogram under replace neighbours is not, because a moved record lowers one count and raises another, so without the 2 the cost is double.
crumbs: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
section: 23.4 Accuracy, and the cost of many candidates
text:
23.4 Accuracy, and the cost of many candidates
The number of candidates \(|\mathcal R|\) costs no privacy but costs accuracy, because more candidates means more bad ones to pick. Call the best score minus the score of the chosen candidate the gap. On average it is at most \[\frac{2\Delta u}{\varepsilon}(\ln|\mathcal R| + 1), \tag{23.2}\] so twice the candidates add only \(\ln 2\) to the bracket.
Suppose that you trained 50 models and want to release the best one on a private validation set of 1,000 records. Model \(r\), numbered from 1, gets \(900 - r\) records right, so model 1 is the best. The score is that count, which one record moves by at most 1, so \(\Delta u = 1\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\), the mechanism picks the best model only 39% of the time. But it loses only 1.54 correct predictions on average, or 0.15% accuracy, because its mistakes are mostly near-ties. Hyperparameter tuning picks models this way.
crumbs: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
section: 23.5 A private quantile or clipping norm
text:
23.5 A private quantile or clipping norm
A median or a clipping norm read from the data leaks the data, so pick it with the exponential mechanism. Before you look at the data, fix a range. Then clip every record into it. The score of each point of the range is how close the share of records below it is to the quantile that you want. For the median, that quantile is one half. One added or removed record moves each score by at most 1. The score stays the same between consecutive sorted records, so the mechanism picks one of these intervals, called pieces, and returns a uniform point inside it. It prefers long pieces near the quantile.
diffprivlib’s tools.quantile and tools.median take an epsilon and the range as bounds. OpenDP’s .dp.quantile and .dp.median work on Polars data frames and pick one value from a finite list of candidates. The script practitioner_adult_statistics.py takes the median age of the Adult census data, 48,842 people with one row each, at \(\varepsilon = 1\). The range of 17 to 90 comes from the survey’s documentation.
age = adult["age"].to_numpy()
private = tools.median(age, epsilon=1.0, bounds=(17, 90), random_state=seed)
print(f"true median age: {np.median(age):.1f}  diffprivlib median: {private:.2f}")
With random_state=0, it prints a true median of 37.0 and a private one of 37.72. Ages are whole numbers, so every point between 37 and 38 has the same score, and the mechanism picked a random point in that piece. OpenDP does not run the median without a public upper bound on the number of rows, declared as a Margin. Choose a large bound from public facts, because it must be at least the true number of rows, and a larger bound costs almost nothing.
context = dp.Context.compositor(
    data=adult.lazy(),
    privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=1),  # one row per person
    privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=1.0),
    split_evenly_over=1,
    margins=[dp.polars.Margin(max_length=100_000)],  # a public bound on the number of rows
)
age_col: Any = pl.col("age")  # OpenDP adds .dp to Polars expressions when it is imported
query = context.query().select(age_col.dp.median(candidates=list(range(17, 91))))
print(query.summarize(alpha=0.05))
released = query.release().collect()  # changes on every run: OpenDP's noise has no seed
Its summary shows ExponentialMin with a scale of 2.0, because OpenDP 0.16 adds exponential noise to the score of every candidate and reports the best. That is permute-and-flip (McKenna & Sheldon 2020), which has the guarantee of the exponential mechanism and never a worse error on average. The accuracy is null, because OpenDP gives no error bar for a quantile. The noise has no seed, so the released value changes on each run of uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/practitioner_adult_statistics.py.
The error bar that you can state is about rank, not value. With probability \(1 - \beta\), the gap of the exponential mechanism is at most \((2\Delta u/\varepsilon)(\ln|\mathcal R| + \ln(1/\beta))\), the tail form of Equation 23.2. For a median, with \(\Delta u = 1\), the gap is the number of records by which the output misses the middle rank. So \(\beta = 0.05\) gives its 95% bar in ranks. A bar in value would need the number of records near the median, which the release does not show. If a dashboard needs values, spend budget on a few noisy counts below candidate values. A large range costs little, because its width changes the gap only through the logarithm of the number of candidates.
Two things go wrong in practice. Where the data near the quantile are sparse, the best piece is long and the output can be anywhere in it. Then a small error in rank is a large error in value. And the range or the candidates must not come from the data. For example, an upper end set to the observed maximum brings back the leak. diffprivlib warns with a PrivacyLeakWarning when you leave out bounds (Sensitivity).
crumbs: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
23.6 Report-noisy-max and Gumbel noise
Report-noisy-max adds independent Laplace noise to the score of each candidate and outputs the candidate with the largest noisy score. It is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any number of candidates when the noise has scale \(2\Delta u/\varepsilon\), or \(\Delta u/\varepsilon\) when one record pushes all scores the same way. Release only the index of the winner, and pay for a fresh noisy answer if you need its score.
Gumbel noise of scale \(2\Delta u/\varepsilon\) in place of the Laplace noise gives exactly the exponential mechanism. Libraries sample it with this Gumbel-max trick, because the exponential of a score in the thousands overflows, but noisy scores do not. The \(c\) largest scores with Gumbel noise give the top \(c\) at once (Durfee & Rogers 2019).
crumbs: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
23.7 The sparse vector technique
Sometimes queries come one at a time, and you want the first one that is high enough. The sparse vector technique (Dwork et al. 2009) compares each query with one noisy threshold and pays only for the query that fires. Its basic form, AboveThreshold, takes a threshold \(\tau\) and a stream of queries \(f\), all with the same sensitivity \(\Delta f\). It divides the budget into \(\varepsilon_1\) for the threshold and \(\varepsilon_2\) for the queries.

Draw one threshold noise, written \(\nu\), from \(\mathrm{Lap}(\Delta f/\varepsilon_1)\) for the whole run.
For each query, draw a fresh noise from \(\mathrm{Lap}(2\Delta f/\varepsilon_2)\) and add it to the answer of the query. If the result is at least \(\tau + \nu\), output “above” and stop. If not, output “below” and continue.

AboveThreshold is \((\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2)\)-DP for any number of “below” answers, even when each query is chosen after the earlier answers. All the “below” answers together pay \(\varepsilon_1\), through the one threshold noise, and the single “above” pays \(\varepsilon_2\).
But the accuracy depends on the stream length \(k\), which you must fix before the run. Write \(\beta\) for the chance that the accuracy guarantee fails. With an equal split, \(\varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_2 = \varepsilon/2\), every query gets the correct answer unless its true value is within a margin \[\alpha = \frac{8\Delta f\big(\ln k + \ln(2/\beta)\big)}{\varepsilon} \tag{23.3}\] of the threshold. Monitor 1,000 counts, each with \(\Delta f = 1\), against a threshold of 500 at \(\varepsilon = 1\). At \(\beta = 0.05\), the margin is 84.77. So with probability 0.95, only a count that near the threshold can get the wrong answer.
To find the first \(c\) queries above the threshold, start AboveThreshold again after each “above”, with fresh threshold noise and \(\varepsilon/c\) per run. Stop after the \(c\)-th. The margin then grows with \(c\), so ask for as few alarms as you can. Lyu, Su and Li keep one threshold for all \(c\) alarms and multiply the query noise by \(c\).
crumbs: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
section: 23.8 When the sparse vector technique goes wrong
text:
23.8 When the sparse vector technique goes wrong
Several published variants do not have the privacy they claim (Table 23.2).



Table 23.2: Variants of the sparse vector technique and their actual privacy, from Lyu, Su & Li (2017).










Variant (as numbered by Lyu, Su & Li)
What it changes
Actual privacy




Algorithm 3
Outputs the noisy value of each “above”
\(\infty\)


Algorithm 4
Query noise does not grow with \(c\)
\(\frac{1 + 6c}{4}\varepsilon\)


Algorithm 5
No noise on the queries
\(\infty\)


Algorithm 6
Never halts
\(\infty\)






The variant that never stops is the one to remember. It adds exactly as much noise per query as AboveThreshold, so a reviewer who checks noise scales does not find it. But at \(\varepsilon = 1\), its privacy loss gets to 18.1246 on 80 queries.
So review the accounting, not only the noise. Draw one threshold noise per run. If you draw the threshold again for each query, every “below” answer costs budget that nobody counted. Draw fresh noise for every query, because one noise draw for all of them is the same as Algorithm 5. Stop after the permitted number of “above” answers. Never publish the noisy values that you compared.

title: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
24.1 Why this matters
Analysts ask for every two-way table over a few columns, or for a synthetic file to query as often as they like. Both must satisfy differential privacy (DP). Such tables are marginal tables. Each one counts the records for each combination of values of a few attributes, and each count is a cell.
These releases add noise to whole tables, not to single cells, and scale it to how much one person can change the table. One person is in one cell of a table, so a whole table costs about as much as one count. All later computation on the noisy tables is free. When the queries are too many for noise on every cell, use synthetic data fitted to a few noisy tables.
crumbs: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
24.2 Which method to use
The choice depends on how many queries you have, compared with the number of records, and on the number of attributes of a record (Table 24.1).



Table 24.1: Which query-release method to use.





Situation
Use




A few marginal tables, with a public list of cells
Noisy counts on every cell, one budget share per table


Hundreds of tables or thousands of cells
Gaussian noise on every cell, scaled to the whole set of tables


A table whose list of values is not public
Noisy counts, keeping only cells that clear a noisy threshold (Release statistics with a library)


Far more queries than records, or queries not known in advance
Synthetic data from AIM or MST


Queries that arrive one at a time, perhaps adaptively
Online private multiplicative weights






One person is in every table, so the tables form a dense query, and the dense-query rule of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms tells where “a few” tables end. At a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) of 1 and a slack \(\delta\) of \(10^{-5}\), Gaussian noise is better from 7 tables on.
crumbs: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
24.3 Noise on every cell
Under add/remove neighbours, a person with one record changes one cell of a marginal table by 1, so the whole table has sensitivity 1. Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) on every cell then makes the table \(\varepsilon\)-DP, by parallel composition. Under replace neighbours, a person can move from one cell to another, so two cells change and the sensitivity doubles.
Several tables of the same people compose. With Laplace noise, you split the budget among the tables, so the error per cell grows in proportion to their number. Gaussian noise scales with the square root of the sum of squared changes. For one person in a number \(m\) of tables, that is \(\sqrt m\), so the Gaussian error grows only like \(\sqrt m\).
For example, a table of 10,000 records has eight yes/no attributes, so \(2^8 = 256\) possible records. The release is every cell of the marginal table of every set of attributes, 6,560 cells in all. Each cell is a fraction of the records, under replace neighbours. A uniform guess, which ignores the data, has a largest error of 0.232 on these cells. At \(\varepsilon = 1\), Laplace noise on every cell is worse, with 0.497. Gaussian noise at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) is much better, with 0.037.
Two mistakes are common. If you scale the noise of each cell to its own sensitivity, as if it were the only query, you silently spend \(\varepsilon\) once per table. And basic composition over thousands of separate cells wastes most of the budget. Calibrate to the whole set of tables instead.
crumbs: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
24.4 Releasing a marginal with OpenDP
The script practitioner_adult_statistics.py releases the education-by-income table of the Adult census data, 48,842 people with one row each, at \(\varepsilon = 1\). The survey’s documentation lists 16 levels of education and two income classes, so the keys are public and the table has 32 cells. The release includes empty cells too, because a missing cell would show that nobody has those values. Map a missing value to a listed key such as “Unknown”, because OpenDP drops a row whose key is not in the list. In OpenDP, a Margin (a setting, not a marginal table) with invariant="keys" makes the list of cells public, and with_keys limits the release to exactly those cells.
keys = pl.LazyFrame({"education": EDUCATION}).join(pl.LazyFrame({"income": INCOME}), how="cross")
context = dp.Context.compositor(
    data=adult.lazy(),
    privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=1),
    privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=1.0),
    split_evenly_over=1,
    margins=[dp.polars.Margin(by=["education", "income"], invariant="keys")],  # the cells are public
)
query = context.query().group_by("education", "income").agg(dp.len(signed=True)).with_keys(keys)
print(query.summarize(alpha=0.05))
released = query.release().collect()  # all 32 cells, zeros included; changes on every run
Run it with uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/practitioner_adult_statistics.py. The summary is deterministic.
shape: (1, 5)
┌────────┬──────────────┬─────────────────┬───────┬──────────┐
│ column ┆ aggregate    ┆ distribution    ┆ scale ┆ accuracy │
│ ---    ┆ ---          ┆ ---             ┆ ---   ┆ ---      │
│ str    ┆ str          ┆ str             ┆ f64   ┆ f64      │
╞════════╪══════════════╪═════════════════╪═══════╪══════════╡
│ len    ┆ Frame Length ┆ Integer Laplace ┆ 1.0   ┆ 3.375618 │
└────────┴──────────────┴─────────────────┴───────┴──────────┘
Each cell gets integer Laplace noise of scale 1 (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms). The 95% accuracy of 3.38 means that each noisy count is that close to the truth 95% of the time. Print that error bar next to every cell, and note that it covers only the noise, not sampling error or mistakes in the data. OpenDP’s noise has no seed, so these four cells come from one run, next to the true counts.
  Doctorate >50K: 432  true 431  accuracy 3.38
  HS-grad <=50K: 13281  true 13281  accuracy 3.38
  Preschool <=50K: 82  true 82  accuracy 3.38
  Preschool >50K: 0  true 1  accuracy 3.38
The large cells barely move, but the smallest true cell, one person with a preschool education and a high income, is smaller than the noise. So if small cells matter, merge rare categories in advance. With signed=True, a count can come out negative, which keeps it unbiased. A clamp at zero, rounding, and scaling the cells to a total already released are post-processing, so they cost nothing.
Three things go wrong. First, a list of cells from the data, such as unique() on a private column, shows rare values by itself. Without a codebook, use partition selection (Release statistics with a library). Second, each extra table of the same people needs its own share of the budget, so set split_evenly_over to the number of tables. Third, for many tables, give the budget as dp.loss_of(rho=...), with the \(\rho\) that converts to your \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) (Release statistics with a library shows how). OpenDP then uses Gaussian noise, which composes far better, and accounts in zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) (Concentrated differential privacy).
crumbs: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
24.5 Synthetic data
When the queries are too many for noise on every cell, or nobody knows them in advance, release synthetic data, in four steps.

Select a set of marginal tables to measure, from domain knowledge or privately with the exponential mechanism, scoring each table by how badly the current model fits it.
Measure each whole table with Gaussian noise, scaled to the whole set.
Generate a compact graphical model that fits the noisy tables.
Sample synthetic rows from the model.

All steps after the measurements are post-processing. So you can query and share the synthetic rows at no more privacy cost. The standard methods are MST and AIM, by McKenna and coauthors, and AIM selects the tables to measure as it goes. SmartNoise Synth, the snsynth package, gives the two methods one interface. This book’s environment does not include it, so the call below did not run. Install it in an environment of its own.
# smartnoise-synth 1.0.8: not installed in this book's environment, not run
from snsynth import Synthesizer

synth = Synthesizer.create("aim", epsilon=1.0, delta=1e-6)
synth.fit(adult_pandas, categorical_columns=["education", "sex", "race", "occupation", "income"])
rows = synth.sample(48_842)
A synthetic table is accurate on the tables that it measured, by construction. So evaluate it on other queries, but not freely on the private data. If you keep the best of several runs, judged against the private data, you select on that data. Also, each extra run spends the generator’s budget again. So score candidate settings on a public dataset of the same shape, or charge the comparisons to the budget. A generator trained without DP is not anonymised, however synthetic its rows look.
crumbs: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
24.6 Private multiplicative weights
The synthetic-data tools keep the select, measure and update loop of the multiplicative weights exponential mechanism (MWEM) of Hardt, Ligett and McSherry (2012). MWEM is the practical form of private multiplicative weights, and it keeps a guessed histogram with one weight for each possible record, 256 in the eight-attribute example. In each of a fixed number of rounds, it uses the exponential mechanism to select a query that the guess answers badly. Then it measures that query with fresh Laplace noise and moves the guess toward the measurement. The number of corrections has a limit for all numbers of queries, so the error grows only with the logarithm of the number of queries.
That pays off only for very large sets of queries. On the eight-attribute example at privacy level 1, with 38 rounds, the largest error of MWEM is 0.078. That is better than Laplace noise, but about two times worse than Gaussian noise. Its running time also grows with the number of possible records, which limits it to a few attributes.
If you implement it, fix the number of rounds before you see the data, from the error bound, which uses only public quantities. Measure each query with fresh noise, because the scores of the selection step are exact and must not leak. Release the average of the guesses, not the last one, because the accuracy guarantee covers only the average. For queries that arrive one at a time, an online form pays only for its corrections (Adaptive data analysis).

title: 25  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
25.1 What it is
The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms set their noise by the global sensitivity, the most one record can move the answer over all pairs of neighbouring datasets. The median of ages between 0 and 100 has global sensitivity 100. So under differential privacy (DP) at a privacy level of \(\varepsilon = 1\), the Laplace mechanism’s median error is \(100\ln 2 = 69.31\) years. But on a simulated sample of 1,001 ages, one person moves the median by only 0.1386 years. That smaller number is the local sensitivity, the most one record can move the answer \(f\) from the dataset \(D\) you hold: \[\mathrm{LS}_f(D) = \max_{D' \text{ a neighbour of } D}|f(D) - f(D')|. \tag{25.1}\]
The techniques of this page add noise on the scale of the data you hold, under one rule. A noise scale, bound or threshold that you compute from the data is itself a statistic of the data, so it must be private too. On this page, datasets have a fixed size \(n\), and neighbours replace one record.

title: 25  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
25.2 When you meet it
You meet these techniques when a statistic has no useful worst case (Table 25.1).



Table 25.1: Which technique releases what, and where you meet it.










You release
Technique
Where you meet it




A sum, mean or gradient of unbounded values
Clipping to a bound fixed in advance
Every library’s bounds, and the clipping norm of private training


A median or quantile
Inverse sensitivity
diffprivlib.tools.quantile, OpenDP’s dp.quantile


A discrete answer with a clear winner
Stability-based release
The threshold of private partition selection


A black-box model or estimator
Subsample-and-aggregate
Teacher ensembles for private prediction






A stability-based release publishes a discrete answer exactly, such as the most common value. It does so if a noisy test shows that the answer leads the runner-up by about \(2\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) records, for a slack \(\delta\). Otherwise it refuses, so plan for refusals downstream. The same test selects the keys a group-by can release (Release statistics with a library).
Subsample-and-aggregate runs an estimator on disjoint blocks and averages their clipped answers with noise. Private aggregation of teacher ensembles (PATE) is its voting form (Private prediction).
Propose-test-release proposes a bound on the local sensitivity, and refuses unless a noisy test shows that the data are far from it. Smooth sensitivity scales heavy-tailed noise to a bound that cannot jump between neighbours. PATE uses it for the \(\varepsilon\) of its votes, but on the 1,001 ages it is about twelve times less accurate than inverse sensitivity (below).

title: 25  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
25.3 How to use it
Most of the time you bound the inputs. Clipping replaces each value \(x\) by \(\min(x, C)\), for a clip bound \(C\) that you fix before you see the data. If the values cannot be negative, one record then moves the mean of \(n\) records by at most \(C/n\). So Laplace noise of scale \(C/(n\varepsilon)\) on the clipped mean gives \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and a larger \(C\) gives less bias but more noise.
Choose \(C\) from domain knowledge, such as a legal maximum or a sensor range. Otherwise, spend a small part of the budget, charged by composition, on a private high quantile and clip there. If you give no bound, diffprivlib computes it from the data and issues a PrivacyLeakWarning. Make that warning an error with warnings.simplefilter("error", PrivacyLeakWarning), as practitioner_adult_statistics.py does.
For a median or quantile, use inverse sensitivity. This exponential mechanism favours each candidate output by how few records must change before the median equals it. Give it bounds or a candidate grid fixed in advance. On the 1,001 ages at \(\varepsilon = 1\), its median error is 0.0783 years, less than even the local sensitivity of 0.1386.

title: 25  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
25.4 What goes wrong
Noise scaled to the local sensitivity is not private. The five ages \((0, 0, 0, 0, 100)\) have median 0. No single change moves it, so they get no noise. Their neighbour \((0, 0, 0, 100, 100)\) gets continuous noise, so its output is never exactly 0, and an output of exactly 0 names the first dataset. The same leak hides in a clip bound set to the observed maximum, a candidate grid made from the values of the data, or keys read from the data. In review, search for a max(), quantile() or unique() on the private data that sets a parameter.
A clip from above always moves a mean down. A two-sided clip removes that bias only when the range has the data at its centre (Private mean estimation). If neighbours add or remove a record, \(n\) is not public. Then release a noisy clipped sum and a noisy count, and divide the two.
Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 26  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
26.1 What it is
The proof of the Laplace mechanism is about densities on the real line. But a computer samples floating-point numbers, a finite set with uneven gaps. The textbook sampler adds \(\pm b\ln(1/U)\) to the true answer, for a noise scale \(b\) and a uniform draw \(U\). Mironov (2012) showed that in double precision this sampler leaks the true answer through the last bits of its output. Floats are dense near 0 and sparse far from it. So many outputs can come from a true answer of 0 or of 1, but not from the two. Such an output names its input with certainty.
Differential privacy (DP) cannot cover that leak. DP limits how much one record can change the chance of an output, by a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and a slack \(\delta\) (The definition of differential privacy). Take a set \(S\) of outputs that a dataset \(D\) can reach but its neighbour never can. No factor \(e^\varepsilon\) lifts the neighbour’s probability of \(S\) above 0, so for a mechanism \(M\) the slack must cover all of \[\delta \ge \Pr[M(D) \in S]. \tag{26.1}\] In a toy sampler with 12-bit floats, such outputs carry probability 0.4791, and more bits do not shrink it.
So DP is a property of the distribution that the code actually produces. There are two repairs. The snapping mechanism keeps floats. It clamps the answer, adds noise, rounds to a coarse power-of-two grid and clamps again. The other repair makes the query integer-valued and adds exact discrete Laplace or discrete Gaussian noise.

title: 26  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
26.2 When you meet it
You meet this problem when you review code that adds noise itself, such as the unsafe x + np.random.laplace(0, b), and when you choose a library. OpenDP’s samplers are exact, and on integer data they give discrete Laplace and discrete Gaussian noise. diffprivlib has mechanisms.Geometric (its name for the discrete Laplace), mechanisms.GaussianDiscrete and mechanisms.Snapping. Its continuous Laplace, which its tools functions use, is a mitigation, not an exact sampler: it draws four uniform variates against this attack (Holohan & Braghin 2021). Secure aggregation needs integer noise too (Local, shuffle and distributed trust models).
In private training, Opacus adds continuous Gaussian noise in floating point, so the proof of Private stochastic gradient descent covers only idealized code. Its secure_mode=True takes the noise from a cryptographic generator, which makes these attacks harder. For a released model, make sure that it used this mode and that its guarantee names the idealized mechanism.

title: 26  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
26.3 How to use it
Use a library on integer data. Its discrete Laplace noise gives each integer \(z\) a probability proportional to \(e^{-|z|/b}\), and you calibrate it like continuous noise. For an integer query with sensitivity \(\Delta f\), it gives \(\varepsilon = \Delta f/b\). At \(b = 1\), a count comes out exact with probability 0.4621.
The discrete Gaussian gives each integer \(x\) a probability proportional to \(e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), for a width \(\sigma\). Its exact privacy curve is a little worse than the continuous one. At sensitivity 1 and \(\sigma = 1\), its \(\delta\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) is 0.1414, against 0.1269. So report the discrete curve, or account as OpenDP does in zero-concentrated DP. In that accounting, the discrete Gaussian has the same privacy parameter as the continuous one, \(\rho = (\Delta f)^2/(2\sigma^2)\). In the snippet, map(1) gives each guarantee at sensitivity 1.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
integers, distance = dp.atom_domain(T=int), dp.absolute_distance(T=int)
laplace = dp.m.make_laplace(integers, distance, scale=1.0)
print(laplace.map(1))  # 1.0
gauss = dp.m.make_gaussian(integers, distance, scale=2.0)
print(gauss.map(1))  # 0.125
print(gauss.output_measure)  # ZeroConcentratedDivergence
To make a real-valued query integer, such as a sum of clipped values, divide it by a step much smaller than the noise. Round up with probability equal to the fractional part, and down otherwise, so that the result has no bias. Compute the sensitivity again in those units, because rounding can move neighbours a little further apart. Then add discrete noise and multiply back.

title: 26  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
26.4 What goes wrong
Ask these questions of each implementation.

Is every sensitivity computed from bounds fixed in advance, with no max(), quantile() or unique() on the private data (Beyond global sensitivity)?
Does a vetted library draw the noise, or an exact sampler with no floating-point exp, log or random() inside? Search for np.random, random., scipy.stats, default_rng, .laplace( and .normal(.
Does integer data get integer noise, and is every floating-point output snapped and clamped to a fixed range?
Does each release draw fresh noise from a cryptographic source, such as secrets.SystemRandom(), rather than a fixed seed that makes it removable?
Is the running time fixed or padded? The rounds of a rejection sampler depend on the value it draws, and Jin et al. (2022) use that time as a leak.
Does the stated guarantee match the mechanism, including the discrete Gaussian’s own curve and the sensitivity after rounding?

Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
27.1 Why this matters
Every mechanism so far in this part assumed a trusted curator, which holds the raw data and releases only the output of the mechanism. In this central model, the differential privacy (DP) guarantee protects what the curator publishes. It does not protect against a breach of its database, a curious engineer or a court order. A browser vendor that collects usage statistics often does not have that much trust.
Three other models trust less. In the local model, you trust nobody, and each person randomizes their own record before it leaves their device. The shuffle model trusts a shuffler only to cut the link between each report and its sender. The distributed model trusts cryptography that shows only a sum, run by enough honest participants. The closer to each person you add the noise, the fewer parties you trust, and the more noise reaches the answer.
crumbs: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
27.2 Choosing a trust model
Less trust costs more noise. As the population grows, the noise on a private count stays fixed in the central model, but grows with its square root in the local model. The shuffle and distributed models close most of that gap.
So use the central model when you can trust a curator with the raw data, as Release statistics with a library does end to end. Choose local only when nobody can see a raw record and the population is large enough, which you check with the standard deviation of Section 27.3. In all cases, state the trust model next to the privacy parameters, because the same \(\varepsilon\) protects against a different adversary in each model.
crumbs: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
27.3 Central and local differential privacy
In the local model, each person sends only a report, the output of a local randomizer \(R\) on their own record. Write \(\varepsilon_0\) for the privacy level of one report. The randomizer is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP when no set of possible reports becomes more than \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\) times as likely when the record changes. That is, all sets of reports \(S\) and all pairs of records \(x\) and \(x'\) satisfy \[\Pr[R(x) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon_0}\Pr[R(x') \in S]. \tag{27.1}\] A change to one person’s record changes only their own report, so the whole collection is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP in the central sense, with neighbours that differ in one replaced record. The guarantee covers only the randomized value, so a network address stored with a report links the report back to the person.
The basic local randomizer is randomized response on one bit. Each person reports their true bit with a probability \(p = e^{\varepsilon_0}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0})\), and the flipped bit otherwise. To remove the expected flips, the analyst subtracts \(1 - p\) from the share of reported ones and divides by \(2p - 1\). The standard deviation of the estimate then depends only on the level and the number of people \(n\): \[\operatorname{sd}(\hat\pi) = \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0/2}}{(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)\sqrt n}. \tag{27.2}\]
The script practitioner_adult_statistics.py runs the two models at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\) on the 48,842 people of the Adult census data. Each bit says whether a person’s income is more than $50K. In the local model, diffprivlib’s Binary mechanism randomizes each bit, and the analyst sees only the reports.
answers = (adult["income"] == ">50K").cast(pl.Int8).cast(pl.String).to_list()  # "1" or "0"
n, eps = len(answers), log(3)
coin = Binary(epsilon=eps, value0="0", value1="1", random_state=seed)
reports = [coin.randomise(a) for a in answers]  # each person randomizes their own answer
p = exp(eps) / (1 + exp(eps))  # chance a report is truthful: 0.75
reported = reports.count("1") / n
local = (reported - (1 - p)) / (2 * p - 1)  # undo the expected flips
local_sd = math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n) / (2 * p - 1)  # the randomization noise alone
print(f"true share over 50K: {answers.count('1') / n:.4f}")
print(f"local estimate: {local:.4f}  sd {local_sd:.4f}")
In the central model, a trusted curator counts the true bits with diffprivlib’s tools.count_nonzero at the same level. This call adds Laplace noise with standard deviation \(\sqrt2/\varepsilon\) to the count.
rich = (adult["income"] == ">50K").to_numpy()
central = tools.count_nonzero(rich, epsilon=log(3), random_state=seed) / len(rich)
central_sd = math.sqrt(Laplace(epsilon=log(3), sensitivity=1).variance(0)) / len(rich)  # the count's noise
print(f"central estimate: {central:.4f}  sd {central_sd:.6f}")
Its seed-0 run, uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/practitioner_adult_statistics.py, prints this.
true share over 50K: 0.2393
local estimate: 0.2359  sd 0.0039
central estimate: 0.2393  sd 0.000026
local sd / central sd: 149
So at the same guarantee, the local estimate is 149 times noisier, and the factor grows like the square root of the population. This cost comes from the model, not from randomized response, because no local protocol can estimate a fraction with an error below order \(1/((e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)\sqrt n)\), and randomized response reaches that order. That is why Apple, Google and Microsoft use local DP only for the most frequent items in very large populations.
crumbs: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
section: 27.4 Frequency estimation: \(k\)-ary randomized response and unary encoding
text:
27.4 Frequency estimation: \(k\)-ary randomized response and unary encoding
Most deployed local DP does frequency estimation. Each person has one value from a known list, such as an emoji, and the analyst wants the share of people with each value. A report votes for a value with some probability \(p_1\) if the person has it, and with a smaller probability \(p_0\) otherwise. Suppose that \(c_v\) of the \(n\) reports vote for a value \(v\). When you remove the false votes on average, you get the unbiased estimate \[\hat f_v = \frac{c_v/n - p_0}{p_1 - p_0}. \tag{27.3}\]
Two designs set \(p_1\) and \(p_0\) for a list of \(k\) values. In \(k\)-ary randomized response, each person reports their true value with probability \(e^{\varepsilon_0}/(e^{\varepsilon_0} + k - 1)\), and another value otherwise. Optimized unary encoding sends one bit per value, and keeps the 1 of the person’s value only half the time, but almost never changes a 0 into a 1. The variance for a rare value sets the smallest share that you can see, so compare the designs by it. Use \(k\)-ary randomized response when \(k < 3e^{\varepsilon_0} + 2\), and unary encoding otherwise, at the cost of a \(k\)-bit report. The pure-ldp Python package has the two designs.
Take a keyboard app that wants the share of each of 128 emoji from a million users at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\). The estimate for a rare emoji has a standard deviation of 0.0019 under unary encoding, against 0.0066 under \(k\)-ary randomized response. By convention, an estimate must be three standard deviations above zero before you can tell it from noise. So even the better design loses all emoji that fewer than about \(3 \times 0.0019\), or 0.6%, of users choose. Size the population from that floor before you collect. For lists too large to send, local hashing and heavy-hitter protocols send a few bits per report (Wang et al. 2017; Bassily et al. 2017).
crumbs: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
section: 27.5 Numbers in one bit: local mean estimation
text:
27.5 Numbers in one bit: local mean estimation
For numbers between 0 and a known bound, such as minutes in an app, one bit per person is enough (Ding, Kulkarni & Yekhanin 2017). The chance of a 1 increases in a straight line with the value, so the analyst inverts that line to get an unbiased mean. For a million users, a bound of 1,440 minutes and \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\), the mean has a standard deviation of 1.420 minutes. Fix the bound before collection and clip to it on the device. A bound from the reports would let one person’s value change the randomizer of all users.
crumbs: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
27.6 Collecting every day: memoization
Telemetry asks the same question every day. If a value does not change, an analyst can average its daily reports to remove their fresh noise. Composition counts that leak as the sum of the \(\varepsilon_0\) of each report. The fix is memoization. The device draws one permanent randomized response per value and sends it each day, so an unchanged value costs only the level of that response, written \(\varepsilon_\infty\). RAPPOR, Google’s collection of the homepages of Chrome users, has \(\varepsilon_\infty = 2.043\).
Memoization fails when the value changes, because each new value costs another \(\varepsilon_\infty\). A user who changes their homepage every month gets to \(12 \times 2.043 = 24.5\) in a year.
crumbs: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
section: 27.7 The shuffle model and amplification by shuffling
text:
27.7 The shuffle model and amplification by shuffling
In the shuffle model (Cheu et al. 2019), each person sends a local report to a shuffler. The shuffler removes identifiers and timing, and sends the reports on in random order. Each report then hides among the others, so the collection meets central \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP at an \(\varepsilon\) far below \(\varepsilon_0\) (Amplification by shuffling and by iteration). The closed-form bound of Feldman, McMillan & Talwar (2021) gives that \(\varepsilon\) only when there are enough people to hide among: \[\varepsilon_0 \le \ln\frac{n}{16\ln(2/\delta)}. \tag{27.4}\]
In practice, you fix the central target and solve for the largest \(\varepsilon_0\) that it allows. For a central \((1, 10^{-6})\), ten thousand people can each randomize at \(\varepsilon_0 = 3.504\). But at a thousand people, the condition above limits it to 1.460. These targets use a \(\delta\) below the book’s default (How small δ must be). At ten thousand people, the closed form gives an \(\varepsilon\) 2.6 to 4.6 times too large, so plan with it, but deploy with the paper’s numerical bound.
Three things remove the amplification. A shuffler that colludes with the analyst leaves each report at \(\varepsilon_0\). So choose an \(\varepsilon_0\) that you can defend on its own, within the tiers of the definition. Fake senders give no cover, so count only honest ones in \(n\). And timing and sizes can leak, so real shufflers batch and pad their traffic.
crumbs: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
27.8 Distributed DP: splitting the noise
In the distributed model, each client adds a small share of the central noise, and secure aggregation shows only the sum to the server (Cryptography basics). Gaussian noise splits cleanly, because the variances of independent shares add. If each of \(n\) clients adds normal noise of variance \(\sigma^2/n\), the sum has noise with standard deviation \(\sigma\). That is as private as the central Gaussian mechanism.
But the small shares are also the weakness. A client that colludes with the server can show its share, and a client that drops out adds none. With \(t\) such clients, only the noise of the honest clients is left, with standard deviation \[\sigma\sqrt{\frac{n - t}{n}}. \tag{27.5}\] So fix in advance the largest fraction \(\rho\) of clients that may collude or drop out, and have each client add variance \(\sigma^2/(n(1 - \rho))\). The honest clients alone then supply the full noise.
For example, a server sums a histogram of about a hundred thousand users through 100 clients, at \((1, 10^{-6})\). A user who changes value moves one count down and another up, so the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity is \(\sqrt 2\). The analytic Gaussian calibration of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms gives a total \(\sigma\) of 5.975. That is \(5.975/\sqrt{100} = 0.597\) per client. Without over-provisioning, if a fifth of the clients collude, the guarantee weakens to \(\varepsilon = 1.128\) at the same \(\delta\).
Secure aggregation works on integers, so clients add integer noise. This noise is Skellam or the distributed discrete Gaussian of Discrete mechanisms, as in TensorFlow Federated’s tff.aggregators.DistributedDpSumFactory. Secure aggregation also does not check inputs, so a malicious client can still send any vector.
