title: 28  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
28.1 What it is
A lower bound says that no mechanism with differential privacy (DP) can be more accurate than some floor. It holds for all mechanisms at once, so you can use it as a feasibility check. Accuracy has two numbers here. The error \(\alpha\) is how far the output may land from the true answer, and the failure probability \(\beta\) is the chance that it lands further away.
The floor you meet most is for a histogram over \(N\) bins under pure DP, with a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and no slack. Suppose that such a histogram is within \(\alpha\) records of every count with probability at least \(1 - \beta\). Then \[\alpha \ge \frac12\left(\frac{\ln\big(N(1 - \beta)\big)}{\varepsilon} - 1\right). \tag{28.1}\] The floor grows only with the logarithm of the number of bins, but under pure DP it never stops. Under approximate DP, which allows a small slack \(\delta\), it stops at about \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) records for all numbers of bins.
crumbs: 28  Lower bounds: what privacy costs

title: 28  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
28.2 When you meet it
You meet a lower bound when a design looks too good. Take a request for a histogram over a million locations at \(\varepsilon = 1\) with no slack, accurate to five records in every bin with 95% probability.
First ask if one person moves one statistic, as in the disjoint cells of a histogram, or all of them, as in the means of many attributes. The histogram floor applies to the first case, and the fingerprinting and reconstruction floors below to the second. Then the floor tells you whether to tune more. A target below it needs more data, a coarser answer or a weaker guarantee. A mechanism within a small factor of the floor is done, because no algorithm can gain more than that factor.
crumbs: 28  Lower bounds: what privacy costs

title: 28  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
28.3 How to use it
For the million locations, all pure-DP histograms have an error of 6.38 records or more in some bin. So the five-record promise is impossible. The Laplace histogram of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, with an error of 16.79, is about 2.6 times the floor and so already near the best. With \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), the floor stays below about \(\ln(10^6) = 13.82\) records. A stability-based histogram, which releases only non-empty bins, has an error that does not grow with \(N\) (Beyond global sensitivity). So when a large, mostly empty universe puts the floor too high, change to approximate DP.
The same floor gives the size of a dataset, because an error in records divided by the number of records \(n\) is an error in frequencies. A pure-DP histogram whose frequencies must all be within \(\alpha\) needs \[n \ge \frac{\ln\big(N(1 - \beta)\big) - \varepsilon}{2\alpha\varepsilon}. \tag{28.2}\] If the data are a sample from a population, sampling costs records too, about \(\ln(2N/\beta)/(2\alpha^2)\) by Hoeffding’s inequality. You need the larger of the two. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 95% probability, a million cells at an error of 0.01 need at least 638 records for privacy, but 87,522 for sampling. So at \(\varepsilon = 1\), fine answers run short of records because of sampling, which no mechanism can fix.
When one person moves many statistics, the cost grows faster. Under pure DP, the means of \(d\) yes/no attributes cost records in proportion to \(d\). Under approximate DP, the fingerprinting bound puts the cost at about \(\sqrt{d\ln(1/\delta)}/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) records. The Gaussian mechanism is within a factor \(\sqrt{\ln d}\) of it. So use approximate DP for outputs with many coordinates, such as a gradient. After you calibrate the Gaussian noise, search for more records, not a better mechanism. For about \(n\) counting queries on \(n\) records, the reconstruction attack of Dinur and Nissim puts the floor at an error of order \(\sqrt n\) per answer (Reconstruction attacks).
crumbs: 28  Lower bounds: what privacy costs

title: 28  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
28.4 What goes wrong
Aggregates are not a defence. The attack behind the fingerprinting bound (Homer et al. 2008) found whether a given person took part in a genome study, from its published frequencies of genetic variants. It scores how far the released means lean towards the target’s record and away from the population means, attribute by attribute. Members score higher, because each member pulls the means toward their own record. On the means of 50 people over 2,000 attributes, it reaches a true positive rate (TPR) of 0.242 at a false positive rate (FPR) of 1%. A \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP Gaussian mechanism cuts that TPR to 0.014.
So use the score to audit a release of many averages, with population means from a separate sample. Compare its TPR at a low FPR with the cap \(\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\) from the definition. If an audit beats the cap, it has found a bug in the mechanism or its accounting. Passing proves nothing, because an attack only bounds \(\varepsilon\) from below (Auditing private training).
Each approximate-DP floor here assumes a small \(\delta\), such as the book’s default (How small δ must be), or it means little. A mechanism that publishes each record with probability \(\delta\) is \((0, \delta)\)-DP, so a claim with \(\delta\) near \(1/n\) lets about one record out in full.
Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.
crumbs: 28  Lower bounds: what privacy costs

title: 29  Private mean estimation
text:
29.1 Why this matters
Private machine learning computes the mean more often than any other statistic. Each step of private gradient descent averages clipped per-example gradients, and a survey share is a mean of 0/1 answers. Before you release a mean, you must know how many records it needs, and how to choose a clipping range without a look at the data.
Differential privacy (DP) must hold for every dataset, also for datasets that your assumptions exclude (The definition of differential privacy). So an assumption such as “the records are normal” can make a mechanism more accurate, but never enters the privacy argument. For this reason, every mechanism below clips each record to a range. The noise grows with the width of that range, and you must not read a narrow range off the data. So spend a small part of the budget to find where the data are, then clip there.

title: 29  Private mean estimation
section: 29.2 Bounded data: privacy adds a lower-order term
text:
29.2 Bounded data: privacy adds a lower-order term
In this chapter, datasets have a fixed size \(n\), and neighbours differ in one replaced record. The measure of an estimate is its root-mean-square error (RMSE), the typical distance from the estimate to the mean of the population.
Start with records in a known interval of width \(w\), such as yes/no answers coded 0 and 1, and write \(\sigma^2\) for the variance of a record. Release the average plus Laplace noise with scale \(w/(n\varepsilon)\), which is \(\varepsilon\)-DP because one record moves the average by at most \(w/n\) (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). Laplace noise has variance twice its scale squared, and it is independent of the sampling error, so the two variances add: \[\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2}{n} + \frac{2w^2}{n^2\varepsilon^2}}. \tag{29.1}\] To plan a study, set the RMSE equal to a target error \(\alpha\) and solve for \(n\), as the snippet in the Code section does. The number of records that you need is at most \[\frac{\sigma^2}{\alpha^2} + \frac{\sqrt2\,w}{\alpha\varepsilon}. \tag{29.2}\]
So sampling alone needs about \(\sigma^2/\alpha^2\) records, and privacy adds at most about \(w/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) more. Take a yes/no survey of a population that is half yes, the worst case for sampling. An RMSE of 0.05 then needs 100 people, and privacy at \(\varepsilon = 1\) raises that to 108. The privacy term grows only like \(1/\alpha\), against \(1/\alpha^2\) for sampling, so it matters most at a coarse target and a small \(\varepsilon\). It also grows with the width \(w\), and the rest of the chapter makes the range narrower.
Libraries ask you for the range. In diffprivlib, tools.mean(x, epsilon=..., bounds=(lower, upper)) clips to the bounds and adds noise. Without bounds, it takes the observed minimum and maximum, which leaks them, and raises a PrivacyLeakWarning.
Bounds that are too tight cause a different problem, because they clip real records. The script practitioner_adult_statistics.py releases the mean weekly hours of work of the 48,842 people in the Adult census data at \(\varepsilon = 1\), with loose and with tight bounds.
hours = adult["hours-per-week"].to_numpy()
loose = tools.mean(hours, epsilon=1.0, bounds=(1, 99), random_state=seed)
tight = tools.mean(hours, epsilon=1.0, bounds=(20, 60), random_state=seed)
clipped = np.clip(hours, 20, 60).mean()  # what the tight bounds can at best recover
print(f"true mean hours: {hours.mean():.3f}")
print(f"bounds (1, 99): {loose:.3f}  bounds (20, 60): {tight:.3f}")
print(f"bias of (20, 60): {clipped - hours.mean():+.3f}")
Its seed-0 run, uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/practitioner_adult_statistics.py, prints these lines. The last two come from code next to the excerpt.
true mean hours: 40.422
bounds (1, 99): 40.421  bounds (20, 60): 40.361
bias of (20, 60): -0.061
people outside (20, 60): 8.7%
noise scale (1, 99): 0.0020  (20, 60): 0.0008
The tight bounds decrease the noise scale from 0.0020 to 0.0008 hours. But they clip the 8.7% of people outside them, and this moves the mean by 0.061 hours, much more than the noise they save. No budget removes that bias, so report the error in three parts, which are sampling, clipping bias and noise. Choose the bounds from the schema or public data, and measure the share that they clip on data that you may look at.
The formulas also treat \(n\) as public, which is true only because neighbours replace a record. If the size is private, divide a noisy sum by a noisy count, and split the budget between the two.

title: 29  Private mean estimation
section: 29.3 The cost of an unknown range
text:
29.3 The cost of an unknown range
Now let the records be normal with variance 1, with a mean that you know only to be within a distance \(R\) of zero. Write \(\tau\) for a distance from the mean that holds all the records, except with a small failure probability \(\beta\). For 1,000 records at \(\beta = 0.05\), \(\tau\) is 4.604.
The naive estimator clips every record to the widest range where the data can be, \(R + \tau\) on each side of zero. It then adds Laplace noise for that width, so its error grows in proportion to \(R\). With 1,000 records at \(\varepsilon = 1\), its RMSE is 2828.44 when \(R\) is a million. But Lower bounds shows that an unknown range needs only about \(\ln R/\varepsilon\) more records.
Coarse then fine (Karwa & Vadhan 2018) comes close to that floor in two steps. The coarse step cuts the range into bins of width \(2\tau\). It then uses a part \(\varepsilon_1\) of the budget to pick the fullest bin with the exponential mechanism. The records it needs grow only with the logarithm of the number of bins. The data can be across two bins, so the fine step clips every record to the chosen bin and its two neighbours. It releases the average with Laplace noise for that window and the rest of the budget, so by composition the two steps are \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
With a quarter of the budget on the coarse step, the same 1,000 records give an RMSE of 0.0609 for every \(R\) from 10 to a million. But the fine step has only three quarters of the budget and a window three bins wide. So for small ranges the naive estimator is better, here up to \(R = 13.81\). For larger ranges, use coarse then fine, or find the data with a private quantile such as diffprivlib’s tools.quantile. Under approximate DP, with its slack \(\delta\), a stability-based histogram does the coarse step with about \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) records, so \(R\) goes away (Beyond global sensitivity).
Two things go wrong. A budget split, bin width or \(\beta\) that you choose after a look at the data leaks it. And a coarse step with too few records can pick an empty bin and clip all records to the wrong place.

title: 29  Private mean estimation
text:
29.4 Many dimensions: clip the norm
Vectors in \(d\) dimensions, such as embeddings or gradients, use the same recipe with a different measure of size. Here the size is the \(\ell_2\) norm, or length. Clip each record to a radius \(C\), so that one replaced record moves the average by at most \(2C/n\). Then add Gaussian noise for that sensitivity (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). This is the step of private gradient descent, and private training tells how to choose its clipping norm.
The radius sets the cost. With unit variance per coordinate, records are about \(\sqrt d\) from their mean, so the radius must grow like \(\sqrt d\). The noise in all coordinates then grows like \(d\) in total, against \(\sqrt d\) for the sampling error. So in high dimension privacy is the larger cost, and the fingerprinting lower bound shows that no mechanism avoids it.
If you do not know where the mean is, a grid of bins pays for the range once per dimension. The shrinking balls of CoinPress (Biswas, Dong, Kamath & Ullman 2020) need no grid. Each round clips to a ball around a noisy guess of the mean, then makes the ball smaller. Fix the number of rounds and their budget split before the run.

title: 29  Private mean estimation
section: 29.5 Heavy tails: clip into the data
text:
29.5 Heavy tails: clip into the data
Incomes, session lengths and per-example gradient norms have heavy tails. If you know only that the variance is at most \(\sigma^2\), a range that clips no record is very wide. So clip into the data on purpose, and accept a bias.
Now let \(\tau\) be a clipping half-width. A coarse step finds a centre near the mean, and you clip every record to within \(\tau\) of it. Only the rare records beyond \(\tau\) move, so with the centre at the mean the bias is at most \(\sigma^2/\tau\). But the noise grows in proportion to \(\tau\). The bound on the total error is smallest at \[\tau_b = \sigma\sqrt{\frac{n\varepsilon}{2\sqrt2}}, \tag{29.3}\] which uses only \(n\), \(\varepsilon\) and the variance bound. At this width, an error \(\alpha\) needs about \(\sigma^2/\alpha^2 + 8\sqrt2\,\sigma^2/(\alpha^2\varepsilon)\) records. Both terms grow like \(1/\alpha^2\), so privacy now costs as much as sampling.
Table 29.1 shows the trade-off on Pareto records, a heavy-tailed distribution scaled to variance 1. The first width clips a record only with probability 0.05, and noise is most of its error. The worst-case width \(\tau_b\) decreases the error to 0.0607, and the best width for this distribution is better again.

title: 29  Private mean estimation
text:
29.6 Code
The snippet computes the records that a bounded mean needs, checks its noise with OpenDP, and computes the default clipping width for heavy tails. The RMSE equal to \(\alpha\), times \(n^2\), is a quadratic in \(n\), and the first function rounds its positive root up.
from math import ceil, sqrt

import opendp.prelude as dp


def records_for_bounded_mean(alpha: float, sd: float, width: float, eps: float) -> int:
    """Smallest n with sd^2/n + 2 (width/(n eps))^2 <= alpha^2."""
    a, c = sd**2, 2 * (width / eps) ** 2
    return ceil((a + sqrt(a * a + 4 * c * alpha**2)) / (2 * alpha**2))


def heavy_tail_width(n: int, eps: float, sd: float) -> float:
    """The clipping half-width that balances the bias bound sd^2/tau against the noise."""
    return sd * sqrt(n * eps / (2 * sqrt(2)))


n = records_for_bounded_mean(0.05, 0.5, 1.0, 1.0)
print(n)  # 108
print(f"{dp.laplacian_scale_to_accuracy(1.0 / (n * 1.0), alpha=0.05):.4f}")  # 0.0277
print(f"{heavy_tail_width(1000, 1.0, 1.0):.2f}")  # 18.80
OpenDP gives accuracy as a half-width that holds the noise with a chosen probability. So laplacian_scale_to_accuracy changes the noise scale \(w/(n\varepsilon)\) of a range of width \(w\) at the planned 108 records into the half-width at 95%.

text:

Rules of thumb

Never clip to the observed minimum and maximum. Take bounds from the schema or public data, or spend a quarter of the budget or less, a simple default, finding the data.
Bounds that clip real records bias the mean whatever \(\varepsilon\) is, so put the clipping bias into every reported interval.

title: 30  Release statistics with a library
text:
30.1 Why this matters
Suppose that you are the analytics engineer of an online shop. The business wants a dashboard of purchase lines, revenue and the typical sale, overall and per country, and of how many customers bought each product. The figures describe customers, so they need a differential privacy (DP) guarantee. But one customer has many rows, and a guarantee for one row protects a single purchase, not the person behind a hundred. This chapter does the job with OpenDP, from the unit to the written guarantee.
The data are the Online Retail set from the University of California, Irvine (UCI) Machine Learning Repository, with 541,909 invoice lines of a British online shop. Each line records one product on one invoice, with its quantity, unit price, customer and country. The script practitioner_release_statistics.py does every step in less than a minute, with OpenDP 0.16.0 and Polars 1.36.1.
OpenDP takes its noise from a cryptographic generator that has no seed, so the released values change on every run. So this page quotes scales, error bars and thresholds, which contain no noise, and shows released values only in a block marked as one run.

title: 30  Release statistics with a library
section: 30.3 Decide the unit and the budget
text:
30.3 Decide the unit and the budget
The unit of privacy, which the guarantee protects, is a customer. So two neighbouring datasets differ by one customer with all their lines, added or removed (The definition of differential privacy). The script removes returns, lines with a zero price and lines with no customer identifier, which belong to nobody. Each filter looks only at the line itself, so a customer who is added or removed still changes only their own lines.
raw = practitioner_datasets.online_retail()
lines, stats = clean(raw)
n_customers = stats.customers
delta = delta_for(n_customers)  # 1/n^1.1, rounded down to a power of ten
per_line = per_customer(lines)
print(f"customers: {n_customers:,}  purchase lines: {lines.height:,}")
print(f"delta: {delta:.0e}")
p50, p90, p99, top = quantiles(per_line, [0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 1.0])
print(f"lines per customer: p50={p50} p90={p90} p99={p99} max={top}")
customers: 4,372  purchase lines: 397,884
delta: 1e-05
lines per customer: p50=41 p90=208 p99=662 max=7847
The slack \(\delta\) follows the book’s default for \(n\) people (How small δ must be), which gives \(10^{-5}\). OpenDP warns that \(\delta\) must be at most \(10^{-6}\), but this book ties \(\delta\) to the number of people. The privacy level is \(\varepsilon = 1\) for the whole release, because all its tables describe the same customers and their costs add up (Post-processing, group privacy and composition).
With a guarantee per line, the largest customer is a group of 7,847 records, and group privacy multiplies \(\varepsilon\) by the size of the group. You can print that maximum only because this set is public.
crumbs: 30  Release statistics with a library

title: 30  Release statistics with a library
text:
30.4 Bound each customer’s contribution
Write \(k\) for the largest number of lines that a customer may give, so that every query keeps at most \(k\) lines of each customer. A small \(k\) means little noise but removes data, and a large \(k\) keeps the data but needs more noise. The script measures this trade-off on the public set.
k=10: lines kept 10.2%  customers truncated 84.8%
k=25: lines kept 22.4%  customers truncated 64.6%
k=50: lines kept 36.9%  customers truncated 44.0%
k=100: lines kept 55.1%  customers truncated 24.9%
k=200: lines kept 72.7%  customers truncated 10.4%
k=500: lines kept 88.2%  customers truncated 1.8%
The default \(k\) is a high percentile of lines per customer in public or historical data, never in the data that you release. If you have neither, spend a small share of the budget on a private high quantile, over candidates fixed in advance (Selection). This chapter takes \(k = 100\), which is less than the 90th percentile of 208 because the noise grows with \(k\). It keeps 55.1% of the lines and truncates a quarter of the customers.
The first \(k\) lines by date bias every statistic towards early purchases, so the script keeps a random sample of \(k\) lines per customer. The filter below does what OpenDP’s truncate_per_group(k, keep="sample") does, but with a seed, so that the true values of the check stay fixed.
def sample_per_customer(k: int, seed: int, *by: str) -> pl.Expr:
    """True for at most k randomly chosen lines of each customer (within each value of `by`)."""
    return pl.int_range(pl.len()).shuffle(seed=seed).over("CustomerID", *by) < k
Values need bounds too. The value of a line is its quantity times its unit price, and the script clips it to between £0 and £200. The lower end is true because the script removed the returns. The upper end is a bound that the business sets, and it clips 1.02% of the lines. So one customer can move the revenue by at most 100 lines of £200 each. Take value bounds from the domain, never from the minimum or maximum of the data (Beyond global sensitivity).
A group-by can use two more bounds. The bound \(L_0\) is the number of groups that one customer may touch. The bound \(L_\infty\) is the number of lines that a customer may put in one group. Countries need neither, because the \(k\) lines of a customer change the country counts by at most \(k\) in total, and the noise already covers that. Products need both bounds for partition selection (Section 30.8).
crumbs: 30  Release statistics with a library

title: 30  Release statistics with a library
text:
30.5 Set up the context
OpenDP keeps the whole release in a context, which holds the data, the unit, the total budget and its split between queries. Contexts need dp.enable_features("contrib"), which turns on components that are not formally vetted. So a reviewer who needs vetted code must examine each call in the documentation of OpenDP.
context = dp.Context.compositor(
    data=lines.lazy(),
    privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=1, identifier="CustomerID"),
    privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(rho=rho, delta=delta / 2),  # Gaussian noise; delta/2 for thresholds
    split_by_weights=WEIGHTS,  # scalars, countries, products
    margins=[dp.polars.Margin(by=[], max_length=MAX_LINES)],
)
The identifier column makes the unit a customer. So contributions=1 means one customer with all their lines, added or removed, and the truncation filters bound those lines. For replace, OpenDP takes changes= instead. The budget is in zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) (Concentrated differential privacy), which gives privacy as one number, written \(\rho\). Values of \(\rho\) add up across queries and change to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) at the end.
With a zCDP budget, the context adds Gaussian noise to every count and sum. That suits the product counts, where one customer touches many groups (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). The script’s rho_for finds \(\rho = 0.0284\), the largest value that the conversion of OpenDP turns into \(\varepsilon \le 1\) with half of \(\delta\). The other half pays for the threshold of Section 30.8. The margin gives a public upper bound on the number of lines, which OpenDP needs before it adds floating-point values.
The weights give a quarter of the budget to the overall statistics, a quarter to the countries and half to the products, which need it most. The script prints the split and converts the whole release back to the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) of the statement.
budget scalars: rho=0.0071 delta=1.25e-06
budget countries: rho=0.0071 delta=1.25e-06
budget products: rho=0.0142 delta=2.50e-06
whole release as (epsilon, delta): (1.0000, 1e-05)
A query takes its share of the budget when you build it, but spends the share only when you release it. Each new query gets the next unspent share. So if you build all the queries first, each one gets the first share. The product query then gets the noise of a quarter but costs half. Build, check and release each query in turn, as the script does.
crumbs: 30  Release statistics with a library

title: 30  Release statistics with a library
section: 30.6 Release overall statistics with error bars
text:
30.6 Release overall statistics with error bars
The first query releases the count of lines, the revenue and the median line value. The context holds the raw lines, so each query truncates them itself.
value = clipped_value()  # the line value, clipped to [low, high]
scalars = (
    context.query()
    .filter(sample_per_customer(K, seed))  # at most K lines per customer
    .select(
        dp.len(signed=True),
        value.dp.sum((low, high)).alias("revenue"),
        value.dp.median(candidates=MEDIAN_CANDIDATES).alias("median"),
    )
)
scalar_summary = scalars.summarize(alpha=0.05)
scalars_hat = scalars.release().collect()
signed=True keeps negative noisy counts, and summarize reports, before anything is released, each statistic’s noise and 95% error bar.
scalars len: Frame Length, Integer Gaussian, scale=1,453.38 95% accuracy=2,850.0
scalars revenue: Sum, Float Gaussian, scale=290,804.33 95% accuracy=569,966.0
scalars median: 0.5-Quantile, GumbelMin, scale=1,453.38 95% accuracy=none
With probability 0.95, the released count of lines is within 2,850 of the truth, and the revenue within £569,966. These bars depend only on the bounds and the budget, so you can read them before the release and decide if the budget is sufficient.
The output also shows how OpenDP splits the share of a query among its statistics. Each statistic gets the same noise scale relative to its sensitivity. So the count and the median both get 1,453.38, and the revenue, with 200 times the sensitivity of the count, gets about 200 times that. To give one statistic more budget, put it in a query of its own with its own weight. The exponential mechanism, sampled by GumbelMin, chooses the median among candidates in steps of £0.50. So its error bar is in ranks, and summarize gives none (Selection).
The error bars cover only the noise, not the bias of truncation and clipping, which together keep only 48.5% of the revenue. So the private revenue estimates a truncated total, not the takings of the shop. Say so in the release. If the full total is more important than the noise, choose a larger \(k\).
crumbs: 30  Release statistics with a library

title: 30  Release statistics with a library
section: 30.7 Group by a public key list
text:
30.7 Group by a public key list
The next query gives lines and revenue per country, and its key list must not come from the data. The distinct values of the Country column tell which countries are in the private data, and no noise covers that. So the script fixes its keys in advance. The 38 keys are the United Kingdom, the 27 EU member states and the 4 states of the European Free Trade Association. Then come the United States, Canada, Australia, Japan, China and “Other”. A rule renames three spellings, such as EIRE to Ireland, and maps every other value to Other.
by_country = (
    context.query()
    .filter(sample_per_customer(K, seed))
    .group_by("Market")
    .agg(dp.len(signed=True), value.dp.sum((low, high)).alias("revenue"))
    .with_keys(pl.LazyFrame({"Market": MARKETS}))  # every key is released, zeros included
)
country_summary = by_country.summarize(alpha=0.05)
countries_hat = by_country.release().collect()
per country len: Frame Length, Integer Gaussian, scale=1,185.25 95% accuracy=2,324.0
per country revenue: Sum, Float Gaussian, scale=237,698.48 95% accuracy=465,880.5
The query releases every key, also the 11 with no purchase lines, whose counts are only noise. So the release tells nothing about which markets have customers. The count of each market has a 95% error bar of 2,324, and its revenue one of about £466,000. The true count of 5,379 for Germany is still useful, but its revenue of £131,902 is less than its error bar. So publish the error bar with every cell, or merge small markets into Other before the release.
crumbs: 30  Release statistics with a library

title: 30  Release statistics with a library
section: 30.8 Group by unknown keys with partition selection
text:
30.8 Group by unknown keys with partition selection
The list of products is not public. If one customer buys a product, its row in the table shows that purchase. So the release uses partition selection to choose privately which products to show. It releases only the products whose noisy count is above a threshold, so a product with few customers almost never appears. The threshold is what costs \(\delta\) (Beyond global sensitivity).
To count customers, not lines, the query first keeps one line per customer and product. So \(L_\infty\), the lines per customer in one group, is 1. It then keeps at most a number \(m\) of products per customer, so \(L_0\), the groups per customer, is \(m\). The script measures the trade-off that \(m\) sets on this public set.
m=1: pairs kept 1.6%  customers truncated 97.9%  scale=5.93  threshold=29  products above it: 1
m=5: pairs kept 7.9%  customers truncated 92.4%  scale=13.27  threshold=66  products above it: 9
m=10: pairs kept 15.1%  customers truncated 83.6%  scale=18.77  threshold=96  products above it: 19
m=20: pairs kept 27.5%  customers truncated 68.3%  scale=26.54  threshold=138  products above it: 30
m=50: pairs kept 52.7%  customers truncated 38.6%  scale=41.96  threshold=225  products above it: 50
The threshold grows with \(m\), from 29 to 225, because each customer can push more groups over it. But the counts grow faster, so the number of products whose true count is above the threshold goes from 1 to 50. The script takes \(m = 50\) (M in the code), again chosen on public data.
by_product = (
    context.query()
    .filter(sample_per_customer(1, seed, "StockCode"))  # one line per customer and product
    .filter(sample_per_customer(M, seed))  # at most M products per customer
    .group_by("StockCode")
    .agg(dp.len(signed=True).alias("customers"))
)
product_summary = by_product.summarize(alpha=0.05)
products_hat = by_product.release().collect()
per product customers: Frame Length, Integer Gaussian, scale=41.96 95% accuracy=83.0 threshold=225
The release shows a product only if its noisy count is 225 or more, and a released count has a 95% error bar of 83. Never publish how many products were left out, or which, because both come from the private data. A product just below the threshold gets in when its noise is positive. So treat a count near 225 as a sign of popularity, not as a measurement.
In OpenDP 0.16.0, truncate_num_groups should bound the groups per customer, but it does not work. With the default keep="sample", summarize accepts the query, but release fails after it spends the share of the query. So run each query end to end on public data first. With keep="first", it keeps one group fewer than asked, and this biases the counts. The filters above avoid both problems only because \(L_\infty = 1\) makes groups into lines. For \(L_\infty > 1\), this book knows of no unbiased group bound in this version.

text:
30.9 Check the release before publishing
To make sure that the code does what the plan says, the script compares the private values with the true values after the same truncation and clipping.
true lines after truncation: 219,291 (all purchase lines: 397,884)
true revenue after truncation and clipping: 4,318,947 (all lines, unclipped: 8,911,408)
true median line value after truncation: 15.00 (all lines: 11.80)
The release is random, and one run printed the following.
released (one run):
  lines 218,972  revenue 4,397,410  median 14.50
  United Kingdom: lines 196,311  revenue 3,927,959
  Germany: lines 7,151  revenue 643,094
  Spain: lines -546  revenue -37,048
  country line counts within their 95% accuracy: 34 of 38
  products released: 63
Compare it with the error bars, which must hold about 95% of the market counts. Negative values are noise on small markets, and you can round them up to zero, because post-processing costs no budget. Expect more than the 50 products whose true count is above the threshold, for the reason above. Compare the private median with the truncated £15.00, not with the £11.80 of all lines.
The check fails if a value is far outside its error bar, which shows a wrong sensitivity. It also fails if far more or far fewer than 95% of the cells are inside. And it fails if the true count of a released product is far below the threshold. In production you cannot compare with the truth, because a decision to publish that uses the true values is a release of them. So run this check on historical or public data during development. Then release the real data once, with the code that you checked.

30.10 Write the guarantee down
The script prints the claim from the variables that set the bounds and the budget, so the claim always agrees with the code.
This release satisfies (epsilon = 1, delta = 1e-05)-differential privacy for adding or
removing one customer and all their invoice lines, with at most 100 lines per customer
(sampled at random), at most 50 random products per customer in the product counts, and
line values clipped to [0, 200] pounds, under the central model, using OpenDP 0.16.0 with
Gaussian noise (accounted as 0.0284-zCDP plus 5e-06 for thresholds, converted to epsilon
and delta). The market list was fixed in advance; the product list is not public.
The statement names all that a reviewer needs to compute the claim again (Writing the guarantee down). Next to it, say what it does not cover. Another release about the same customers adds its own budget to the claim. If that release is pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP, you can add the two \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pairs. Or you can add its \(\rho = \varepsilon^2/2\) to this release’s \(\rho\) and then convert. Use the smaller total (Concentrated differential privacy). Also, the dashboard must say that the figures describe truncated data. Release and governance maps such a claim to data-protection law.

title: Privacy accounting
text:
A model trained with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) under differential privacy (DP), the method called DP-SGD, takes thousands of noisy steps. Yet you report one guarantee for the run, a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) with a small slack \(\delta\). The composition theorems of Part 3 are far too loose for that. An accountant does better, because it keeps a summary of the cost of each step that composes tightly. It converts the total to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) once, at the end.
The running example is a DP-SGD run of 10,000 steps. Each step samples every record with probability 0.01 and adds noise with multiplier 1. At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), advanced composition certifies \(\varepsilon = 24{,}379.55\), while the privacy loss distribution accountant of Google’s dp_accounting certifies 6.19. So an \(\varepsilon\) means nothing until you name its accountant, with the sampler and the neighbouring relation that the accountant assumed.
The part starts with two jobs. Choosing an accountant says which accountant fits a mechanism and how to check that it matches the code. Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run turns a target \(\varepsilon\) into a noise multiplier for the Adult run of Part 5.
Two full chapters explain what those jobs rely on. Amplification by subsampling shows how much a random batch helps, if the data loader samples as the accountant assumes. Rényi differential privacy defines the curve most libraries track.
Short reference pages follow. Three finish the DP-SGD story: the conversion from Rényi DP, numerical accounting, and Gaussian DP, which reads a guarantee as a limit on attacks. Then come adaptive composition for budgets decided during training, concentrated DP for analytics ledgers, and shuffling and iteration.
Every number comes from code you can run with Opacus or dp_accounting. By the end, you will be able to calibrate a DP-SGD run, account for it with two libraries, and report \(\varepsilon\) so that others can reproduce it.

title: 31  Choosing an accountant
text:
31.1 Why this matters
You report a model trained with differential privacy (DP) with a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and a small slack \(\delta\). The code that computes \(\varepsilon\) is an accountant, and the same run can get 6.24 from one accountant and 24,379.55 from another. Table 31.1 runs three accountants on one run of private stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD. They are advanced composition, Rényi differential privacy (RDP) and the privacy loss distribution (PLD). Each record joins each batch with probability \(q = 0.01\), the sampling rate. The noise multiplier \(\sigma\), the noise as a multiple of the clipping norm, is 1.
The true \(\varepsilon\) lies between the two PLD columns, because the lower PLD column is a lower bound. Advanced composition, which adds up the guarantees of the steps, is useless here. RDP is much closer, but it still overstates \(\varepsilon\), by 14.6% on the shorter run and by 7.6% on the longer one. This gives the rule of the chapter. Report the tightest upper bound whose assumptions hold for the code you ran, and give enough detail that someone else can recompute it.

31.2 Which accountant
An accountant is tight only when its summary of each step fits the mechanism. So let the mechanism choose the accountant (Table 31.2).

Mechanism

The GDP CLT is an approximation, not a bound. After 1,000 steps it gives 1.6177, which is below the certified lower value of the PLD, 1.8232. So it claims a guarantee that the run does not have. Opacus’s "gdp" accountant is this CLT, so do not report it. The default PRV accountant of Opacus is safe.

title: 31  Choosing an accountant
section: 31.3 The inverse problem: noise for a target ε
text:
31.3 The inverse problem: noise for a target ε
Usually you fix the target \(\varepsilon\), the batch size and the number of epochs, and you ask for the smallest \(\sigma\) that meets them. A looser accountant overstates \(\varepsilon\), so it asks for more noise. For a target of 3 on the 10,000-step run, RDP needs a noise multiplier of 1.662 and the PLD only 1.584. So calibrate with the accountant that you will report. Opacus’s get_noise_multiplier uses "rdp" by default, so give it accountant="prv" (Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run).

title: 31  Choosing an accountant
text:
31.4 Choosing δ
Choose \(\delta\) by the rule of this book, which for \(n\) people is at most \(1/n^{1.1}\), rounded down to a power of ten (How small δ must be). Count \(n\) in the unit that the claim protects, which at the user level means users, not records. For example, run the 10,000 steps of Table 31.1 on 50,000 records. At \(q = 0.01\), that is 100 epochs. For 50,000 records the rule gives \(10^{-6}\), so the \(10^{-5}\) of the table fails it. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) recommends the stricter \(1/n^2\), so report \(\varepsilon\) there too.
Publish the upper value of the accountant that you name, rounded up, because the accountant does not certify a lower value. Write the statement shows the full privacy statement that carries these numbers.

title: 31  Choosing an accountant
section: 31.5 Matching the accountant to the code

31.5 Matching the accountant to the code
The number of an accountant holds only if the code does what its theorem assumes. Many papers reported the number for Poisson sampling but trained with shuffled batches of fixed size, a different algorithm (Ponomareva et al. 2023). So check the code against Table 31.3 before you report.

The sampler has the largest effect. Under Poisson sampling, the PLD of dp_accounting gives 6.19 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), but batches of fixed size raise this to 43.37. Shuffle and partition raise it to 91.82, and that number holds only for zero-out neighbours (Subsampling).
A review of someone else’s claim also uses this checklist, in the order that Review someone else’s claim gives.

title: 31  Choosing an accountant
text:
31.6 Checking an accountant
An accountant is code, so test it on known answers. With sampling rate \(q = 1\), each step is a plain Gaussian mechanism, and the composition of such steps is exact (f-DP and Gaussian DP). Ten such steps at noise multiplier 1 are exactly \((17.8566, 10^{-5})\)-DP. So an upper bound must be above 17.8566, and a PLD bracket must contain it. Also, \(\varepsilon\) must not decrease when you add steps, and it must not increase when you add noise.
Then compare two maintained libraries at pinned versions. This snippet recomputes Table 31.1 with Google’s dp_accounting.
import dp_accounting
from dp_accounting.pld import PLDAccountant
from dp_accounting.rdp import RdpAccountant

step = dp_accounting.PoissonSampledDpEvent(0.01, dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(1.0))
run = dp_accounting.SelfComposedDpEvent(step, 10_000)  # q = 0.01, sigma = 1, 10,000 steps
pld = PLDAccountant(value_discretization_interval=1e-4).compose(run)
rdp = RdpAccountant(orders=list(range(2, 65))).compose(run)  # integer orders only
print(f"{pld.get_epsilon(1e-5):.4f} {rdp.get_epsilon(1e-5):.4f}")  # 6.1877 6.7194
print(f"{pld.get_epsilon(1e-6):.4f} {rdp.get_epsilon(1e-6):.4f}")  # 6.9074 7.4869
Each PLD value is inside the bracket of the table. Each RDP value is just above the value in the table, because the table also tries fractional orders. When libraries disagree, look for three causes. If two RDP values differ by an amount that depends only on the order, such as 0.3612 at order 10, the libraries use different conversions (RDP conversions). If two PLD brackets do not overlap, one library has a bug. A factor of two often comes from different neighbouring relations.

title: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
text:
32.1 Why this matters
An accountant turns the settings of a training run into its privacy level \(\varepsilon\) under differential privacy (DP). Before the run, it finds the noise for your target, and after it, the \(\varepsilon\) the run spent. Both jobs can fail without a sign. The noise may come from one accountant and the report from another. The loader may not sample as the accountant assumes, or a restart may reset the step count. Each makes the claim false, and none changes the loss curve.
This chapter does the accounting for a run of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with DP, called DP-SGD, on the Adult census data from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. It trains nothing. The run uses 30,000 people in batches of 1,000 for ten epochs, with a target of \(\varepsilon = 4\). Train a model with DP-SGD trains it.
The script practitioner_calibrate.py runs the seven steps below in one to two minutes, with Opacus 1.6.0 and dp-accounting 0.6.0. Its defaults give the run of Part 5. Options such as --n, --batch, --epochs and --epsilon set your own, as the second command does for MNIST.

title: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
section: 32.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
text:
32.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
The guarantee protects exactly one record, so first decide what a record is. In Adult, each row is one person. If one person could own many rows, \(n\), the number of records, would have to count people, as in User-level differential privacy.
The slack \(\delta\) is roughly the chance that the guarantee fails. Set it by the rule of this book, at most \(1/n^{1.1}\) rounded down to a power of ten (How small δ must be).
def delta_for(n: int) -> float:
    """The book's default delta: at most 1/n^1.1, rounded down to a power of ten."""
    return 10.0 ** math.floor(math.log10(n**-1.1))
Adult rows: 48,842; Part 5's training split: n=30,000
delta_for(30,000) = 1e-05
delta_for(60,000) = 1e-06
delta_for(569) = 1e-04
Here \(n\) counts the people of the training split, not all the rows of Adult. So \(\delta\) is \(10^{-5}\). Set the validation rows aside first, because the run neither trains on them nor protects them. The other two lines show that each dataset needs its own \(\delta\).
crumbs: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run

title: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
text:
32.3 Choose the sampler
The accountants here assume Poisson sampling, in which each record joins each batch independently with probability \(q\), the sampling rate. So the batches vary in size. Other samplers cost far more privacy (Section 32.6). With an expected batch size \(B\), the rate is \(q = B/n\). A run of \(E\) epochs then takes \(E/q\) steps, rounded down, which the output calls \(T\).
Poisson: B=1000, E=10: q=0.033333, T=300
Opacus DPDataLoader.from_data_loader: q=1/30=0.033333, 30 steps an epoch, 300 in 10 epochs
chosen run uses the loader's q and steps; get_noise_multiplier at that q counts int(E/q)=300: equal True
The second line is what training will run, because Opacus replaces your loader with a Poisson DPDataLoader. The rate of that loader is one over the number of batches of your loader, \(\lceil n/B \rceil\), and it takes that many steps per epoch. Here \(B\) divides \(n\), so the two lines agree. When it does not, training runs the numbers of the loader, so the script takes \(q\) and \(T\) from it. The third line checks that the calibration of Opacus counts the same steps.
This step goes wrong if the training code builds its own loader with shuffle=True and a fixed batch_size. Then all batches in the logs have the same size (Amplification by subsampling).

title: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
crumbs: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run

title: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
section: 32.5 Check ε with a second accountant
text:
32.5 Check ε with a second accountant
Train with the calibrated \(\sigma\) unrounded, as Part 5 does with the 0.9729 of Opacus. If you round it, round up to the three decimals that the statement prints, because less noise gives a larger \(\varepsilon\). Before you train, compute the \(\varepsilon\) of the planned run with every accountant at hand.
def crosscheck_epsilon(sigma: float, q: float, steps: int, delta: float) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Epsilon of one planned run by five accountants (GDP is the trap: it is not an upper bound)."""
    epsilons: dict[str, float] = {}
    for name, opacus_accountant in [("Opacus RDP", RDPAccountant()), ("Opacus PRV", PRVAccountant())]:
        opacus_accountant.history = [(sigma, q, steps)]  # what `steps` calls of .step() would record
        epsilons[name] = opacus_accountant.get_epsilon(delta)
    run = SelfComposedDpEvent(PoissonSampledDpEvent(q, GaussianDpEvent(sigma)), steps)
    epsilons["dp_accounting RDP"] = RdpAccountant().compose(run).get_epsilon(delta)
    epsilons["dp_accounting PLD"] = PLDAccountant().compose(run).get_epsilon(delta)
    gdp = GaussianAccountant()
    gdp.history = [(sigma, q, steps)]
    epsilons["Opacus GDP"] = gdp.get_epsilon(delta)
    return epsilons
chosen cell: Adult, B=1000, E=10, eps=4: sigma=0.972900 (Opacus PRV, as Part 5)
Opacus RDP         eps=4.50
Opacus PRV         eps=3.99
dp_accounting RDP  eps=4.50
dp_accounting PLD  eps=3.98
Opacus GDP         eps=3.34
PLD <= target: True; RDP >= PLD: True; |PRV - PLD|/PLD < 3%: True
crosscheck: pass
PLD bracket (grid 1e-4): lower 3.9656 (optimistic), upper 3.9806 (pessimistic); width 0.0150
The two tight accountants, PRV and the PLD, agree at 3.99 and 3.98, and both meet the target. The two RDP accountants agree at 4.50, above the target, as a looser bound should be. The trap is the Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) value of 3.34. It comes from a central limit theorem (CLT), which approximates the run but does not bound it, and it is below the certified values. So do not report it.
The pass line makes three checks. The PLD value must be at most the target, which fails if \(\sigma\) was rounded down or the steps differ from the plan. RDP must be at or above the PLD, up to the grid error, and PRV must agree with the PLD within 3%. If one of these two fails, the accountants got different runs.
The last line is the error bar of the PLD. Rounding the privacy loss of each step up to the grid gives the reported 3.9806, and rounding it down gives an optimistic 3.9656. So the true \(\varepsilon\) is between the two. Claim the upper value, with the lower value as its error bar (Which accountant). The bracket gets wider with more steps, so a long run needs a finer grid.
crumbs: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run

title: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
section: 32.6 If the loader is not Poisson
text:
32.6 If the loader is not Poisson
Not every training loop uses Poisson sampling, with its batches of random size, so find the cost of the others before you train. The script accounts the chosen run under the four samplers of Amplification by subsampling.
Poisson (PLD)                              eps=3.98
fixed size, add/remove, sigma/2 (PLD)      eps=23.03
fixed size, replace-one (RDP)              eps=52.60
shuffle, zero-out, no amplification (PLD)  eps=18.51
PLDAccountant supports sampling without replacement: add/remove False, replace-one False
Random batches of fixed size cost more, because a record that joins a full batch pushes another out. So the clipped sum can move by twice the clipping norm \(C\). Under add/remove neighbours, the Poisson accountant at \(\sigma/2\) covers them, which turns 3.98 into 23.03. Under replace-one neighbours, only RDP can account them, also at \(\sigma/2\) (last line). Its 52.60 protects the value of a record, not its presence, so it is not comparable with the add/remove values.
A loader that shuffles once per epoch and cuts the data into batches gets no amplification. All that is certain is one Gaussian step per epoch, 18.51 here. It holds for zero-out neighbours, in which one gradient becomes zero, so the statement must name that relation. A sum then moves by at most \(C\), as under add/remove, so the value is comparable with the add/remove values. It beats fixed-size batches here, but the order reverses on the 100-epoch run of Matching the accountant to the code. So the fix for a loader that is not Poisson is to keep the Poisson loader of Opacus’s make_private.
crumbs: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run

title: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
text:
32.7 Train, stop early and resume
During training, the optimizer of Opacus calls accountant.step once per noisy update. That is once per logical batch, even when BatchMemoryManager splits it into smaller physical batches. The script simulates the 300 calls and asks for \(\varepsilon\) after each epoch.
def train_epochs(
    accountant: PRVAccountant, sigma: float, q: float, steps_per_epoch: int, epochs: int, delta: float
) -> list[float]:
    """Step the accountant once per logical batch for `epochs` epochs; epsilon at the end of each epoch."""
    epsilons: list[float] = []
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for _ in range(steps_per_epoch):
            accountant.step(noise_multiplier=sigma, sample_rate=q)  # what the optimizer's step does
        epsilons.append(float(accountant.get_epsilon(delta)))
    return epsilons
Suppose that the validation loss stalls and the run stops after six of its ten epochs. An early stop is safe, because the planned guarantee covers each prefix of the planned run. But report the planned maximum, because the decision to stop depended on what the run released. So the \(\varepsilon\) at the stop is not a valid claim, and only a privacy filter that runs from the first step could certify it (Adaptive composition). Still log \(\varepsilon\) every epoch. It must never decrease, so a drop shows that something reset the accountant.
Training past the maximum is not safe. If you add epochs after you see the model, the number of steps depends on what the run released. So the longer run needs a new plan, accounted from the first step. Plan the longest run that you might want, and treat a shorter run as an early stop.
A job that stops and restarts must keep its accountant. Save the state_dict of the accountant with the model, and load it before the first new step. Opacus’s PrivacyEngine.save_checkpoint and load_checkpoint do this.
state = accountant.state_dict()  # saved with the model; PrivacyEngine.save_checkpoint stores it too
# ... the job stops, and later restarts ...
restarted = PRVAccountant()
restarted.load_state_dict(state)  # without this, epsilon would restart from zero
resumed = train_epochs(restarted, sigma, q, steps_per_epoch, epochs - stop, delta)
steps_recorded = sum(steps for _, _, steps in restarted.history)
steps per epoch: 30; planned: 10 epochs = 300 steps
epoch  1: eps=1.70
epoch  2: eps=2.09
epoch  4: eps=2.69
epoch  6: eps=3.18
epsilon never decreases over 10 epochs: True
stopped early at epoch 6: eps=3.18; report the planned maximum: eps=3.99
after resuming at epoch 6: eps at epoch 10=3.99; uninterrupted run: eps=3.99; equal: True
steps recorded: 300; planned (the loader's 10 x 30): 300; equal: True
The resumed run ends at 3.99, like a run that never stopped, with all 300 steps in its history. A fresh accountant would have counted only the last four epochs and reported 2.69.

title: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
text:
32.8 Write the statement
The last step writes the claim with every input that a reviewer needs to recompute it. The script fills the template from the run. It rounds up the PLD’s \(\varepsilon\) at two values of the slack, the rule’s \(\delta\) and \(1/n^2\), where \(n\) is still the number of training records.
def privacy_statement(
    unit: str, dataset: str, n: int, batch: int, epochs: int, sigma: float, clip: float, delta: float, calibration: str
) -> str:
    """The filled template of the reporting page: every input a reviewer needs to recompute epsilon."""
    q, _, steps = opacus_loader_plan(n, batch, epochs)  # the steps the Poisson loader runs
    run = SelfComposedDpEvent(PoissonSampledDpEvent(q, GaussianDpEvent(sigma)), steps)
    epsilon = round_up(PLDAccountant().compose(run).get_epsilon(delta))
    epsilon_tiny_delta = round_up(PLDAccountant().compose(run).get_epsilon(1 / n**2))
    return f"""\
Unit: one {unit} (a row of {dataset}); neighbouring datasets differ by adding or removing one {unit}
Data: n = {n:,}; Poisson sampling with q = {q:.6f} (B = {batch}); T = {steps:,} steps ({epochs} epochs)
Mechanism: DP-SGD, clipping norm C = {clip}, noise multiplier sigma = {sigma:.3f}
Accountant: PLD, dp-accounting {version("dp-accounting")}; {calibration}
Guarantee: (epsilon = {epsilon:.2f}, delta = {delta:.0e}); epsilon = {epsilon_tiny_delta:.2f} at delta = 1/n^2 = {1 / n**2:.1e}
Not covered: hyperparameter tuning runs (see Part 5), and any model released before this one"""
Unit: one person (a row of Adult); neighbouring datasets differ by adding or removing one person
Data: n = 30,000; Poisson sampling with q = 0.033333 (B = 1000); T = 300 steps (10 epochs)
Mechanism: DP-SGD, clipping norm C = 1.0, noise multiplier sigma = 0.973
Accountant: PLD, dp-accounting 0.6.0; calibrated with Opacus 1.6.0 (PRV)
Guarantee: (epsilon = 3.99, delta = 1e-05); epsilon = 6.30 at delta = 1/n^2 = 1.1e-09
Not covered: hyperparameter tuning runs (see Part 5), and any model released before this one
The guarantee reads 3.99 because the script rounds the PLD value up, while the cross-check above printed it to the nearest value, 3.98. The unit, the dataset and the clipping norm come from options, because the accountant never sees them. The last line matters most to a reviewer, because it names privacy spent outside this \(\varepsilon\). Examples are tuning on the private data (Hyperparameter tuning) and earlier models trained on the same people.
A published statement also gives what the script cannot know (Write the statement). That is the setting, the grid and bracket of the PLD, and the data outside the run, such as pretrained weights and the unprotected validation rows.

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.1 Why this matters
Most private training uses stochastic gradient descent (SGD) made to satisfy differential privacy (DP), a method called DP-SGD. Each step clips every record’s gradient to a maximum length, the clipping norm, sums the clipped gradients and adds Gaussian noise. The noise’s standard deviation is the clipping norm times the noise multiplier \(\sigma\). Suppose every record paid the cost of a full Gaussian step each time. Then ten thousand steps at \(\sigma = 1\) would cost a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) of 5425.5 at a slack \(\delta\) of \(10^{-5}\), no guarantee at all (Rényi DP).
DP-SGD avoids this cost because each step uses only a small random batch. Write \(q\) for the sampling rate, the probability that a given record is in the batch. An attacker must then first guess whether the step used the record at all, and that doubt is worth a lot. This amplification by subsampling depends on how the batch was drawn. So the accountant, the code that adds up a run’s privacy cost, must assume the sampler that the training code runs. A wrong sampler is the largest single error in DP-SGD accounting, far larger than the choice of accountant (Section 33.4).

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.2 One step under Poisson sampling
The simplest sampler is Poisson sampling: each record enters the batch by its own coin flip, with probability \(q\), independently of every other record. It goes with add/remove neighbours, two datasets of which one has an extra record. For this pair, Balle, Barthe and Gaboardi (2018) give the best possible one-step result. Suppose a step is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP when it uses every record, where \(\delta\) is the small slack of Part 3. Then the same step on a Poisson sample is \((\varepsilon', \delta')\)-DP with \[\varepsilon' = \ln\big(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\big), \qquad \delta' = q\delta. \tag{33.1}\]
Small and large \(\varepsilon\) behave very differently. For small \(\varepsilon\) the amplified cost is about \(q\varepsilon\). So a 1% sample makes a step about a hundred times cheaper, and a 1-DP step costs 0.0170. For large \(\varepsilon\) the amplified cost is about \[\varepsilon' \approx \varepsilon - \ln(1/q), \tag{33.2}\] so sampling only subtracts a fixed amount, and a 10-DP step on the same sample still costs 5.3993. The change happens where \(\varepsilon\) is near \(\ln(1/q)\). So amplification helps most when each step is already fairly private, which is why DP-SGD takes many cheap steps.
The result has two conditions. First, each record’s coin must be independent of the others, so that every record is drawn with probability exactly \(q\), whatever else is in the batch. Second, the batch must stay secret, because an attacker who reads the list of drawn records, for example in a log, knows whether the step used the target.

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
section: 33.3 Match the sampler to the accountant
text:
33.3 Match the sampler to the accountant
Most training code does not draw Poisson batches. Some draws a new random batch of a fixed size \(B\) from the \(n\) records at each step. More often, it shuffles the data once per epoch and cuts it into consecutive batches, which is shuffle and partition.
Each sampler needs its own accounting under each neighbouring relation. Besides add/remove, two relations are in use. Under replace-one, the two datasets have the same size and differ in one record’s value, and under zero-out, the target’s gradient becomes zero. Table 33.1 gives DP-SGD’s accounting for each case as events of Google’s dp_accounting library, which a Rényi differential privacy (RDP) or privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant then composes.



Table 33.1: What to account for under each sampler and neighbouring relation in DP-SGD.











Sampler
Neighbours
What to account for

The same event, at \(\sigma\), in a PLD accountant built with NeighboringRelation.REPLACE_ONE, which models the swap itself

The factor of two for fixed-size batches comes from the gradient sum. Under Poisson sampling, to add or remove a record moves the clipped sum by at most the clipping norm. A fixed-size batch has no space for an extra record. So a drawn record takes the place of another, and the sum can move twice as far (Lebeda et al. 2025). Twice the shift with the same noise is the same as the original shift with half the noise multiplier. Replace-one swaps a record by definition, so its shift doubles too, and for it only the RDP accountant of dp_accounting covers fixed-size batches.
Shuffle and partition is worse, because it has no source of amplification. In an epoch the record is in exactly one batch and is never absent, so the attacker only has to find which batch held it. Chua et al. (2024) build a dataset in which the target’s gradient points against all the others, so that its batch stands out. There, at \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\), one shuffled epoch provably has an \(\varepsilon\) of at least 4.06, but a Poisson accountant reports at most 1.21. The honest bound is the table’s last row, one full Gaussian release per epoch, because each epoch uses the record exactly once.
So read the data loader before you trust a reported \(\varepsilon\). A PyTorch DataLoader with shuffle=True and a batch_size is shuffle and partition. Opacus replaces the loader with a Poisson one by default, because PrivacyEngine.make_private sets poisson_sampling=True unless you turn it off. Its batch_sampler is then a UniformWithReplacementSampler, which flips one coin per record despite its name. So batch sizes change from step to step, which you can check in the training log. If you cannot use Poisson sampling, report under the matching row of Table 33.1. Name the sampler next to \(\varepsilon\).

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.4 Accounting each sampler
Never account DP-SGD step by step with Equation 33.1. That route gives each step a tiny share of \(\delta\), and a tiny \(\delta\) forces a large per-step \(\varepsilon\), which sampling barely reduces, as for the 10-DP step above. On 10,000 steps, advanced composition then gives 24379.55, worse even than 5425.5 without sampling. An RDP accountant instead adds the steps’ Rényi curves order by order and converts the total to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) once, which gives 6.71 (Rényi DP). A PLD accountant is tighter still (Numerical accounting).
The snippet below accounts that run under four rows of Table 33.1, with 50,000 records in batches of 500, so \(q = 0.01\). It uses \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) to compare with the rest of the part, not the smaller \(\delta\) of a report (How small δ must be).
from dp_accounting import GaussianDpEvent, NeighboringRelation, PoissonSampledDpEvent
from dp_accounting import SampledWithoutReplacementDpEvent, SelfComposedDpEvent
from dp_accounting.pld import PLDAccountant
from dp_accounting.rdp import RdpAccountant

n, batch, sigma, steps, delta = 50_000, 500, 1.0, 10_000, 1e-5  # q = 0.01, 100 epochs
poisson = SelfComposedDpEvent(PoissonSampledDpEvent(batch / n, GaussianDpEvent(sigma)), steps)
fixed_size = SelfComposedDpEvent(PoissonSampledDpEvent(batch / n, GaussianDpEvent(sigma / 2)), steps)  # add/remove
shuffled = SelfComposedDpEvent(GaussianDpEvent(sigma), 100)  # one Gaussian release per epoch, no amplification
pld = [PLDAccountant(value_discretization_interval=1e-3).compose(e) for e in (poisson, fixed_size, shuffled)]  # 1e-3: the PLD's grid spacing
print(" ".join(f"{accountant.get_epsilon(delta):.2f}" for accountant in pld))  # 6.19 43.37 91.82
replace_one = RdpAccountant(neighboring_relation=NeighboringRelation.REPLACE_ONE)
swap = SampledWithoutReplacementDpEvent(n, batch, GaussianDpEvent(sigma / 2))  # replace-one: the sum moves by up to 2C
replace_one.compose(SelfComposedDpEvent(swap, steps))
print(f"{replace_one.get_epsilon(delta):.2f}")  # 118.73
Poisson sampling costs 6.19. With the same noise, fixed-size batches cost 43.37 under add/remove neighbours, about seven times more, and shuffling costs 91.82 under zero-out. The replace-one value, 118.73, protects a record’s value, not its presence, so compare it only with other replace-one numbers. Thus the sampler changes \(\varepsilon\) sevenfold or more, while the accountant changes it by less than 10%, from 6.71 by RDP to 6.19 by PLD.
Before you compose an unusual event, check it with PLDAccountant().supports(event), which returns False for a SampledWithoutReplacementDpEvent, for example.

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.5 Batch size, epochs and noise
Amplification also changes how you plan a run. Write \(E\) for the number of epochs, so that a run takes \(E/q\) steps at sampling rate \(q\). For small \(q\) and a large noise multiplier, the run’s Rényi curve, its cost at each order \(\alpha\), is then roughly \[\varepsilon(\alpha) \approx \frac{E\,q\,\alpha}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{33.3}\] So at a fixed number of epochs a smaller sampling rate costs less privacy, because each step costs about \(q^2\) while the number of steps grows only as \(1/q\). Use this only to plan, never as the reported number, because at high orders the true curve rises far above it (from about order 9 at \(\sigma = 1\) and \(q = 0.01\)).
Privacy is not the only cost, because the noise also changes the averaged gradient. With \(C\) for the clipping norm, the noise on the average of \(B\) records has standard deviation \(\sigma C/B\). So compare plans by \(\sigma/B\), not by \(\sigma\). At the same \(\varepsilon\), a ten times larger batch needs a larger \(\sigma\), but its \(\sigma/B\) is six times smaller (Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run).
So plan in this order. First fix the batch size \(B\) and the epochs \(E\) that your accuracy needs. They set \(q = B/n\) and the number of steps, where \(n\) is the size of the dataset you actually train on, after any filters. Then let the accountant find \(\sigma\). Name the numerical accountant in the Opacus call get_noise_multiplier, because its default is RDP (Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run).

Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 34  Rényi differential privacy
text:
34.1 Why this matters
Training a model runs thousands of private steps, but you report one differential privacy (DP) guarantee for all of them, a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) with a small slack \(\delta\). The advanced composition of Part 3 adds up the pairs of the steps, and the result is far too pessimistic (Composition). Take 1000 steps of full-batch noisy gradient descent, each with Gaussian noise whose standard deviation is 20 times the most one record can move the gradient. At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), advanced composition gives \(\varepsilon = 68.01\), nine times the exact 7.51. So a run calibrated to it adds more noise than it needs.
Rényi differential privacy (RDP) fixes this, because it keeps a whole curve of privacy costs for each step instead of one point. The curves of the steps add, with no \(\delta\) spent along the way, and you convert the total into \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) once, at the end. Even with Mironov’s original conversion (Section 34.6), the same run then costs 8.84, only 18% above the exact value. Opacus and Google’s dp_accounting both have an RDP accountant.

title: 34  Rényi differential privacy
text:
34.2 The RDP curve
A DP guarantee compares the outputs of a mechanism on two neighbouring datasets, which differ in one person’s record. RDP measures the distance between those two output distributions with the Rényi divergence of Divergences. That divergence has a dial, the order \(\alpha\), which is any number above 1. A small order looks at the typical output. A large order gives more weight to the rare outputs that are much more likely on one dataset than on the other.
A mechanism is \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP if, at order \(\alpha\), the divergence is at most \(\varepsilon\) for every pair of neighbours. The smallest such \(\varepsilon\) at each order gives the RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) of the mechanism, and a higher curve means less privacy. The curve never decreases with the order. At order infinity, it is the largest privacy loss of any output, which is what pure DP, the case \(\delta = 0\), bounds. You never compute the divergence yourself, because accountants know the curves of the standard mechanisms on a grid of orders.

title: 34  Rényi differential privacy
section: 34.3 RDP curves of the basic mechanisms
text:
34.3 RDP curves of the basic mechanisms
To account for a mechanism, you need its curve, and the basic mechanisms have one in closed form (Mironov 2017). For the Gaussian mechanism, write \(\sigma\) for its noise multiplier. That is the standard deviation of the noise in units of the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, the most one record can move the answer. Its curve is the straight line \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{34.1}\] Table 34.1 gives the curves of the Gaussian, Laplace and randomized-response mechanisms at a few orders, each at sensitivity 1.



Table 34.1: RDP curves of the three basic mechanisms with sensitivity 1.

The Laplace and randomized-response curves level off at their pure DP level. The Gaussian curve has no limit, so the Gaussian mechanism is not \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any \(\varepsilon\). But an accountant converts only at finite orders, where the curve is finite. These curves are for steps on the whole dataset. The private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD, runs each step on a random batch, and libraries compute its much smaller curves for you (Amplification by subsampling).

title: 34  Rényi differential privacy
text:
34.4 Composition adds curves
Training runs thousands of mechanisms in sequence, and each may depend on what the earlier ones released, as a gradient step depends on the current model. RDP composes these mechanisms by adding their curves, order by order. Write \(\varepsilon_i\) for the curve of the \(i\)-th step. Then a whole run of \(k\) steps has a curve \(\varepsilon_M\) with \[\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le \sum_{i=1}^k \varepsilon_i(\alpha) \qquad\text{for every order } \alpha. \tag{34.2}\] Different mechanisms mix freely, because you only add numbers at the same order.
Two conditions come with the sum. First, every curve must describe the same neighbouring relation, such as add/remove or replace-one, and the same unit of privacy, such as one record or one user. Second, the curve of each step must be fixed before the run. Steps may adapt to earlier outputs, but if the data choose the noise level or the number of steps, the curves depend on the data too. An early stop when a validation metric looks good is such a choice, and it needs Adaptive composition instead.
The sum is simplest for Gaussian steps, because their curve is the straight line \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\). Adding \(k\) such lines multiplies the slope by \(k\), which gives the line of one step with noise multiplier \(\sigma/\sqrt k\). So \(k\) Gaussian steps cost as much privacy as one step with \(\sqrt k\) times less noise, which is bad news for training. If 10,000 steps with noise multiplier 1 each used the whole dataset, they would cost as much as one step with noise multiplier \(1/\sqrt{10{,}000} = 0.01\), whose \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) is 5425.5, no guarantee at all. DP-SGD escapes this by running each step on a small random sample. This part’s running example is such a run: 10,000 steps with noise multiplier 1, each on a random 1% of the data.

title: 34  Rényi differential privacy
text:
34.5 Post-processing and group privacy
Post-processing is free in RDP, because a computation on the output that does not look at the data again cannot make the curve larger. So the release of the trained model or its predictions costs nothing beyond the training run.
Groups of records are harder, and the generic group rule of RDP is loose. So when one user gives \(m\) records and the noise is Gaussian, use the sensitivity of the group instead, which is at most \(m\) times that of one record. The curve becomes \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{group}}(\alpha) = \frac{m^2\alpha}{2\sigma^2}, \tag{34.3}\] which is \(m^2\) times the curve of one record, so ten records per user cost a hundred times as much. The fix is to clip the whole contribution of each user to one clipping norm and to account per user (User-level privacy).

title: 34  Rényi differential privacy
text:
34.6 Compose, then convert once
After composition, you have a curve, but you report an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair. Both libraries turn the curve into a pair with the improved conversion (Balle et al. 2020, and independently Canonne, Kamath and Steinke 2020). From the value \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) of the curve at one order and a target \(\delta\), it gives the privacy level \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{34.4}\] Report the smallest \(\varepsilon'\) over the grid of orders, or 0 if that is negative. Libraries call the order that gave it the best order.
Older papers and code use Mironov’s original conversion, which gives 7.43 instead of 6.71 on the DP-SGD running example. The moments accountant of the original DP-SGD paper (Abadi et al. 2016) is the RDP curve with that conversion, so its \(\varepsilon\) is loose but not wrong (From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests).

title: 34  Rényi differential privacy
text:
34.7 Check the order grid
A conversion can use only the orders on the grid of the accountant, so the grid must contain the best order. That order moves with the run, towards 1 for long runs with little noise and up for short runs with much noise. For the noisy gradient descent at the start of the chapter, it falls from 128 after one step to 4 after 1000.
The default grid of Opacus, RDPAccountant.DEFAULT_ALPHAS, stops at order 63, and that of dp_accounting, DEFAULT_RDP_ORDERS, at 1024. A best order at either end of the grid means that the true optimum is outside it, so give a longer list, with alphas=[...] in Opacus or orders=[...] in dp_accounting. Opacus warns you, but dp_accounting does not, so compare the returned order with the ends of the list yourself.

title: 34  Rényi differential privacy
text:
34.8 Accounting with a library
In practice, you describe each step to a library, and it composes and converts. In dp_accounting, a DP-SGD step is a GaussianDpEvent inside a PoissonSampledDpEvent, which samples each record independently, with probability 0.01 in the running example. This snippet composes the 10,000 steps and prints \(\varepsilon\) with the best order.
import dp_accounting

step = dp_accounting.PoissonSampledDpEvent(0.01, dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(1.0))
accountant = dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant()
accountant.compose(step, count=10_000)
eps, order = accountant.get_epsilon_and_optimal_order(1e-5)
print(f"{eps:.4f} {order:g}")  # 6.7128 4.1
In Opacus, the accountant is attached to the optimizer, which calls step after every noisy update. The same calls by hand give the same \(\varepsilon\) to the fourth decimal, at the same order, 4.1, which is well inside both grids.
from opacus.accountants import RDPAccountant

accountant = RDPAccountant()
for _ in range(10_000):  # what the optimizer does at each step of training
    accountant.step(noise_multiplier=1.0, sample_rate=0.01)
eps, order = accountant.get_privacy_spent(delta=1e-5)
print(f"{eps:.4f} {order:g}")  # 6.7127 4.1
Opacus’s defaults mix two accountants, so name the one that you want. In Opacus 1.6.0, PrivacyEngine uses "prv", a numerical accountant, by default, and accountant="rdp" selects this class. But get_noise_multiplier, which solves for the noise multiplier \(\sigma\), uses RDP by default. Both give valid upper bounds, but different ones, and the numerical accountant gives 6.19 for the running example.
Two more checks catch most mistakes. The event must match the sampler of your data loader, because shuffled batches of fixed size get none of the amplification of a Poisson event (Amplification by subsampling). And a manual call to step on top of the optimizer’s own call charges each update twice.
