title: 35  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
35.1 What it is
An accountant that tracks Rényi differential privacy (RDP) ends a run with a curve (Rényi differential privacy). The curve gives a privacy level, written \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), at each order \(\alpha\) above 1. A report needs a differential privacy (DP) guarantee, a privacy level \(\varepsilon'\) with a small slack \(\delta\). A conversion turns each point of the curve into such a pair, and you keep the smallest \(\varepsilon'\).
Two conversions are in use. The original one, Mironov’s conversion (Mironov 2017), gives at each order \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{35.1}\] The improved conversion (Balle et al. 2020) gives \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{35.2}\] Both are valid, but at the same order the improved one is always lower, by 0.3612 at order 10 and more at smaller orders. If the improved value is negative, report 0.
For example, one Gaussian release with noise multiplier 1 has the curve \(\alpha/2\). At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) its exact \(\varepsilon\) is 4.377, Mironov’s conversion gives 5.299 and the improved one 4.729.
crumbs: 35  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests

title: 35  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
35.2 When you meet it
You meet the conversion when you compare RDP numbers from two sources. Opacus 1.6.0 and dp_accounting 0.6.0 use the improved one, and older papers and code use Mironov’s. This part’s running example is 10,000 steps of the private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD, each on a random 1% of the data with noise multiplier 1. There, Mironov’s conversion gives 7.43 and the improved one 6.71.
The saving depends only on the order. So two RDP accountants that report values about 0.36 apart for one run, with a best order near 10, use different conversions. Recompute both with one library before you compare them.
crumbs: 35  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests

title: 35  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
35.3 How to use it
In dp_accounting, get_epsilon_and_optimal_order converts at the best order of the grid and returns both. One curve gives every \(\delta\), so get_epsilon can report several pairs at no extra privacy cost. This snippet converts the single Gaussian release above.
from dp_accounting import GaussianDpEvent
from dp_accounting.rdp import RdpAccountant

accountant = RdpAccountant()
accountant.compose(GaussianDpEvent(1.0))  # one release, noise multiplier 1
eps, order = accountant.get_epsilon_and_optimal_order(1e-5)
print(f"{eps:.4f} {order:g}")  # 4.7285 5.4
print(f"{accountant.get_epsilon(1e-8):.4f}")  # 6.0864
A \(\delta\) a thousand times smaller raises \(\varepsilon\) only from 4.7285 to 6.0864, because \(\delta\) enters the conversion through a logarithm. The best order comes from a fixed grid. Short runs with much noise can need orders above 63, where the Opacus default grid stops. So if the returned order is at an end of the grid, extend the grid and convert again (Rényi differential privacy).
crumbs: 35  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests

title: 35  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
35.4 What goes wrong
No conversion closes the whole gap to the exact value, because the curve is only a summary. Other mechanisms with the same curve have a larger exact \(\varepsilon\), and the conversion must hold for them too. For the plain Gaussian, the improved conversion is 5 to 10% above the exact value, and more for the subsampled steps of DP-SGD. A privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant keeps the whole distribution instead, and gets the exact 4.377 for the single release (Numerical accounting).
The conversion works in one direction only, because a guarantee with \(\delta\) above 0 gives no RDP curve. For example, a mechanism that publishes your record with probability \(\delta\) is \((0, \delta)\)-DP, but its Rényi divergence is infinite. So never put an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair into an RDP accountant. Take the curve from the mechanism instead.
A conversion also loses what the curve says about attacks. Take a membership attack on the single release above, at a false-positive rate of \(10^{-3}\). The curve limits the attack’s true-positive rate to \(2.4910 \times 10^{-2}\). But the pair at \(\varepsilon = 4.729\) limits it only to 0.1131 (f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy).

title: 36  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
36.1 What it is
A privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant computes the privacy level \(\varepsilon\) of a whole differential privacy (DP) run numerically. Take a dataset and a neighbour that differs in one record, and run the mechanism on the first. The privacy loss \(L\) of that run is the logarithm of how much likelier the output is on the first dataset than on the second. The output is random, and the distribution of its loss is the PLD. Only outputs whose loss is more than \(\varepsilon\) add to the slack \(\delta\), so the smallest slack is the following, where \((\cdot)_+\) sets a negative value to 0: \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \mathbb E\big[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\big]. \tag{36.1}\]
When steps draw their noise independently, their losses add, so the PLD of a run is the convolution of the steps’ PLDs. All the error comes from the grid of losses that holds each PLD, with a spacing \(h\) between points. To round every loss up can only make \(\delta\) larger, so the \(\varepsilon\) it gives is an upper bound, the pessimistic side. To round down gives a lower bound, the optimistic side. Each rounding moves a step’s loss by at most \(h\), so after \(T\) steps the two values are at most \(Th\) apart.
crumbs: 36  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions

title: 36  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
36.2 When you meet it
You meet a PLD accountant each time you train with Opacus, whose default "prv" is the privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant of Gopi, Lee and Wutschitz (2021). It rounds each loss to the nearest grid point, adds a proven error bound and reports the upper value. Google’s dp_accounting has PLDAccountant, which by default rounds up with connect the dots, the tightest pessimistic rounding on a grid.
Table 36.1 compares a PLD with Rényi differential privacy (RDP) and with the central limit theorem (CLT) estimate of Gaussian differential privacy (GDP). The run is the part’s example of the private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD, with sampling rate 0.01 and noise multiplier 1.

title: 36  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
36.3 How to use it
In dp_accounting, compose the run as an event and read \(\varepsilon\) at your \(\delta\). The method get_delta goes the other way, from a claimed \(\varepsilon\) to a bound on its \(\delta\).
from dp_accounting import GaussianDpEvent, PoissonSampledDpEvent, SelfComposedDpEvent
from dp_accounting.pld import PLDAccountant
from opacus.accountants import PRVAccountant

run = SelfComposedDpEvent(PoissonSampledDpEvent(0.01, GaussianDpEvent(1.0)), 10_000)
pld = PLDAccountant(value_discretization_interval=1e-4).compose(run)  # h, 10x the table's
print(f"{pld.get_epsilon(1e-5):.4f}")  # 6.1877
print(f"{pld.get_delta(6.24):.1e}")  # 8.5e-06

prv = PRVAccountant()
prv.history = [(1.0, 0.01, 10_000)]  # (noise multiplier, sample rate, steps)
print(f"{prv.get_epsilon(delta=1e-5):.4f}")  # 6.1980
Both answers are upper bounds inside the bracket of Table 36.1, so you can report either. A reviewer can use get_delta to confirm the claim \((6.24, 10^{-5})\), because it bounds the run’s slack at that \(\varepsilon\) by \(8.5\times10^{-6}\).
Each library has one accuracy setting. In dp_accounting it is the grid spacing value_discretization_interval, and a grid ten times finer makes the bracket ten times narrower, for about ten times the memory. In Opacus it is eps_error, the error allowed in \(\varepsilon\). The error grows with the steps, so set either for your longest run.
crumbs: 36  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions

title: 36  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
36.4 What goes wrong
The most frequent mistake is to report the wrong side of the bracket. Only the pessimistic value, or the PRV accountant’s upper value, is a guarantee. The optimistic value and the midpoint are estimates.
Under add/remove neighbours, a subsampled step has one PLD for an added record and another for a removed one, and neither is larger in general. So an accountant must compose both and report the larger, as dp_accounting does by default. The PRV accountant of Opacus models only removal, which is the larger direction in the running example. Both libraries assume Poisson sampling, and shuffled or fixed-size batches break it (Amplification by subsampling).
A run that adapts its steps or noise to the outputs needs a filter instead (Adaptive composition).
crumbs: 36  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions

title: 37  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
37.1 What it is
Every differential privacy (DP) guarantee limits how well an attacker can tell whether the data held a target’s record. That attacker runs a hypothesis test, so the fullest guarantee is a trade-off curve, the lowest false negative rate any test can get at each false positive rate. A mechanism is \(f\)-DP when its curve is never below a given curve \(f\) (Dong, Roth and Su 2022). A privacy level \(\varepsilon\) with its slack \(\delta\) is only a summary of that curve.
For Gaussian noise the curve has one parameter. Write \(\sigma\) for the noise multiplier, the noise’s standard deviation in units of the query’s \(\ell_2\) sensitivity. In those units the attacker must tell a standard normal draw from one shifted by \(\mu = 1/\sigma\). So the mechanism satisfies Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) with parameter \(\mu\), written \(\mu\)-GDP. Write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal distribution function. Then no membership attack at a false positive rate \(\alpha\) gets a true positive rate above \[1 - \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - \mu\big). \tag{37.1}\]
crumbs: 37  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy

title: 37  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
37.2 When you meet it
You meet GDP when you decide whether a guarantee is enough, and as a trap in Opacus (Section 37.4). Table 37.1 reads \(\mu\) as the best true positive rate (TPR) of an attack at a given false positive rate (FPR), whatever else the attacker knows.

For example, at a false positive rate of 1%, no attacker on a 1-GDP release finds the record in more than 9.24% of the trials where it is present. That is the ceiling for any membership inference attack, and the value a privacy audit tests. Dong et al. suggest that \(\mu \le 0.5\) is a reasonable guarantee and that \(\mu \ge 6\) promises almost nothing. So report \(\mu\) next to a Gaussian pipeline’s \((\varepsilon, \delta)\).
crumbs: 37  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy

title: 37  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
37.3 How to use it
Gaussian releases compose exactly in GDP, also when each one depends on the earlier ones. Write \(\mu_i\) for the parameter of the \(i\)-th release. The run is then \(\mu\)-GDP with \[\mu = \sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \mu_2^2 + \dots + \mu_k^2}, \tag{37.2}\] so the quantity that adds up is \(\mu^2\). For releases on the whole dataset, such as analytics queries and full-batch noisy gradient descent, no accountant does better. So keep a ledger of \(\mu^2\) and convert once, at the end. For example, four 1-GDP releases compose to 2-GDP, which is \((9.9973, 10^{-5})\)-DP. If you convert each release first, with a quarter of the slack, the four values of \(\varepsilon\) add to 18.7607, almost twice as much.
The snippet computes the attack ceiling and converts both ways. The dp_accounting functions take a noise multiplier, so for \(\mu\)-GDP you give \(1/\mu\).
from statistics import NormalDist

import dp_accounting

N = NormalDist()


def attack_power(mu: float, fpr: float) -> float:
    """Best true positive rate of any membership attack on mu-GDP at a false positive rate."""
    return 1 - N.cdf(N.inv_cdf(1 - fpr) - mu)


print(" ".join(f"{attack_power(mu, 0.001):.4f}" for mu in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0)))  # 0.0048 0.0183 0.1378
print(f"{dp_accounting.get_epsilon_gaussian(1.0, 1e-5):.4f}")  # 4.3772
print(f"{dp_accounting.get_sigma_gaussian(1.0, 1e-5):.4f}")  # 3.7306
The last print finds the noise multiplier of a single \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP release. It uses the exact curve, which needs less noise than the classical formula of the Gaussian mechanism.
crumbs: 37  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy

title: 37  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
37.4 What goes wrong
Opacus has accountant="gdp" for the private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD. It estimates \(\mu\) with the central limit theorem (CLT) of Bu et al. (2020), which says that many steps that each leak little compose to nearly a Gaussian curve. This estimate is an approximation, not a bound, and its error is on the unsafe side. A small \(\delta\) depends on rare, large losses, and a CLT fits those tails badly. On the part’s running example of 10,000 steps, the CLT gives 6.0071, but a numerical accountant proves that the true \(\varepsilon\) is at least 6.1377. So report with the default numerical accountant of Opacus, "prv".
A mix of Laplace and Gaussian releases needs a numerical accountant, because a curve that is not Gaussian takes the composition out of GDP. But for Gaussian pipelines without subsampling, GDP is the best accountant. Even the best conversion from a Rényi DP curve loses: for 1-GDP at \(\varepsilon = 1\), it gives a \(\delta\) of 0.2149 against the exact 0.1269.
crumbs: 37  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy

title: 38  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
38.1 What it is
The composition theorems of differential privacy (DP) assume that you fix each step’s privacy parameter and the number of steps before the run (Composition). Actual runs often choose them from the outputs, for example when training stops on the validation loss. Then the theorems do not hold for the actual values (Rogers et al. 2016). This plug-in mistake can make the bound fail about three times as often as its \(\delta\) claims.
A privacy filter fixes a total budget in advance and refuses any step that would go past it, so the run keeps the budget’s guarantee for any stopping rule. A privacy odometer, for open-ended analyses, reports the spend so far instead. Its value holds at every step, at a higher \(\varepsilon\).
crumbs: 38  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 38  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
38.2 When you meet it
Early stopping with a planned maximum needs neither. Fix the noise, sampling rate and maximum number of steps in advance, then stop when the validation loss stops falling. Report the \(\varepsilon\) of the planned maximum, not of the steps you ran. The steps you ran are the start of the planned run, so the planned guarantee covers them. If 100 planned full-batch Gaussian steps with noise multiplier 10 are \((5.299, 10^{-5})\)-DP, a run that stops at step 60 reports that.
The rule has three conditions. The stop signal must come from the released models or from held-out data, so that the stop is post-processing. To train past the maximum, make a new plan and account it from the first step. A resumed run must restore its accountant (the calibration workflow).
You meet filters when training changes the noise in response to the outputs, and in analytics services, such as OpenDP’s make_privacy_filter or Tumult Analytics’ Session.
crumbs: 38  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 38  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
38.3 How to use it
The Rényi filter of Feldman and Zrnic (2021) works in Rényi differential privacy (RDP) at one order, written \(\alpha\) and fixed in advance. It charges each step its spend at that order (Rényi DP). The spend can depend on earlier outputs, but the filter must know it before the step runs. The filter refuses a step that would take the total past a budget \(B\). For a target privacy level \(\varepsilon_g\) with slack \(\delta\), use the conversion from RDP in reverse, which sets \[B = \varepsilon_g - \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{38.1}\]
A Gaussian step with a noise multiplier, written \(\sigma\), spends \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\) at order \(\alpha\). At order 5.8, the best order for this target, the budget is \(B = 2.900\), enough for 100 full-batch steps at \(\sigma = 10\). Suppose that the validation loss stops falling at step 60 and you halve the noise. Each later step then costs four times as much, so the budget left for 40 steps pays for 10, and the run still meets the target.
OpenDP’s filter works in zero-concentrated DP (zCDP). Its single budget number, written \(\rho\), bounds the RDP spend at every order at once (Concentrated DP).
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
domain, metric = dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False), dp.absolute_distance(T=float)
odometer = dp.c.make_fully_adaptive_composition(domain, metric, dp.zero_concentrated_divergence())
queryable = dp.c.make_privacy_filter(odometer, d_in=1.0, d_out=0.5)(0.0)  # rho = 0.5, i.e. 2.9 at order 5.8

answered = 0
try:
    for _ in range(1000):  # sigma = 10: rho = 1 / (2 sigma^2) = 0.005 each
        queryable(dp.m.make_gaussian(domain, metric, scale=10.0))
        answered += 1
except dp.OpenDPException:  # the release that would exceed the budget
    pass
print(answered)  # 99
OpenDP lets 99 releases through, not 100, because it rounds each charge up for floating-point safety. For pure-DP queries, the Whitehouse filter (Whitehouse et al. 2023) holds many more small queries than a plain sum of their \(\varepsilon\).
crumbs: 38  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 38  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
38.4 What goes wrong
An odometer costs more than a filter. The Ville odometer converts the RDP spend at the best order of a grid fixed in advance. It pays for that late choice with \(\delta\) divided by the grid’s size, which raises \(\varepsilon\) from 5.299 to 6.253 on the 100-step run above.
Individual accounting charges each training record by its own clipped gradient norm, because a small gradient moves the model less. It drops a record when its spend would pass the budget. In the full edition’s simulation, the median record ends at an individual \(\varepsilon\) of 3.17, against 5.299 for the worst case. But it comes from the actual norms, so it is an estimate, not a guarantee. It is also sensitive, because a small value says that the model fits that record well. And the records with large gradients, which go first, are often those the model serves worst (Disparate impact).
crumbs: 38  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

38.5 References

Feldman & Zrnic, “Individual Privacy Accounting via a Rényi Filter” (NeurIPS 2021).

title: 39  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
39.1 What it is
Zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) keeps a differential privacy (DP) budget as one number that adds up. It starts from the curve of Rényi differential privacy (RDP), which bounds how far apart a mechanism’s outputs on neighbouring datasets can be at each order \(\alpha\). A mechanism is \(\rho\)-zCDP when that curve lies under the straight line \(\rho\alpha\), so \(\rho\) is a slope. Composition adds the slopes, also when each step depends on the earlier outputs.
The Gaussian mechanism’s curve is such a line. Write \(\sigma\) for the standard deviation of its noise. Write \(\Delta_2 f\) for the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity of the query \(f\), the most one record can move it in Euclidean distance. One release then costs \[\rho = \frac{(\Delta_2 f)^2}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{39.1}\] So a release with noise multiplier 1, where \(\sigma = \Delta_2 f\), costs \(\rho = 0.5\), and twice the noise cuts \(\rho\) to a quarter.

title: 39  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
39.2 When you meet it
You meet zCDP in releases that add Gaussian noise to the whole dataset, such as noisy counts or the marginals behind a synthetic dataset. The 2020 United States Census used it with the discrete Gaussian mechanism (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms). Tumult Analytics and OpenDP also keep budgets in \(\rho\).

title: 39  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
39.3 How to use it
Keep a ledger of releases, and charge each its \(\rho\) from Table 39.1.



Table 39.1: What each kind of step costs in a zCDP ledger.










Step
Charge in \(\rho\)
Notes




Gaussian, sensitivity \(\Delta_2 f\), noise \(\sigma\)
\((\Delta_2 f)^2/(2\sigma^2)\)
Exact


Any pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP step
\(\varepsilon^2/2\), or \(\varepsilon^2/8\) for an exponential mechanism
Above the plain \(\varepsilon\) once \(\varepsilon \ge 2\): keep such a step in RDP


An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP step
\(\varepsilon^2/2\), plus \(\delta\) in a second column that also adds
Approximate zCDP


Poisson-subsampled Gaussian
\((\Delta_2 f)^2/(2\sigma^2)\), as without sampling
No amplification






Add the charges. Then convert the total to a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and a small slack \(\delta\) once, at the end, so that you pay the conversion’s slack only once. An all-Gaussian total \(\rho\) costs the same as one Gaussian release with noise multiplier \(1/\sqrt{2\rho}\), so get_epsilon_gaussian converts it exactly. The snippet does this, then calibrates a \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP release.
from math import sqrt

import dp_accounting

rho = 1 / (2 * 1.0**2)  # one Gaussian release, noise multiplier 1
print(f"{rho:.1f} {dp_accounting.get_epsilon_gaussian(1 / sqrt(2 * rho), 1e-5):.4f}")  # 0.5 4.3772
sigma = dp_accounting.get_sigma_gaussian(1.0, 1e-5)  # one release that must be (1, 1e-5)-DP
budget = 1 / (2 * sigma**2)
quarter = budget / 4  # four releases share it
print(f"{budget:.5f} {sigma:.3f} {1 / sqrt(2 * quarter):.3f}")  # 0.03593 3.731 7.461
So the budget for \((1, 10^{-5})\) is \(\rho = 0.03593\), which one query meets with noise multiplier 3.731. Four queries that share it get a quarter each, and each needs twice the noise. Split the budget in \(\rho\), which adds exactly, never in \(\varepsilon\). A histogram in which each person is in one cell costs one charge, not one per cell (Parallel composition).
A ledger with steps that are not Gaussian has no exact conversion. At \(\rho = 0.5\), the simple conversion of Bun and Steinke (2016) is 21% above the exact Gaussian value. The improved conversion of Canonne, Kamath and Steinke (2020) is only 8% above, and the RDP accountant in dp_accounting uses it. Use it, or the exact one for an all-Gaussian ledger. Name the conversion in the report.

title: 39  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
39.4 What goes wrong
The most frequent error is to read \(\rho\) as \(\varepsilon\). A Gaussian release at \(\rho = 0.5\) is \((4.3772, 10^{-5})\)-DP. So if you read it as \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), you overrate the protection by far. Also, \(\rho\) covers only what passed through the noise. The Census Bureau released some counts exactly, and such invariants are outside the guarantee, so list them next to the budget.
Keep subsampled steps out of zCDP, because it gives them no amplification. On this part’s running example, a run of the private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD, zCDP gives \(\varepsilon = 5475.8\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) where RDP gives 6.719. So keep a pipeline with DP-SGD in RDP or a numerical accountant. A \(\rho\)-zCDP release joins it without loss as a GaussianDpEvent with noise multiplier \(1/\sqrt{2\rho}\).
Several records of one user cost more, because a group of \(m\) records costs \(m^2\rho\). For example, four records in a 0.1-zCDP release cost \(\rho = 1.6\).
A budget never renews, because next year’s releases about the same people compose with this year’s. So fix the period and its total in advance (Release and governance). Keep a long ledger in \(\rho\), not in diffprivlib’s BudgetAccountant, which adds \(\varepsilon\) by plain composition (Keeping a budget).

title: 39  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
39.5 References

Bun & Steinke, “Concentrated Differential Privacy: Simplifications, Extensions, and Lower Bounds” (TCC 2016): the definition.
Canonne, Kamath & Steinke, “The Discrete Gaussian for Differential Privacy” (NeurIPS 2020): the improved conversion.

Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 40  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
40.1 What it is
In the shuffle model, each of \(n\) users randomizes their own data, so each report satisfies local differential privacy (DP) at a level \(\varepsilon_0\). A shuffler removes identities and mixes the order, so each report hides among the others. The set of reports then satisfies central DP at a much smaller \(\varepsilon\), which falls like \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/n}\) for a slack \(\delta\) above 0. All results here are for replace-one neighbours.
For binary randomized response, the analyst learns only the count of 1-reports, so you can compute the shuffled guarantee exactly. For any other local randomizer, use the clone bound of Feldman, McMillan and Talwar (2021). With probability \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\), the report of another user looks exactly like one you could have sent, and such clones hide yours. The numeric clone bound computes this exactly, while the paper’s closed form is looser and needs enough users.

title: 40  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
40.2 When you meet it
You meet shuffling in telemetry systems such as Prochlo (Bittau et al. 2017), where the decision is how large \(\varepsilon_0\) can be. No maintained library accounts for it, so use the full edition’s shuffling_iteration.py.
Two other things have the same name but get none of this amplification. A data loader that shuffles once per epoch is a sampler (Match the sampler to the accountant). Federated clients that join rounds when available pass through no shuffler either, so account for them without amplification or with matrix mechanisms.

The choice of bound can decide whether a design is possible. For example, for 100,000 users and a target of 0.2, the closed form allows \(\varepsilon_0\) up to 2 but the numeric bound allows 4, so use the numeric bound.
Before you report a shuffled \(\varepsilon\), check the assumptions below. If one fails, for example if the order leaks, only \(\varepsilon_0\) remains.

The order is uniformly random and hidden, with no metadata such as arrival time or network address.
The shuffler does not collude with the analyst.
Only honest users count in the number of users \(n\), because colluders reveal their reports to the analyst.
The count of users is the number of reports shuffled, so with several batches it is the size of the smallest batch.
Each user sends one report per batch, or the reports compose like any other releases.

title: 40  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
40.4 What goes wrong
Shortcuts fail when users are few or \(\varepsilon_0\) is large. For 1,000 users at \(\varepsilon_0 = 4\), a normal approximation of the count of 1-reports gives 0.9667 against the exact 1.6910.
In amplification by iteration, later training noise protects earlier records. It covers one pass of noisy stochastic gradient descent (SGD) that keeps the weights in a fixed convex set (Feldman et al. 2018). It has two conditions. You can release only the final model, and every step must be a contraction, which never moves two sets of weights further apart. That needs a convex, smooth loss and a small enough step.
Even then the gain depends on the record. Over 10,000 records with noise multiplier 1, the middle record gets \(\varepsilon = 0.0707\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). But the last record gets 5.2985, the cost of one Gaussian step, so report the worst record’s value.
Deep learning breaks both conditions. Checkpoints, logged models and a best checkpoint chosen from several all release more than the final model. Steps on a non-convex loss are not contractions, and Annamalai (2024) builds a loss whose final model leaks as much as all the intermediate models. So claim amplification by iteration only for convex models, such as logistic regression, that release only their final weights.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
text:
This part is for anyone who trains, ships or reviews a model under differential privacy (DP). It builds on the Gaussian mechanism and composition from Part 3 and an accountant from Part 4. Its audits reuse the membership-inference attacks of Part 2.
Every private training method has two halves. The privacy half, the guarantee \(\varepsilon\), is computed by an accountant, while the utility half, accuracy, can only be measured. The main private algorithm is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipped per-example gradients and Gaussian noise, called DP-SGD. Its accountant needs just three settings: the noise multiplier, the sampling rate and the number of steps. So every page asks whether the \(\varepsilon\) is correct and whether the accuracy at that \(\varepsilon\) is good enough.
Three pages are workflows, each a whole job done with real libraries on public data. Train a model with DP-SGD trains a classifier on the Adult census data with Opacus. Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA adapts a small public language model to a private text and checks it for memorized secrets. Release and governance recomputes the guarantee, writes it down, maps it to the law and lists what to check before a model ships.
The other pages explain the decisions those jobs make, in the order a project meets them. A short page on private empirical risk minimization for convex models leads to DP-SGD. Then come hyperparameter tuning, the privacy unit in User-level differential privacy and the budget in Choosing ε. Public data and private fine-tuning explains why a public starting model helps so much. Disparate impact and Auditing private training are the checks before release. Three reference pages cover rarer methods: private prediction, correlated noise across steps and adaptive data analysis.
Every number on these pages comes from a script you can run.

title: 41  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
41.1 What it is
Most of machine learning is empirical risk minimization (ERM), which picks the weights \(\theta\) with the least average loss over a training set. Write \(D\) for that set and \(n\) for its number of records. A ridge penalty usually keeps the weights small. Its strength is a number \(\lambda\), and training minimizes \[\mathcal L(\theta; D) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\theta; z_i) + \frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2, \tag{41.1}\] where \(\ell(\theta; z)\) is the loss of the weights on one record \(z\). Differential privacy (DP) asks that replacing one record barely change the released weights, so noise must enter the trained weights, the objective or each gradient step.
Output perturbation trains as usual and adds Gaussian noise to the final weights, with a small slack \(\delta\). The noise is scaled to the most that the trained weights \(\theta^*\) can move between datasets \(D\) and \(D'\) that differ in one record. For a convex loss, the ridge limits that move to \[\|\theta^*(D) - \theta^*(D')\| \le \frac{2L}{\lambda n}. \tag{41.2}\] Here the constant \(L\) bounds the length of each record’s loss gradient. It is 1 for logistic regression with labels \(\pm1\) and features of length at most 1.
Objective perturbation adds a random linear term to the objective and minimizes the result exactly. Part of the privacy budget \(\varepsilon\) pays for the loss’s curvature, which is at most a constant \(c\), one quarter for the logistic loss. The noise is scaled to what is left, \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon - 2\ln\Big(1 + \frac{c}{n\lambda}\Big). \tag{41.3}\] The subtracted term grows as \(n\lambda\) shrinks, so with little data the ridge must grow to keep \(\varepsilon'\) positive.
Gradient perturbation adds noise to every gradient step instead. With random batches and clipped per-record gradients, it becomes noisy stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD, the only option for a model that is not convex.

title: 41  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
41.2 When you meet it
You meet these methods for linear models, such as a linear probe on features from a public pretrained network (Public data and private fine-tuning). Objective perturbation is usually the most accurate, because the objective’s full curvature damps its noise, while only the ridge damps output perturbation’s. So use output perturbation only when training is a black box.
Whether you have enough data depends on \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\). On the training objective they matter only through their product, so halving \(\varepsilon\) costs as much as halving the data. On new data, with \(d\) features, privacy adds less error than sampling does once \(n\) is well above \(d\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon^2\).

title: 41  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
41.3 How to use it
IBM’s diffprivlib offers objective perturbation as LogisticRegression(epsilon=..., data_norm=...), with data_norm bounding each row’s length. Its version 0.6.6 fails with scikit-learn 1.8, so the snippet calls the mechanism it wraps, mechanisms.Vector, with the curvature bound \(c\) as function_sensitivity. The breast-cancer data has no public data dictionary for feature bounds. So the snippet treats 500 rows as private and 69 as a public stand-in. It clips the private rows to the stand-in’s log-transformed ranges and maps them to \([-1, 1]\). A constant 1 replaces the intercept, and dividing by \(\sqrt{31}\) keeps each row’s length at most 1.
import numpy as np
from diffprivlib.mechanisms import Vector
from scipy.optimize import minimize
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
data = load_breast_cancer()
public, private = np.log1p(data.data[:69]), np.log1p(data.data[69:])  # 69 stand-in rows fix the bounds
lo, hi = public.min(axis=0), public.max(axis=0)
X = np.hstack([2 * (np.clip(private, lo, hi) - lo) / (hi - lo) - 1, np.ones((500, 1))]) / np.sqrt(31)
y = 2 * data.target[69:] - 1
Xt, yt, n = X[::2], y[::2], 250  # even rows train, odd rows test
lam = 1 / n  # diffprivlib's default ridge, fixed in advance

def objective(w):  # J(w) and its gradient
    m = yt * (Xt @ w)
    return np.logaddexp(0, -m).mean() + lam / 2 * w @ w, lam * w - Xt.T @ (yt / (1 + np.exp(m))) / n

def accuracy(eps, seed):  # eps = inf adds no noise
    vector = Vector(epsilon=eps, function_sensitivity=0.25, dimension=31, alpha=n * lam, n=n, random_state=seed)
    w = minimize(vector.randomise(objective), np.zeros(31), jac=True, options={"gtol": 1e-9}).x
    return np.mean(np.sign(X[1::2] @ w) == y[1::2])

print(" ".join(f"{np.mean([accuracy(e, s) for s in range(20)]):.3f}" for e in [1, 4, np.inf]))  # 0.783 0.946 0.964
Averaged over 20 noise draws, test accuracy is 0.783 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 0.946 at \(\varepsilon = 4\), against 0.964 without noise. So with only 250 training records, accuracy comes close only at \(\varepsilon = 4\). Nothing was tuned on the private rows, so the guarantee is pure DP for the 250 training rows, against replacing one record. The 69 stand-in rows get none.

title: 41  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
41.4 What goes wrong
The most common failure is a bound taken from the data. Left unset, data_norm is computed from the training rows with a PrivacyLeakWarning, and the guarantee is gone. A range table computed from the same rows is no better, because each minimum and maximum is one record’s value. So take every bound from public knowledge or public rows, and clip the private rows to it.
The second failure is the solver, because output and objective perturbation assume the exact minimizer. A solver that stops where the gradient still has length \(g\) adds \(2g/\lambda\) to the sensitivity. That is small beside the exact sensitivity \(2L/(\lambda n)\) only when \(g\) is well below \(L/n\). So set the tolerance there, and check the final gradient rather than the number of steps.
The third failure is an unpenalized weight, because the sensitivity bound needs the ridge’s curvature in every direction. Scikit-learn’s loss, which diffprivlib reuses, leaves the intercept out of the ridge, so the snippet adds a constant feature. Fix \(\lambda\) by a rule or on public data, since tuning it on private data is a search that must be paid for (Hyperparameter tuning). Finally, these guarantees assume replaced records, unlike the add/remove accountants of later chapters, and the two do not convert freely. So state the relation next to every \(\varepsilon\).
Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 42  DP-SGD
text:
42.1 Why this matters
Nearly every deep-learning system that satisfies differential privacy (DP) runs one algorithm. It is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipped per-record gradients and Gaussian noise at every step, called DP-SGD (Abadi et al. 2016). Clipping limits how far one record moves the model at each step, and the noise hides that move. An accountant adds up the cost of the steps into the guarantee’s \(\varepsilon\), with a small additive slack \(\delta\).
The accountant sees only the noise, the sampling rate (the chance that a record joins a batch) and the number of steps, never the model. So those three decide \(\varepsilon\), and you can tune the clipping norm and learning rate for accuracy alone. Most failures come from code that breaks an assumption of the privacy proof, so the checks matter as much as the settings. Train a model with DP-SGD does the whole job in Opacus.

title: 42  DP-SGD
text:
42.2 The algorithm and its guarantee
A training set holds \(n\) records. The gradient of one record’s loss is its per-example gradient, written \(g_i\) for record \(i\). Each step of DP-SGD does five things.

Sample a batch. Each record enters independently with probability \(q\), the sampling rate, which is called Poisson sampling.
Compute the per-example gradient of each record in the batch.
Clip each gradient longer than the clipping norm \(C\) to length \(C\).
Sum the clipped gradients, and add Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(\sigma C\) to each coordinate, where the noise multiplier \(\sigma\) measures the noise in units of \(C\).
Divide the noisy sum by the expected batch size \(B = qn\), a fixed public number, and step against it, scaled by the learning rate \(\eta\).

Write \(\theta_t\) for the weights at step \(t\) and \(S_t\) for its batch. With Gaussian noise \(\xi_t\) drawn afresh on each coordinate, the update is \[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \frac{\eta}{B}\Big(\sum_{i\in S_t}g_i\min\Big(1, \frac{C}{\|g_i\|}\Big) + \xi_t\Big), \qquad \xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2I). \tag{42.1}\] Releasing every intermediate set of weights then satisfies \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for add/remove neighbours, datasets that differ by one record (Amplification by subsampling).
This part’s running example (Section 42.7) trains a small network on 10,000 synthetic records. It runs 10,000 steps with \(\sigma = 1\), and each record joins a batch with probability \(q = 0.01\). For this run, the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant, a standard and slightly loose upper bound, gives \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at the \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) of the book’s rule (How small δ must be). To pick \(\sigma\) for a target \(\varepsilon\), let the accountant you will report solve for it (Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run).

title: 42  DP-SGD
text:
42.3 The implementation checklist
The guarantee rests on four properties of your code. Code that breaks one still trains and reports as before.
First, one record must move the clipped sum by at most \(C\). Batch normalization breaks this, because its statistics let one record change every other record’s gradient. So private models use group or layer normalization, which works on each record alone. With strict=False, Opacus’s validator lists the layers to replace instead of raising an error.
from opacus.validators import ModuleValidator
from torchvision.models import resnet18

model = resnet18(weights=None)
print(len(ModuleValidator.validate(model, strict=False)))  # 20
model = ModuleValidator.fix(model)
print(len(ModuleValidator.validate(model, strict=False)))  # 0
Also fix \(C\) in advance, from public data or a private estimate. A \(C\) read off the current batch makes the noise depend on the data.
Second, the accountant must assume the sampler the code actually runs (Amplification by subsampling). The Poisson accountant’s saving comes from each record’s chance of being left out of a batch. A loader that shuffles once per epoch and cuts fixed batches puts every record in exactly one batch per epoch. That chance is then gone, and the true \(\varepsilon\) can be far above the Poisson number.
Fixed-size batches drawn afresh at every step can still use a Poisson accountant, at the batch’s share of the data and half your noise multiplier. The noise counts as halved because a record that enters a fixed-size batch pushes another out, so the sum can move by \(2C\). This raises the running example’s \(\varepsilon\) from 6.71 to 47.42, and it holds only for add/remove neighbours.
Third, divide the noisy sum by the public number \(B\), never by the actual batch size. The actual size is one larger when the protected record is drawn, so dividing by it reveals whether it was.
Fourth, the accountant must count every step that touched the data, including those of runs discarded in tuning.
Beyond the proof, state the neighbouring relation next to every \(\varepsilon\), and make data-dependent preprocessing private too. A person with many records needs user-level privacy. For a model you release, turn on Opacus’s secure_mode=True, because floating-point sampling is not the exact Gaussian noise of the proof (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms).

title: 42  DP-SGD
text:
42.4 Clipping and the learning rate
Clipping must happen per record. PyTorch’s torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_ clips a whole batch’s gradient, which bounds no single record and so gives no privacy at any threshold.
The clipping norm \(C\) does not change \(\varepsilon\), but it costs accuracy either way. A small \(C\) clips more gradients, so records with large gradients count for less, and they are often rare records (Disparate impact). A large \(C\) means more noise, since the noise is \(\sigma C\).
When every gradient is clipped, each has length exactly \(C\) and the noise is proportional to \(C\) too. So the step depends only on the product \(\eta C\) of the learning rate and the clipping norm. Clip hard, and tune that one number. On the running example, holding \(\eta C\) at 0.25 keeps test accuracy at 0.9599 or above for every \(C\) up to 0.3. Holding \(\eta\) at 0.5 instead, \(C = 10\) drops it to 0.8347.
Noise and clipping also move the best learning rate. Noise lowers it (Optimization), while clipping raises it, because clipped gradients are shorter. The two do not cancel predictably, so search the step again whenever \(\sigma\) or \(C\) changes, and count the search’s runs in \(\varepsilon\).
Gradient norms also drift. The running example’s median per-example norm falls from 3.592 to 0.006 in a thousand steps, so a \(C\) that clips everything early clips only a minority later. Adaptive clipping moves \(C\) toward a quantile of the norms, measured by a small private count, and Opacus offers it with clipping="adaptive". The count spends part of the budget, so the gradient gets more noise at the same \(\sigma\).

title: 42  DP-SGD
section: 42.5 Batch size at a fixed budget
text:
42.5 Batch size at a fixed budget
Averaging the noisy sum over \(B\) records divides the added noise by \(B\), so larger batches dilute it. At a fixed budget and number of epochs, a larger batch also means fewer steps. So the noise multiplier must rise to keep \(\varepsilon\), but more slowly than \(B\) does. For a small sampling rate \(q\) and a \(\sigma\) well above 1, the accountant’s cost over a fixed number of epochs depends on \(q/\sigma^2\). So \(\sigma\) only has to grow like \(\sqrt q\). Since \(q = B/n\), with \(n\) the number of records, the noise on the averaged gradient falls with the batch size, \[\sigma \propto \sqrt{\frac Bn}, \qquad \frac{\sigma C}{B} \propto \frac{C}{\sqrt{Bn}}. \tag{42.2}\]
So choose the largest batch your hardware allows, with a larger learning rate for the fewer steps. When it does not fit in memory, Opacus’s BatchMemoryManager splits the sampled batch into physical batches that fit, and still steps once per sampled batch.

title: 42  DP-SGD
text:
42.6 Making it fast
Computed one record at a time, DP-SGD can run tens or hundreds of times slower than ordinary training. Two fixes cost no accuracy. Vectorized per-example gradients, from torch.func.vmap or Opacus’s hooks, compute the same clipped sum in parallel. Ghost clipping also saves memory, because it gets each record’s gradient norm from each layer’s inputs and errors without the gradient itself. Opacus turns it on with grad_sample_mode="ghost".
The third fix, microbatching, costs accuracy. It clips the average gradient of each group of \(m\) records. One record can change its group’s clipped average by up to \(2C\), so the noise doubles. The update then averages over \(B/m\) groups rather than \(B\) records, so the noise on each coordinate of the averaged update becomes \[2m\cdot\frac{\sigma C}{B}. \tag{42.3}\] On the running example at \(\sigma = 1\), groups of 4 cut test accuracy from 0.9589 to 0.9336. So use microbatching only as a last resort.

text:
42.7 What privacy costs in accuracy

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
43.1 Why this matters
You have a PyTorch training loop on sensitive data, and it must become private. The algorithm is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with differential privacy (DP), called DP-SGD, which clips each record’s gradient and adds noise at every step (DP-SGD). Opacus does it with one call that wraps the model. The hard part is the decisions around that call. A mistake in one of them leaves code that trains as before but reports a false privacy level \(\varepsilon\).
This chapter trains on Adult, a census survey of 48,842 people from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, to predict whether a person earns more than $50,000 a year. Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run plans the privacy side of this run, and this chapter keeps training, tuning and utility. The script practitioner_dp_sgd.py runs every step except tuning, which practitioner_tuning.py does. Each runs in one to two minutes without a GPU.

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
section: 43.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
text:
43.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
The guarantee protects exactly one record, so first decide what a record is (User-level differential privacy). Adult has no person identifier, so one row counts as one person because of how the survey was collected. When your data has an identifier, count distinct identifiers, not rows.
The script splits the rows with seed 0 into 30,000 private training rows and 16,842 test rows. The other 2,000, the stand-in rows from here on, play the part of public data. The script chooses settings on them but never trains on them. They come from the same survey, so this is an assumption for the demonstration. In production the role belongs to public data, and without any, tuning costs privacy (Section 43.10).
The slack \(\delta\) depends on the number of people \(n\) in the training set, not in the whole dataset. The book’s rule (How small δ must be) gives \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for \(n = 30{,}000\).
crumbs: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
43.3 Preprocess from public facts
Every statistic computed from the private rows is a release that the accountant does not count. A scaler fitted on the training set leaks each column’s mean and spread. An encoder fitted on it leaks which categories occur, even a country that only one person comes from. So the script takes its category lists from the dataset’s documentation, and scales each number by bounds the survey publishes, such as ages from 17 to 90. Capital gains and losses go on a log scale first, and a missing value becomes its own category.
def features(rows: pl.DataFrame) -> Array:
    """One-hot categories from the documented lists, numbers scaled by public bounds."""
    rows = rows.with_columns(pl.col("capital-gain", "capital-loss").log1p())
    numeric = [
        np.clip((rows[name].to_numpy() - low) / (high - low), 0.0, 1.0) for name, (low, high) in NUMERIC_BOUNDS.items()
    ]
    encoder = OneHotEncoder(categories=list(CATEGORIES.values()), sparse_output=False)
    text = rows.select(pl.col(list(CATEGORIES)).fill_null("?")).to_numpy()
    encoder.fit(text[:1])  # the categories are given, so fitting learns nothing from the rows
    return np.hstack([np.column_stack(numeric), encoder.transform(text)])
This gives 91 features for a network with one hidden layer of 64 units and 6,018 weights. To check this step in other code, find every fit call and ask what data it sees.
crumbs: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
43.4 Train the baselines
A private accuracy means little on its own, so train three baselines with the same model, batch size, epochs and optimizer. The non-private model shows the best you can expect. A model with clipping and no noise separates the cost of clipping from the cost of noise. The majority class shows the floor, where a collapsed private model lands.
non-private: test accuracy 0.847
clip only (C=1, no noise): test accuracy 0.845
always '<=50K': test accuracy 0.759
Clipping alone costs little here. If clip-only accuracy were far below non-private, no budget would fix it, because the problem would be the clipping norm or the learning rate.
crumbs: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
43.5 Check the model
Opacus computes one gradient per record, and some layers break that. Batch normalization is the common case, because its statistics let one record change every other record’s gradient. The validator lists such layers before you train.
errors = ModuleValidator.validate(model, strict=False)
print(f"validator errors: {len(errors)}")
Here it finds none. For a model with such layers, ModuleValidator.fix replaces batch normalization with group normalization (DP-SGD shows it on a ResNet).
crumbs: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
section: 43.6 Choose the clipping norm, batch and epochs
text:
43.6 Choose the clipping norm, batch and epochs
Fix these settings before you touch the private data, because choosing them on it costs privacy. The usual guide for the clipping norm \(C\), the length each record’s gradient is cut to, is the typical gradient norm on public data. So the script measures it on the stand-in rows.
wrapped = GradSampleModule(model)  # adds hooks that keep one gradient per row
wrapped.train()
logits: torch.Tensor = wrapped(split.x)
nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(logits, split.y).backward()  # fills p.grad_sample for every weight p
norms = stacked_norms(wrapped)
at initialisation: median norm 1.444  90th percentile 1.538
fraction clipped at C=1: 1.000
The median rule would give a \(C\) of about 1.4. The script keeps the usual default \(C = 1\), just below the median, so every gradient is clipped at the start. That costs nothing, because when every gradient is clipped, only the learning rate times \(C\) matters (DP-SGD).
Make the batch as large as you can afford. The reason is that the noise on the averaged gradient is \(\sigma C/B\), where \(B\) is the expected batch size and the noise multiplier \(\sigma\) is the noise’s standard deviation in units of \(C\). With \(B = 1{,}000\), Opacus sets the sampling rate \(q\), the chance that a row joins a batch, to \(1/30 = 0.0333\). Ten epochs then make 300 steps. Fix the epochs now, because the noise is calibrated to them.
The optimizer is SGD with momentum 0.9. The script picks its learning rate on the stand-in rows too. It trains a non-private model on 1,500 of them at six rates and scores each on the other 500.
  lr=0.05: 0.814  lr=0.1: 0.816  lr=0.2: 0.826  lr=0.5: 0.792  lr=1: 0.812  lr=2: 0.768
non-private learning rate 0.2; DP-SGD learning rate 2 (x10)
DP-SGD then uses ten times the winning rate, a rule of thumb rather than a measurement. Private runs usually need a larger step, because clipped gradients are shorter (DP-SGD). No private row was used, so this choice costs no privacy.
crumbs: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
43.7 Calibrate the noise
The target is a privacy level of \(\varepsilon = 4\) at the slack \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) of Section 43.2. For this \(q\) and these epochs, Opacus’s get_noise_multiplier finds the smallest \(\sigma\) that meets it. With its privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant it gives \(\sigma = 0.973\), and Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run shows the call. That \(\sigma\) holds only for those epochs and that \(q\), so recompute it if you change either.
crumbs: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
43.8 Train
The privacy engine wraps the model, the optimizer and the data loader. Its optimizer clips each record’s gradient and adds the noise. Its loader draws Poisson batches, in which each row joins each batch independently with probability \(q\), as the accountant assumes. The script’s own loader cuts fixed batches, so make_private must replace it.
engine = PrivacyEngine(accountant="prv")
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr, momentum=0.9)
model, optimizer, data_loader = engine.make_private(
    module=model,
    optimizer=optimizer,
    data_loader=data_loader,
    noise_multiplier=sigma,
    max_grad_norm=CLIP,
)  # Poisson sampling is the default: each row joins each batch with probability q
The training loop runs inside BatchMemoryManager, which splits each logical batch of about 1,000 rows into physical batches of at most 500. The optimizer still steps once per logical batch, so the accounting does not change.
with BatchMemoryManager(
    data_loader=data_loader, max_physical_batch_size=PHYSICAL_BATCH, optimizer=optimizer
) as batches:
    for x, y in batches:  # Opacus splits each logical batch; it steps once per logical batch
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = criterion(model(x), y)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
steps=300  q=0.0333
epsilon (Opacus PRV) = 3.99
test accuracy at epsilon=4: 0.846
The script leaves secure_mode off, so that its noise is seeded and its numbers repeat, and its record says so. For a model you release, pass secure_mode=True to PrivacyEngine. It draws the noise from a secure generator and guards against the floating-point flaws of ordinary Gaussian samples (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms).
crumbs: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
43.9 Cross-check ε
An \(\varepsilon\) from one library is a claim about that library’s arithmetic. So the script recomputes it with Google’s dp_accounting, whose privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant gives 3.98 against Opacus’s 3.99. The looser Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant gives 4.50, so a statement must name its accountant. Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run runs this check and says what a disagreement means.
crumbs: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
43.10 Tune honestly
This run chose every hyperparameter on a public stand-in, so tuning cost nothing. Without public data, tuning runs on the private rows, and every private run that influences the release costs privacy, the discarded ones too (Hyperparameter tuning).
The tuning script measures that cost for six learning rates at a total \(\varepsilon\) of 4. A grid runs all six rates and pays for each by composition. A random search runs a Poisson number of models with mean 4, each at a rate drawn from the six, and releases only the best. Only RDP handles a random number of runs, so the script uses it throughout, and its single-run \(\sigma\) is larger than the PRV value above.
def random_search(sigma: float) -> dp_accounting.DpEvent:
    """A Poisson number of runs with mean 4 (shape=inf selects the Poisson case); only the best is released."""
    return dp_accounting.dp_event.RepeatAndSelectDpEvent(one_run(sigma), mean=MEAN_RUNS, shape=math.inf)


def sigma_for(strategy: Callable[[float], dp_accounting.DpEvent], epsilon: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """The smallest noise multiplier per run that keeps the whole strategy within (epsilon, delta).

    The search starts at 0.1 and tries 1 first.
    """
    return dp_accounting.calibrate_dp_mechanism(
        dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant, strategy, epsilon, delta, dp_accounting.LowerEndpointAndGuess(0.1, 1.0)
    )
one run, no tuning: sigma=1.029
grid of 6, all runs counted: sigma=1.816
random search, Poisson mean 4 runs: sigma=1.256
naive grid of 6 at sigma=1.029: reports epsilon=4.00
naive grid, true epsilon of all 6 runs = 9.84
The naive grid is the common mistake. It trains six models at the single-run noise, reports the \(\varepsilon\) of one, and actually spends 9.84. The random search costs a modest rise in \(\sigma\), from 1.029 to 1.256.
With seed 0, the search drew only two runs, both at the learning rate 0.05. So its model reaches only 0.828 on the test set, against 0.846 for the run tuned on public data. Do not redraw until you like the answer, because the guarantee depends on the randomness of the draw. So spend private runs on tuning only when no public data can stand in.

Train at several budgets with everything else fixed, and compare against the baselines. Fix the released budget beforehand, as the script does with \(\varepsilon = 4\), because the script scores these runs on private rows that no \(\varepsilon\) counts (Choosing ε).

Privacy costs almost nothing on Adult down to \(\varepsilon = 1\). Only at \(\varepsilon = 0.25\) does accuracy drop, by about five points, and the other differences are too small to read on one seed.
Adult is easy. Its training set is large, so a batch of 1,000 still has a small sampling rate and divides the noise by 1,000. Its model is small, and the noise’s total length grows with the square root of the number of trained weights. So expect a steeper curve with millions of weights trained from scratch, a few thousand records, a rare class or many more epochs. crumbs: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 44  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
44.1 Why this matters
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipped gradients and Gaussian noise satisfies differential privacy (DP) at the level its accountant reports for one run. It is called DP-SGD. But nobody trains once. You try several learning rates, score each model and ship the best, and every run and every score touched private data. So the privacy level \(\varepsilon\) you report must pay for the search too.
Releasing only the best of a fixed number of runs can cost as much as releasing all of them. On the Adult census data, a grid of six runs that each meet \(\varepsilon = 4\) really costs 9.84. If instead you draw the number of runs at random, from a distribution fixed in advance, the whole search costs little more than one run.
crumbs: 44  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection

title: 44  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
44.2 The procedure and the report
The cheapest tuning is the tuning you don’t do on private data. Runs on public or proxy data cost nothing, and neither do published settings for similar tasks. Fix a large batch, the number of epochs and a small clipping norm in advance. With the clipping norm below the typical gradient norm, only its product with the learning rate matters, so often only that product needs a search (DP-SGD).
If you must tune on private data, fix the search before you touch the data. Write down the candidate set, the distribution of the number of runs (Section 44.4), the score, which must be private too (Section 44.5), and the validation set. Trying “a few more” later, or restarting a disappointing search, makes the search depend on the data, which no accountant covers.
Then account for the whole search. For two or three candidates, charge for every run (Section 44.3), and for more, use random search with a random number of runs (Section 44.4). Either way, count every run that touched the private data, including crashed and debugging runs and evaluations for early stopping.
Finally, log the candidate set, the drawn number of runs and each run’s settings and score, and report two numbers. The \(\varepsilon\) of the released run says what the model alone would leak if its hyperparameters had been public. The \(\varepsilon\) of the whole procedure is what the release guarantees, and an audit cannot check it, because an audit tests only the released model. With the slack \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) that the book’s rule gives for 30,000 records (How small δ must be), the Adult search of Section 44.6 reports as follows.

DP-SGD ran for 300 steps with Poisson sampling at rate 1/30. It clipped gradients to norm 1 and added noise with multiplier 1.256, so one run satisfies \((2.73, 10^{-5})\)-DP. The learning rate was chosen by random search over \(\{0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2\}\). The number of runs was drawn from a Poisson distribution with mean 4, and each run was scored on 2,000 validation records treated as public. The whole procedure satisfies \((4.00, 10^{-5})\)-DP for add/remove neighbours, datasets that differ by one record. It was computed with dp_accounting from the Rényi bound of Papernot & Steinke (2022).
crumbs: 44  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection

title: 44  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
44.3 Paying for every run
A common argument says that choosing among eight learning rates reveals at most three bits. It is wrong, because the release is a whole private run, picked because of how it came out. If each run says only “good” or “bad”, the best is bad only when every run was bad. So a bad best reveals all of them. Even tuning without privacy and then training once privately leaks. The winning regularization weight can change when you add a few outliers, and so reveal whether they were in the data (Membership inference).
The safe answer is to charge for every run, because the best run is computed from all the runs’ outputs (Composition). For DP-SGD, a grid of \(k\) runs, each of \(T\) steps, costs exactly as much as one run of \(kT\) steps. One run of the synthetic running example of DP-SGD costs \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Ten such runs cost 27.23, about four times one run rather than ten, because the conversion to \(\varepsilon\) pays its \(\delta\) cost only once.
crumbs: 44  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection

title: 44  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
44.4 A random number of runs
The way out is to draw the number of runs \(K\) at random, independently of the data. A search whose runs all came out bad then most likely drew few runs, which says little about the data. So the whole search costs about one run, plus a term that grows with the logarithm of the expected number of runs. For DP-SGD, use the version of Papernot & Steinke (2022), which works with the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) that DP-SGD’s accountants already compute (Rényi DP).
To use it, fix the candidate set and the distribution of \(K\), either Poisson or a truncated negative binomial with a shape parameter \(\nu\). That family includes the geometric distribution, \(\nu = 1\), which is the random stopping of Liu & Talwar, and the logarithmic one, \(\nu = 0\). Then draw \(K\), run that many candidates drawn at random from the set, and release the best one by a private score. To get the cost from Google’s dp_accounting, wrap the event of one run in a RepeatAndSelectDpEvent. Give it \(\nu\) as its shape (infinite for Poisson), and compose it in an RdpAccountant.
NumPy draws \(K\) with rng.poisson(mean), rng.geometric(1 / mean) or rng.logseries(p). The last takes \(p\) rather than a mean, so solve its mean, \(-p/((1 - p)\ln(1 - p))\), for \(p\).

In Table 44.1, the geometric and logarithmic searches barely grow from 10 to 1,000 runs, while composition grows almost linearly. A smaller \(\nu\) gives a cheaper bound, but the search also stops after one run more often. The Poisson bound needs runs that are already very private, which a run at \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) is not, so here it grows almost like composition. A random number of runs may also miss the best candidate. With eight candidates and a geometric number of runs with mean eight, it never tries the best one with probability 0.4667.
The theorems have three conditions, and each is easy to break. First, each run must draw its candidate independently from a fixed distribution, as random search does. Bayesian optimization picks each candidate from earlier scores, so it is not covered and needs adaptive composition. Second, the number of runs must be drawn independently of the data. Third, the score that ranks the runs must be private and counted in each run’s cost.
crumbs: 44  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection

title: 44  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 44.5 Selecting by a noisy validation score
text:
44.5 Selecting by a noisy validation score
Sometimes the candidates are fixed in advance, such as public pretrained checkpoints, and only the choice among them uses private data. That is a selection problem, which Selection solves with the exponential mechanism, a random choice weighted toward high scores. Score each candidate by its number of correct predictions, which one record changes by at most 1, not by an accuracy, which divides by a private set size. The mechanism’s shortfall from the best count then grows only with the logarithm of the number of candidates.
For the random-number bounds, add Gaussian noise to each run’s count of correct predictions, since an exact validation accuracy leaves the validation records unprotected. With noise of standard deviation 20, one noisy count costs \(\varepsilon = 0.182\). If the validation set is disjoint from the training set, each record pays only one of the two costs. So the event for one run is the costlier of its training and its count, not their sum. Otherwise compose both into one event. On the running example the counts are the cheaper, so they add nothing to the total.

44.6 Tuning on Adult
The script practitioner_tuning.py tunes the learning rate of a small network on 30,000 Adult census records, with 300 steps per run. It asks the accountant for the noise multiplier per run that each strategy can afford.

Strategy

One run, no tuning
1.029
4.00

1.029

The second row is the reporting bug of Section 44.3. This snippet recomputes it, together with the numbers of the report in Section 44.2.
import dp_accounting


def one_run(sigma: float) -> dp_accounting.DpEvent:
    step = dp_accounting.PoissonSampledDpEvent(1 / 30, dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(sigma))
    return dp_accounting.SelfComposedDpEvent(step, 300)


def epsilon(event: dp_accounting.DpEvent) -> float:
    return dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant().compose(event).get_epsilon(1e-5)


search = dp_accounting.dp_event.RepeatAndSelectDpEvent(one_run(1.256), mean=4, shape=float("inf"))
naive_grid = dp_accounting.SelfComposedDpEvent(one_run(1.029), 6)
print(f"{epsilon(one_run(1.256)):.2f}")  # 2.73
print(f"{epsilon(search):.2f}")  # 4.00
print(f"{epsilon(naive_grid):.2f}")  # 9.84
With seed 0, the search drew only two runs, both at the smallest learning rate. So its model reaches only 0.828 on the test set, against 0.846 for the run of Train a model with DP-SGD, tuned for free on public stand-in rows.

title: 45  User-level differential privacy
text:
45.1 Why this matters
Every differential privacy (DP) guarantee in this part so far protects one record. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipping and noise, this part’s DP-SGD, gives each record of its running example a privacy loss \(\varepsilon\) of 6.71. But a messaging user contributes hundreds of messages, and together a person’s records can reveal far more than any one of them.
A DP guarantee protects whatever differs between two neighbouring datasets, so the neighbouring relation sets the privacy unit. To show what a user unit costs, this chapter gives the running example’s 10,000 synthetic records to 1,000 users, very unevenly. The median user holds 4 records and the largest 348.

title: 45  User-level differential privacy
text:
45.2 The privacy unit and δ
Take a mechanism \(M\), and call two datasets neighbours, \(D\) and \(D'\), when they differ by adding or removing all the records of one user. The mechanism is user-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, with a small slack \(\delta\), if every such pair and every set \(S\) of outputs satisfy \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta. \tag{45.1}\] Example-level DP is the same inequality for datasets that differ in one record. So every property and accountant of Part 4 holds for user-level DP unchanged. What changes is the sensitivity, because one user can move the computation with all of their records at once.
The right unit, such as a record, a user, a household or a device, answers the question “whose participation do I want to hide?”. Report it with every \(\varepsilon\) (Release and governance). The unit also sets the slack, because the book’s rule for \(\delta\) (How small δ must be) now counts users. For 1,000 users it gives \(10^{-4}\) (Section 45.8), so this chapter’s \(10^{-5}\) is stricter than it needs to be.
The textbook answer for a person with \(k\) records is group privacy (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). An example-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism is also user-level DP for users with at most \(k\) records, at level \(k\varepsilon\) and with slack \[\delta_k = \delta\,\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}. \tag{45.2}\] The fraction grows like \(e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\), so never read a record-level \(\delta\) as a user’s. To hold a user’s slack at \(10^{-5}\), the per-record \(\delta\) must be much smaller, and so the per-record \(\varepsilon\) larger. On the running example a user with two records therefore gets \(\varepsilon = 18.61\), not twice 6.71, and for ten records no per-record \(\delta\) is small enough.

title: 45  User-level differential privacy
section: 45.3 What an example-level model gives a user
text:
45.3 What an example-level model gives a user
Group privacy treats DP-SGD as a black box, but you know how a user’s records enter each step. Each step includes every record independently with the sampling rate \(q\). So it sees some record of a user with \(k\) records with probability about \(kq\). While \(kq\) is small, two of their records rarely share a batch. So a user with \(k\) records looks like one record sampled at rate \(kq\). To screen a user’s exposure, rerun the record-level accountant at rate \(kq\) (Section 45.8). An exact accountant for a user with \(k\) records also exists (Charles et al. 2024).

The rate-\(kq\) screen stays within 8% of the exact value up to ten records, but always a little low. The reason is that it ignores steps that draw several of the user’s records together. So report the exact value when you have an implementation. The libraries this book uses offer only the screen, so report its value, say it can be a few percent low, and keep \(kq\) small. It is not a pessimistic bound, because a person’s similar records do push the gradient partly the same way.

title: 45  User-level differential privacy
text:
45.4 User-level DP-SGD
The better route makes the user the unit that DP-SGD samples, clips and accounts for (McMahan et al. 2018). Starting from weights chosen without looking at the data, each step does five things.

Sample users. Put each user in the batch independently with probability \(q\), now the user sampling rate.
Compute one vector per user. From that user’s records alone, compute their average gradient, or the change in weights after a few training steps on their records.
Clip per user. Rescale that vector to length at most the clipping norm \(C\).
Add noise. Sum the clipped vectors and add Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\), for a noise multiplier \(\sigma\).
Step. Divide by the expected number of sampled users and take a gradient step.

One user moves the sum by at most \(C\), however many records they have. So the guarantee is user-level DP with exactly the accountant of example-level DP-SGD, run at the user sampling rate.
That has two consequences. First, you pay for having fewer units. On a shorter schedule of the running example, 1,000 steps with about 100 units per batch, sampling records needs \(\sigma = 0.778\) for \(\varepsilon = 4\). The same batch drawn from ten times fewer users needs a ten times higher rate, and so \(\sigma = 3.78\). Second, records inside a user are free, since you can average them, train on them for several steps or subsample them without changing \(\varepsilon\).
Carry a user identifier through the pipeline, and split training and test data by user. Opacus clips each row of a batch, so write a data loader that yields users and clip each user’s vector yourself. Three things break the guarantee:

A user’s vector depends on other users’ data, for example through normalization statistics computed over all users.
One person is spread over several accounts, so the unit is the account and the person is again a group.
Users are iterated in a fixed shuffled order instead of Poisson-sampled, which is a different mechanism that this accountant does not cover (Matrix factorization).

title: 45  User-level differential privacy
text:
45.5 Contribution bounding
A pipeline built around records can still protect users. Contribution bounding keeps at most \(k\) records of each user, the cap, and runs example-level DP-SGD on what remains. The result is user-level DP with the \(\varepsilon\) the user accountant gives for \(k\) records. The condition is that each user’s kept records are chosen without looking at other users’ data, for example at random. Otherwise adding one user could change which records other users keep, and neighbours would differ by more than one user’s records. To calibrate the noise for a cap, solve for \(\sigma\) with dp_accounting.calibrate_dp_mechanism at rate \(kq\) (Train a model with DP-SGD).
import polars as pl

rows = pl.DataFrame({"user": ["a", "a", "a", "a", "b", "c", "c"], "x": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]})
k = 2  # the cap, fixed from public knowledge of the population
capped = rows.sample(fraction=1.0, shuffle=True, seed=0).group_by("user").head(k)
print(capped.height)  # 5
print(capped.group_by("user").len()["len"].max())  # 2
Choosing the cap trades noise against bias (Amin et al. 2019). A larger cap keeps more data but needs more noise, while a smaller cap discards records and reweights the data toward light users. On the running example at a user-level \(\varepsilon = 4\), a cap of fifty records instead of one multiplies the noise by 5.8, and accuracy falls from 0.8917 to 0.6401.
So take the cap from public knowledge of the population, or choose it privately and count the cost, for example with a private quantile of records per user (Beyond global sensitivity). Trying caps on test accuracy spends privacy that the accountant does not see.

title: 45  User-level differential privacy
text:
45.6 Heterogeneous users
User-level training also changes the objective. Averaging per user weights users equally, while example-level training weights them by their number of records (Disparate impact). If heavy users should count for more, sum a user’s gradients before clipping. Their influence then rises with their records until clipping caps the sum at \(C\), and \(\varepsilon\) does not change.

title: 45  User-level differential privacy
text:
45.8 Code
The rate-\(kq\) screen needs only a record-level accountant, such as Google’s dp_accounting. This snippet screens users with one and two records, and computes the book’s \(\delta\) for 1,000 users.
import math

import dp_accounting


def screen(k: int, q: float = 0.01, sigma: float = 1.0, steps: int = 10_000) -> float:
    """The epsilon of a user with k records, screened as one record sampled at rate k * q."""
    step = dp_accounting.PoissonSampledDpEvent(k * q, dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(sigma))
    accountant = dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant()
    accountant.compose(dp_accounting.SelfComposedDpEvent(step, steps))
    return accountant.get_epsilon(1e-5)


print(f"{screen(1):.2f}")  # 6.71
print(f"{screen(2):.2f}")  # 15.35
print(10 ** math.floor(math.log10(1_000**-1.1)))  # 0.0001
Its 15.35 is a little above the table’s 15.32, because the two accountants use different Rényi orders, so quote the value you ran and name its accountant. With \(k = 1\) and \(q\) the user sampling rate, the same code accounts for user-level DP-SGD.
