title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.1 Why this matters
Every model trained with differential privacy (DP) ships with a privacy budget \(\varepsilon\). The chapter on private stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD, showed what each budget costs in accuracy. This chapter adds what it means for the people in the data, so that \(\varepsilon\) is not chosen by habit (“everyone uses 8”).
An attacker who wants to know whether a record was used for training runs a membership test. The test catches real members, its true positives, and wrongly flags non-members, its false positives. The budget \(\varepsilon\) and its small slack \(\delta\) cap the first rate in terms of the second (The definition of differential privacy). But each training run also has its own curve of the best rates an attacker can reach, usually far below the cap. So compute that curve, read it at the false positive rate of your threat, and set it beside the accuracy each budget buys.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.2 Justifying a choice
A defensible choice says what the budget protects before it picks the number.

Unit and period. Say whether one unit is a record, a user or a device, and whether neighbouring datasets differ by adding or removing one unit or by replacing one. Say which runs the budget covers, since every tuning run spends budget too (Hyperparameter tuning).
Threat. Say whether the concern is membership, reconstruction or attribute inference, and what the attacker knows and sees. This sets the false positive rate at which you read the curve, a low one for an attacker who must rarely accuse a non-member.
Whole guarantee. Choose \(\delta\) by the book’s rule (Section 46.5), then compute the trade-off curve (Section 46.3) and read it there.
Evidence. The curve is a theorem about an algorithm, not about your code, so run an audit that could refute it (Auditing private training).
Utility. Put accuracy against \(\varepsilon\) next to the risk, and pick the smallest budget past the bend, where accuracy stops improving. Draw it on public or proxy data, because private runs that choose \(\varepsilon\) are a search whose cost the reported \(\varepsilon\) leaves out.
Comparison. Only now compare with deployments (Section 46.6) and with the tiers in the rules of thumb.

Adult, a public census survey, shows step 5 on a real run. Train a model with DP-SGD trains a small network on 30,000 of its people at five budgets, each with \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). title: 46  Choosing ε
section: 46.3 The pair and the whole curve
text:
46.3 The pair and the whole curve
A membership test says “member” or “non-member” about one target record. Its TPR is the chance that it says “member” when the target was in the training set, and its FPR the chance when it was not. Every test against an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} \le \min\big\{1,\ e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta,\ 1 - e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - \mathrm{FPR})\big\}. \tag{46.1}\] The middle term is the one that binds at low FPR, and the last applies the same cap to the members a test misses. Attacks are judged at a low FPR, because an attack that rarely flags a non-member identifies people with confidence (Membership inference). Yet at \(\varepsilon = 8\) and an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), the pair caps the TPR at 0.9997, which constrains almost nothing.
A real training run satisfies DP for a whole range of pairs, one \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) for each \(\varepsilon\), because its accountant can trade \(\varepsilon\) for \(\delta\). Each pair gives a line, the middle term of Equation 46.1, and every test must stay under all of these lines at once. The best test reaches the lowest line exactly, which is called the trade-off curve: \[\mathrm{TPR}^*(\mathrm{FPR}) = \min_{\varepsilon}\big(e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta(\varepsilon)\big). \tag{46.2}\] For DP-SGD, a privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant computes this curve. It can round the privacy loss up or down, and the two curves it gets bracket the true one (Numerical accounting).
Table 46.2 compares the pair with the curve for this part’s running example from DP-SGD, a synthetic run sampled at rate 0.01 for 10,000 steps.

To compute the curve with Google’s dp_accounting, build the run’s PLD, ask it for \(\delta\) on a grid of \(\varepsilon\), and take the lowest line. The snippet’s first print falls inside the bracket of Table 46.2, and its second gives the last column of Table 46.1.
import numpy as np
from dp_accounting.pld import privacy_loss_distribution as pld

EPS_GRID = np.linspace(0.0, 20.0, 2001)


def tpr_at(sigma: float, q: float, steps: int, fpr: float) -> float:
    run = pld.from_gaussian_mechanism(sigma, sampling_prob=q).self_compose(steps)
    deltas = np.array(run.get_delta_for_epsilon(EPS_GRID))
    return float(np.min(np.exp(EPS_GRID) * fpr + deltas))


print(f"{tpr_at(1.36, 0.01, 10_000, 1e-3):.4f}")  # 0.0126
adult = [tpr_at(sigma, 1 / 30, 300, 1e-3) for sigma in (8.125, 2.383, 1.431, 0.973, 0.722)]
print(" ".join(f"{tpr:.4f}" for tpr in adult))  # 0.0013 0.0023 0.0046 0.0123 0.0445
The library’s default PLD rounds the loss up, so its curve is a valid upper bound. A Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant gives a valid but looser curve. The Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) approximation is quick but not a bound, so use it to explain and the PLD to certify.
The curve is a worst case, for an attacker who sees every intermediate model, so a typical record attacked through the final model alone is much safer. The curve bounds reconstruction too, since a guess among \(m\) equally likely records is a membership test at an FPR of \(1/m\) (Reconstruction attacks).

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.4 What an attacker can believe
Most people ask how sure an attacker can become that a person was in the data. Write \(p\) for the attacker’s prior, its probability of “member” before it sees the model. A privacy loss of at most \(\varepsilon\) means that no output is more than \(e^\varepsilon\) times as likely with the person’s record as without it. So the attacker’s belief afterwards is at most \[\Pr[\text{member} \mid \text{output}] \le \frac{p\,e^\varepsilon}{p\,e^\varepsilon + 1 - p}. \tag{46.3}\] So DP bounds the change of belief, not the belief itself.
For example, an attacker who starts at 1% can end at 35.55% when \(\varepsilon = 4\). That is for the worst output, and in DP-SGD the privacy loss of the released model is usually far below \(\varepsilon\).
Base rates matter as much as the loss. An attacker who accuses every person its test flags as a member is right with probability \[\Pr[\text{member} \mid \text{flag}] = \frac{p\,\mathrm{TPR}}{p\,\mathrm{TPR} + (1 - p)\,\mathrm{FPR}}. \tag{46.4}\] Take the running example’s \(\varepsilon = 8\) run and an attacker with a 1% prior who flags at an FPR of \(10^{-2}\). The curve caps its TPR there at 0.2092 (Table 46.2), so at most 0.1744 of its flags are right, and five out of six are false. An insider with a prior of 0.5 would be right far more often, so a statement about beliefs must name the attacker.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.5 How small δ must be
For \(n\) privacy units, the book’s rule sets \(\delta \le 1/n^{1.1}\), rounded down to a power of ten (How small δ must be). The units are people when one person has many records (User-level differential privacy). The rule gives \(10^{-5}\) for both of this page’s runs. When \(n\) is just above a power of ten, as with Adult’s 30,000 people, that \(\delta\) is not far below \(1/n\). NIST SP 800-226, the US guidelines for evaluating DP claims, calls a \(\delta\) above \(10^{-5}\) suspicious unless justified.
For DP-SGD a smaller \(\delta\) is cheap. The RDP accountant that set the running example’s \(\varepsilon = 4\) run puts it at only 5.209 when \(\delta\) falls to \(10^{-8}\). So report \(\varepsilon\) at a second, smaller \(\delta\) too, and never quote a \(\delta\) as large as one over the number of units.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.6 Comparing with deployed values
“Industry uses \(\varepsilon\) between 1 and 10” hides what every \(\varepsilon\) needs, its privacy unit and the period over which it is spent. The Census Bureau’s 2020 redistricting data used zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), which states the guarantee as one number, written \(\rho\), that converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pairs. Its unit was one person’s record under the replace-one relation, and persons got \(\rho = 2.56\), reported as \(\varepsilon = 17.14\) at \(\delta = 10^{-10}\).
So before you compare, convert both budgets to the same unit, neighbouring relation and \(\delta\). A zCDP parameter \(\rho\) converts to a pair by \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}. \tag{46.5}\] For the Census figures this formula gives 17.92, and the Bureau’s 17.14 comes from a tighter conversion. Since a replacement is a removal followed by an addition, an add/remove guarantee \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) implies only the replace-one guarantee \((2\varepsilon, (1 + e^\varepsilon)\delta)\) (The definition of differential privacy). And a budget stated per day adds up over time by composition, to 365 a year at \(\varepsilon = 1\) per day.
So it would be wrong to call the running example’s \(\varepsilon = 8\) run “less than half the Census budget”. At the Census’s \(\delta = 10^{-10}\) it is at 11.627, and under the Census’s replace-one relation that can double.

title: 47  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
47.1 Why this matters
The differential privacy (DP) version of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD, loses much accuracy when it trains a model from random weights, most at a privacy loss \(\varepsilon\) of 1 or below. The most accurate private models avoid this. They start from a model pretrained without privacy on a large public dataset, and only fine-tune it privately on the sensitive data (Tramèr & Boneh 2021).
Fine-tuning only a small part of the model often helps further. DP-SGD adds noise to every weight it trains, while the useful signal does not grow with their number, so fewer weights mean less noise for the same signal. The workflow Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA does the job end to end.
crumbs: 47  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 47  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
47.2 How many weights to train
Which weights you train leaves \(\varepsilon\) unchanged, because DP-SGD’s guarantee needs only that one record moves the clipped sum by at most the clipping norm \(C\). The choice changes only how much noise lands on the model. Anything else computed only from public data is also free, if no choice in it looked at the private data. Examples are the starting weights, a tokenizer and normalization statistics.
The noise grows with the number \(d\) of trainable weights. Write \(\sigma\) for the noise multiplier and \(B\) for the expected batch size, expected because DP-SGD’s Poisson sampling draws batches of random size. Then the noise on the averaged gradient has length about \[\text{noise length} \approx \frac{\sigma C\sqrt d}{B}. \tag{47.1}\] The signal, the average clipped gradient, is at most \(C\) long whatever \(d\) is. It can even get longer when fewer weights train, because clipping then cuts each record’s gradient less.
Take the running example of DP-SGD, a small network with 3,329 weights, pretrained on a similar public task and fine-tuned on the 10,000 private records. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and the pretrained weights, the noise is 92.0 times longer than the signal when all weights train. It is only 6.7 times longer when the 65 weights of the last layer train. That gap is wider than the formula predicts, because the signal is longer when only the last layer trains (0.0250 against 0.0130).
But counting weights overstates the cost of training them all. Noise does harm only along the directions in which the loss is curved, because a step along a flat direction barely changes the loss. Near a pretrained model, few directions are curved (Li, Liu et al. 2022). So on the running example, full fine-tuning trains 51 times as many weights as the last layer, but its noise should raise the loss only 7.5 times as much. A larger learning rate lets the noise into more of the nearly flat directions, so private fine-tuning wants smaller steps than training from scratch.
Training fewer weights has its own cost, a bias, because no private data can move the model along a frozen direction that the task needs.
crumbs: 47  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 47  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
47.3 Linear probing first
The simplest option freezes everything but the last layer and trains a linear classifier on the frozen features, which is linear probing. Because the features are fixed, the probe’s loss is convex. So linear probing turns private deep learning back into Private empirical risk minimization, which makes it the safe first baseline.
A private probe’s error has two parts. One is the error that privacy adds to convex empirical risk minimization (ERM), which grows with the number \(d\) of features. The other is the feature gap, how far the best linear model on the features falls short of the best model of any kind, which no number of records or size of \(\varepsilon\) closes. For example, the running example’s probe without privacy, its ceiling, has a test accuracy of 0.9536, while a non-private network trained from scratch reaches 0.9606. The private probe stays within 0.006 of that ceiling, but never passes it.
So measure the probe’s ceiling first, by fitting it without privacy on labelled public data that resemble the task. If it already meets your target, stop there. To train the probe privately, feed the frozen features to diffprivlib’s LogisticRegression (Private empirical risk minimization), or run DP-SGD on the one layer.
crumbs: 47  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 47  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
47.4 Low-rank adapters and full fine-tuning
When the probe’s ceiling is below your target, only changing the earlier layers can lift it. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022) freezes each pretrained matrix and learns a small correction to it. The correction is the product of two thin matrices that each have \(r\) columns, where \(r\) is the rank. A matrix with \(d_{\text{in}}\) inputs and \(d_{\text{out}}\) outputs has \(d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}\) weights, while its adapter has only \[d = r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}}). \tag{47.2}\]
The adapter comes from Hugging Face’s peft library. This snippet puts a rank-4 adapter on the first layer of a network shaped like the running example, and trains its last layer in full.
import torch
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model

model = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(50, 64), torch.nn.Tanh(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 1))
print(sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()))  # 3329
config = LoraConfig(r=4, lora_alpha=8, target_modules=["0"], modules_to_save=["2"], lora_dropout=0.0)
adapted = get_peft_model(model, config)  # freezes every pretrained weight
print(sum(p.numel() for p in adapted.parameters() if p.requires_grad))  # 521
In the snippet, target_modules and modules_to_save name layers by their index in the Sequential, and lora_alpha scales the correction. It trains 521 weights, the adapter’s \(4 \times (50 + 64) = 456\) and the last layer’s 65. The run in Section 47.5 treats the first layer’s biases as a 51st input, which gives 525. Opacus’s PrivacyEngine computes per-example gradients only for the parameters that require them, so the frozen weights cost nothing. Call model.train() before make_private, because Opacus rejects a model in evaluation mode, as a pretrained model often is after you measure it.
The adapter’s second factor starts at zero, so training begins exactly at the pretrained model. The first factor starts random, and that draw must not depend on the private data.
Yu et al. (2022) showed that private fine-tuning of language models with LoRA matches or beats private full fine-tuning, at a fraction of the compute and memory. Each adapter factor is an ordinary linear layer, so the ghost clipping of DP-SGD applies to it. Still, Li, Tramèr et al. (2022) matched the adapters with full fine-tuning, using large batches and a learning rate tuned for private training.

text:
47.5 Which method at which budget
The numbers in this section come from the full edition’s synthetic running example. No practitioner script reproduces them, so treat them as one task’s evidence. DP-SGD fine-tunes the last layer, a rank-4 adapter plus the last layer, or all weights, against a model trained privately from scratch. Each method’s learning rate was chosen at \(\varepsilon = 1\) on half of the private test set, and accuracy comes from the other half. That choice looked at private data without paying, so the table shows each method at its best, not what a real run could claim (Hyperparameter tuning).

Here pretraining is worth about a factor of eight in \(\varepsilon\), since the adapter at \(\varepsilon = 1\) matches training from scratch at \(\varepsilon = 8\).
At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) the last layer is best, because its noise is 7.2 times shorter than full fine-tuning’s, and its ceiling does not yet bind. From \(\varepsilon = 1\) on, it is stuck near its ceiling while the others keep improving. The adapter is never more than 0.0022 below the best method, so it is the robust middle choice here. But a public task further from the private one can reverse the ranking even when the probe’s ceiling looks fine, so rerun the comparison on a public stand-in for your task.
The learning rate matters as much as the method, since a step three times too large costs full fine-tuning 1.3 percentage points of accuracy. The adapter’s rank matters little, since at \(\varepsilon = 1\) ranks 1, 4 and 16 differ by about the run-to-run spread.

title: 47  Public data and private fine-tuning
section: 47.6 What public data does not buy
text:
47.6 What public data does not buy
Whatever the public data are, training on the private data is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, where \(\delta\) is the small additive slack the guarantee allows. The public data get no guarantee of any kind. Non-private pretraining can memorize individual records (Memorization and training-data extraction), and the fine-tuned model inherits whatever the pretrained weights encode (Tramèr, Kamath & Carlini 2024).
So a person in both datasets has protection only in the private copy. A membership attack against the pretrained model (Membership inference) has no bound at all. Web-scale “public” datasets contain posts, profiles and leaked documents, so private notes or emails may well overlap with them. For text, also mind the privacy unit, because one person’s documents span many training sequences (User-level differential privacy).
Check three things before you train and when you report.

Check that the public data resemble the private task, and deduplicate the private set against them. Deduplication protects copies, not people, since exact matching misses paraphrases.
Choose the public model and the hyperparameters on public data. Otherwise every private run costs privacy (Hyperparameter tuning).
Name the public data and the overlap check, and state that the guarantee covers the private data given the pretrained model.

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
48.1 Why this matters
You have a pretrained language model and private text, such as support tickets or clinical notes. You want the model to learn from that text without being able to repeat it. A model fine-tuned without privacy can write out a phone number or a password that was often in its training text (Memorization and training-data extraction). The fix is to fine-tune with the differential privacy (DP) version of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD. It costs least when it trains only a small adapter on the frozen model, which is often as accurate as training every weight (Public data and private fine-tuning). Here the adapter is low-rank adaptation (LoRA), from Hugging Face’s peft library, and Opacus does the private training.
The model is Pythia-14m, a public language model of 14 million parameters from EleutherAI. The private text is Tiny Shakespeare, a million characters of Shakespeare’s plays. The script fine-tunes the model twice, once without privacy and once at a privacy loss \(\varepsilon\) of 8 for each sequence of training text. First it plants made-up secrets, called canaries, in the text, so that you can see what each model memorized. The script practitioner_lora.py runs in a few minutes without a GPU.

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
section: 48.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
text:
48.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
The guarantee protects one unit, so decide first what the unit is. A language model trains on fixed-length sequences of tokens, the word pieces its tokenizer cuts text into. The script cuts the text into sequences of 32 tokens, about one or two lines of verse, and makes each sequence the unit. To keep the run short, it trains on the first 1,024 sequences and holds out the last 128.
sequences of 32 tokens: 10,632  training n=1,024  held out 128
delta=1e-04 (privacy unit: one training sequence)
For \(n = 1{,}024\) sequences, the book’s rule for the slack \(\delta\) gives \(10^{-4}\) (How small δ must be).
A sequence is the right unit for this demonstration, but rarely in production. One person’s document spans many sequences, and one user writes many documents, so a guarantee per sequence protects a person much less than it seems. In production, make the unit a document or a user, and bound how many sequences each contributes. Then set \(\delta\) from the number of users (User-level differential privacy).
crumbs: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
48.3 Plant canaries
To check memorization later, you need secrets whose presence you control. So the script writes canaries into the training text. Each is a sentence such as “the pin of Alice is 8 6 5 2 3”, whose last five digits are the secret. There are four groups of three canaries, inserted 1, 4, 16 and 64 times each. Three more, the controls, are drawn the same way but never inserted, so they show what an unseen secret scores in the audit of Section 48.9.
def insert_canaries(
    train: torch.Tensor, canaries: list[Canary], tokenizer: PreTrainedTokenizerBase, rng: np.random.Generator
) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Write each copy of each canary over the start of a different training sequence."""
    train = train.clone()
    total = sum(c.copies for c in canaries)
    rows = iter(rng.choice(len(train), size=total, replace=False).tolist())
    for canary in canaries:
        tokens = torch.tensor(tokenizer(canary.text)["input_ids"])
        for _ in range(canary.copies):
            train[next(rows), : len(tokens)] = tokens
    return train
The 255 copies take up a quarter of the training set. That is far denser than secrets in real data, on purpose, because it lets a model this small memorize within a short run, so the audit has a positive control.
canary sequences: 255 (3 canaries each at (1, 4, 16, 64) copies)
tokens per secret: [5]
candidates: 2,000  exposure cap 10.97 bits  (full space 16.61)
The digits are separated by spaces so that every possible secret is exactly five tokens long, which the second line confirms over 1,000 random secrets.
crumbs: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
section: 48.4 Load a public model and tokenizer
text:
48.4 Load a public model and tokenizer
Everything not trained privately must come from outside the private data. That includes the tokenizer, whose vocabulary would leak rare words if it were built from the private text. So the weights and the tokenizer both come from the same public checkpoint, Pythia-14m, pinned to one revision. The script loads the model in float32, because transformers loads some checkpoints in float16, which is far slower on a CPU.
The guarantee then covers the private text given the pretrained model, and says nothing about the model’s own training data. Pythia was pretrained on the Pile, which includes Project Gutenberg’s books and so very likely Shakespeare’s plays. That is harmless here, but with real data, check for overlap with the public model’s training data (Public data and private fine-tuning).
crumbs: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
48.5 Choose what to train
DP-SGD adds noise to every weight it trains. So the noise on the averaged gradient grows with the square root of the number of trained weights, but the clipped signal does not (Public data and private fine-tuning). That makes the choice of trainable weights a main lever on accuracy, with the learning rate. LoRA freezes each pretrained matrix and learns a correction to it, the product of two thin factors whose width is the rank.
attention_and_mlp = ["query_key_value", "dense", "dense_h_to_4h", "dense_4h_to_h"]  # every linear layer
config = LoraConfig(r=rank, lora_alpha=2 * rank, target_modules=attention_and_mlp, lora_dropout=0.0)
lora_model = get_peft_model(model, config)  # freezes the pretrained weights
trainable_count = sum(p.numel() for p in lora_model.parameters() if p.requires_grad)
total_count = sum(p.numel() for p in lora_model.parameters())
print(f"trainable parameters: LoRA {trainable_count:,}  full fine-tuning {total_count - trainable_count:,}")
full model parameters: 14,067,712
trainable parameters: LoRA 98,304  full fine-tuning 14,067,712
By default the adapters have rank 8 and sit on every linear layer, in attention and in the feed-forward blocks. They train 98,304 weights, against about 14 million for full fine-tuning. lora_alpha scales the adapters’ correction, set to the usual twice the rank. For a real task, choose the rank and the layers on public data, because a choice made from private runs costs privacy (Hyperparameter tuning).
crumbs: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
48.6 Make the model Opacus-compatible
Opacus needs one gradient per sequence, and layers that mix the records of a batch, such as batch normalization, make that impossible. Opacus’s ModuleValidator.validate lists such layers before you train.
validator errors: 0
Pythia has none, and only the adapters train in any case. They are ordinary linear layers, which Opacus’s default hooks handle, so the script passes grad_sample_mode="hooks". Opacus computes per-sequence gradients only for the weights that require gradients, so the 14 million frozen weights add no cost. Call model.train() before you wrap a model you have just evaluated, because Opacus rejects one in evaluation mode. After training, the hooks stay attached and slow down everything the model does next, so the script calls remove_hooks() before it evaluates the private model.
crumbs: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
48.7 Calibrate and train
The accountant finds the noise for a fixed target, here \(\varepsilon = 8\) over 3 epochs with an expected batch of 32 sequences. The sampling rate \(q\), the share of the data in an average batch, is then \(32/1{,}024\), so the 3 epochs take 96 steps. The accountant is the privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant, which computes \(\varepsilon\) almost exactly (Choosing an accountant).
privacy_engine = PrivacyEngine(accountant="prv")
private_model, optimizer, loader = privacy_engine.make_private_with_epsilon(
    module=model,
    optimizer=optimizer,
    data_loader=loader,  # replaced by Poisson sampling with rate BATCH / n
    target_epsilon=epsilon,
    target_delta=delta,
    epochs=EPOCHS,
    max_grad_norm=MAX_GRAD_NORM,
    grad_sample_mode="hooks",
)
print(f"noise multiplier: {optimizer.noise_multiplier:.3f}")
The training loop is an ordinary one, with Poisson batches, in which each sequence joins each batch independently with probability \(q\).
for (batch,) in loader:  # each batch holds a random number of sequences
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = private_model(input_ids=batch, labels=batch).loss
    loss.backward()  # Opacus's hooks keep one gradient per sequence
    optimizer.step()  # clips each one to MAX_GRAD_NORM, sums, adds noise
    steps += 1
noise multiplier: 0.553
sample rate q=0.03125  steps=96  noise multiplier=0.553
epsilon (Opacus PRV)=7.99  epsilon (dp_accounting PLD)=7.98  at delta=1e-04
The noise multiplier is the noise’s standard deviation in units of the clipping norm, MAX_GRAD_NORM, which the script sets to 1. The last line cross-checks the \(\varepsilon\) with the privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant of Google’s dp_accounting, as in Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run, and the two agree.
Both runs use AdamW at a learning rate of \(10^{-3}\), and the private run differs only by clipping, noise and Poisson sampling. That learning rate, the rank and the epochs were chosen in a few non-private trial runs on the same text. A real run must choose them on similar public text, such as other public-domain plays, or pay for the trials in \(\varepsilon\) (Hyperparameter tuning).
Two more settings change for a real run. With more data, use batches in the thousands, and let Opacus’s BatchMemoryManager split them into physical batches that fit in memory (Train a model with DP-SGD). And a model you release needs secure_mode=True in PrivacyEngine. Its secure noise cannot be seeded, so the script leaves it off.
crumbs: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
48.8 Evaluate
A language model is judged by how well it predicts held-out text. The script measures the mean cross-entropy per token on the 128 held-out sequences, and its exponential, the perplexity. A perplexity of 159.3 means the model is as unsure as if it chose among about 159 equally likely tokens. So lower is better.
held-out loss pretrained: 5.306 nats/token  perplexity 201.6
held-out loss LoRA non-private: 5.071 nats/token  perplexity 159.3
held-out loss LoRA DP eps=8: 5.044 nats/token  perplexity 155.1
Both fine-tuned models improve on the pretrained one. On one seed, the private model’s slightly lower perplexity means only that DP costs nothing measurable here. Both gains are modest, because a quarter of the training sequences begin with canaries rather than Shakespeare.
Do not expect privacy to be this cheap on every task. This run is short, trains few weights, and uses text that is very likely in the pretraining data already. With a harder task or a smaller \(\varepsilon\), compare the private model with both baselines at several budgets, as Train a model with DP-SGD does.
crumbs: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
48.9 Check memorization
The canaries show what perplexity cannot, whether the model will repeat a secret. The script measures each canary in two ways. The first is extraction. It gives the model the prefix “the pin of Alice is”, lets it write the likeliest next token five times, and checks whether the result is the secret.
@torch.no_grad()
def greedy_completion(model: PeftModel, tokenizer: PreTrainedTokenizerBase, prefix: str) -> str:
    """The five tokens the model writes after the prefix when it always picks the likeliest one."""
    ids = tokenizer(prefix, return_tensors="pt")["input_ids"]
    for _ in range(5):
        next_token = model(input_ids=ids).logits[:, -1].argmax(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        ids = torch.cat([ids, next_token], dim=1)
    return tokenizer.batch_decode(ids[:, -5:])[0].strip()
The second is the exposure of Memorization and training-data extraction. It ranks the canary’s secret among random secrets of the same format by how likely the model finds each, and turns the rank into bits. The script’s likelihood is the summed log-probability of the five digits. Each bit halves the number of guesses an attacker needs.
@torch.no_grad()
def secret_scores(model: PeftModel, tokenizer: PreTrainedTokenizerBase, prefix: str, secrets: list[str]) -> Scores:
    """Summed log-probability of each secret's five digit tokens after the prefix."""
    prefix_ids = tokenizer(prefix)["input_ids"]
    rows = [prefix_ids + tokenizer(" " + s)["input_ids"] for s in secrets]
    ids = torch.tensor(rows)  # every secret is five tokens, so the rows have equal length
    logits = model(input_ids=ids[:, :-1], logits_to_keep=5).logits  # the predictions of the five digits
    logprobs = logits.log_softmax(dim=-1).gather(-1, ids[:, -5:, None])
    return logprobs.sum(dim=(1, 2)).double().numpy()


def canary_exposure(
    model: PeftModel, tokenizer: PreTrainedTokenizerBase, canary: Canary, candidates: list[str]
) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """The exposure of the canary's secret among the candidates, measured and extrapolated past the cap."""
    candidate_scores = scores_batched(model, tokenizer, canary.prefix, candidates)
    score = float(scores_batched(model, tokenizer, canary.prefix, [canary.secret])[0])
    return exposure(score, candidate_scores), extrapolated_exposure(score, candidate_scores, SECRET_SPACE)
No library installed with this book computes exposure, so exposure and extrapolated_exposure come from the book’s helper module practitioner_privacy_tests.py, after TensorFlow Privacy’s versions. With 2,000 random candidates, a canary that beats them all reaches a cap of 10.97 bits. A secret the model has never seen has a random rank and averages about 1.44 bits (\(\log_2 e\)). Each line below gives a group’s mean exposure, the same past the cap, and how many of its three secrets greedy decoding wrote out.
non-private 1 copies: mean exposure 2.0 bits  extrapolated 2.0  extracted 0/3
non-private 4 copies: mean exposure 5.9 bits  extrapolated 5.7  extracted 0/3
non-private 16 copies: mean exposure 10.0 bits  extrapolated 13.0  extracted 0/3
non-private 64 copies: mean exposure 11.0 bits  extrapolated 16.3  extracted 3/3
non-private controls: mean exposure 1.4 bits  extrapolated 1.5  extracted 0/3
DP 1 copies: mean exposure 0.9 bits  extrapolated 0.9  extracted 0/3
DP 4 copies: mean exposure 0.6 bits  extrapolated 0.6  extracted 0/3
DP 16 copies: mean exposure 4.2 bits  extrapolated 4.3  extracted 0/3
DP 64 copies: mean exposure 4.0 bits  extrapolated 3.9  extracted 0/3
DP controls: mean exposure 2.2 bits  extrapolated 2.2  extracted 0/3
The non-private model, the positive control, leaks. Exposure rises with the number of copies, from 2.0 bits for one copy to the cap for 64, and the model writes out all three 64-copy secrets. The extrapolated column sees past the cap by fitting a skew-normal distribution, a normal with one heavier tail, to the candidates’ scores. It puts the 64-copy secrets near the 16.61 bits of the whole space.
The 4-copy canaries are the instructive case. Two of the three reach 6.9 and 8.2 bits, yet none is extracted, so exposure detects memorization that extraction alone would miss.
Greedy decoding extracts nothing from the private model, and its canaries with 1 or 4 copies score no higher than its controls. The controls’ 2.2 bits are within the scatter of a mean over three secrets. Still, DP limits the effect without erasing it, since the canaries with 16 and 64 copies still average about 4 bits.
The guarantee allows that, because \(\varepsilon = 8\) protects one sequence, while a canary with many copies is many sequences. Group privacy bounds a group of units at about their number times \(\varepsilon\). So 16 copies get \(16 \times 8\), far too much to promise anything (User-level differential privacy). A secret that a user repeats across many documents is the same case, one more reason to make the unit the user.
Two cautions apply. Because the canaries are so dense, a real non-private model may leak less than this one, and a real audit should plant fewer copies. And three canaries per group is a small sample. For a fuller assessment before release, run the attacks of Pre-release privacy risk assessment. For a statistical lower bound on \(\varepsilon\), run the one-run audit of Auditing private training.

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
48.10 Variants
Three variants matter for real models. The block below shows ghost clipping, LoRA on GPT-2, and packages that wrap the whole loop, with pinned versions. It was not run.
# opacus==1.6.0: ghost clipping, when per-sequence gradients do not fit in memory
model, optimizer, criterion, loader = privacy_engine.make_private_with_epsilon(
    module=model, optimizer=optimizer, data_loader=loader, criterion=torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss(),
    target_epsilon=8.0, target_delta=1e-4, epochs=3, max_grad_norm=1.0, grad_sample_mode="ghost",
)
logits = model(input_ids=batch).logits[:, :-1]                 # predict each next token
loss = criterion(logits.flatten(0, 1), batch[:, 1:].flatten(), shape=logits.shape)
loss.backward()                                                # norms first, then the clipped sum

# peft==0.21.2: GPT-2 stores its attention as Conv1D, with the weight transposed
LoraConfig(r=8, lora_alpha=16, target_modules=["c_attn"], fan_in_fan_out=True)

# dp-transformers==1.0.0 (Microsoft): Opacus inside the Hugging Face Trainer
# private-transformers (Li et al.): install from its GitHub repository, pinned to a commit
Ghost clipping gets each sequence’s gradient norm without storing the gradient, so memory no longer holds one gradient per sequence (DP-SGD).

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
48.11 Report
Release and governance builds the statement from the run’s record. For this run, it adds three things. The guarantee covers the private text given the pretrained model, named with its revision. The hyperparameters came from non-private trials on the private text, which a real release could not claim for free. And the canary audit is attached as evidence, with its caveats.
What ships is the adapter. With --save-adapter FOLDER, the script saves it after remove_hooks() and loads it back onto the same pinned checkpoint.
private.save_pretrained(path)  # only the adapter weights and config, after Opacus's hooks are removed
base_model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(folder, dtype=torch.float32)  # the same pinned checkpoint
reloaded = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base_model, path)
The folder holds only the adapter, so the statement names the base checkpoint and revision it fits. The guarantee covers the adapter and anything computed from it.

title: 49  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
49.1 What it is
Private prediction applies differential privacy (DP) to each answer instead of to the model. You split the private records into disjoint shards and train an ordinary model, a teacher, on each one. The teachers stay secret. Each query gets the winner of their vote after noise is added to the counts, private at a level \(\varepsilon\) with a small slack \(\delta\). A record lives in one shard, so it can move one teacher’s vote to another label. That changes the counts by at most \(\sqrt2\) in Euclidean length.
GNMax adds Gaussian noise with a standard deviation \(\sigma\) to each count and releases only the label with the largest noisy count. In Rényi differential privacy (RDP), each answer costs a straight line of slope \(1/\sigma^2\) in the order \(\alpha\), and the slopes add (Rényi DP). So write \(\rho(\varepsilon, \delta)\) for the largest slope that still converts to your target. A fixed number \(Q\) of answers, even adaptively chosen, then needs the noise \[\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{Q}{\rho(\varepsilon, \delta)}}. \tag{49.1}\] For example, at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) a budget of \(\varepsilon = 1\) allows a slope of 0.0306, so 1,000 answers need \(\sigma = 181\).
crumbs: 49  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning

title: 49  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
49.2 When you meet it
You meet private prediction when you cannot train a private model. The common case is a large language model (LLM) behind an interface, whose prompt holds private records that its answers leak. The fix splits the records into disjoint groups, prompts the model once per group, and releases the GNMax label (Duan et al. 2023). At \(\varepsilon = 1\), Wu et al. (2024) answered 10,000 sentiment queries this way as accurately as one non-private prompt.
Otherwise the choice is between private answers and a private model, whose accuracy is fixed. The vote’s noise grows with \(\sqrt Q\), so answers win up to a break-even number of queries, and the model wins beyond it. On the full edition’s 10,000-record synthetic task, the vote beats noisy stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD, only on the first 18 queries at \(\varepsilon = 1\). So compare the two at your budget and expected number of queries, with the DP-SGD baseline of Train a model with DP-SGD.
PATE (private aggregation of teacher ensembles) spends the budget once. It labels public, unlabelled inputs by GNMax and trains a new model, the student, on them. Only the student is released, at exactly the cost of its labels, so PATE needs public inputs from the private data’s distribution. Papernot et al.’s MNIST student comes within a percentage point of non-private accuracy, but at a data-dependent \(\varepsilon\) (Section 49.4). On the synthetic task, DP-SGD beats the best student at every budget.
crumbs: 49  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning

title: 49  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
49.3 How to use it
dp_accounting accounts for the vote. One GNMax answer is a GaussianDpEvent whose noise multiplier, the noise over the sensitivity, is \(\sigma/\sqrt2\).
import numpy as np
from dp_accounting import GaussianDpEvent, SelfComposedDpEvent
from dp_accounting.pld import PLDAccountant
from dp_accounting.rdp import RdpAccountant

sigma, queries = 181.0, 1000  # noise per count, answers to release
event = SelfComposedDpEvent(GaussianDpEvent(sigma / np.sqrt(2)), queries)  # sensitivity sqrt(2)
rdp = RdpAccountant().compose(event).get_epsilon(1e-5)
pld = PLDAccountant().compose(event).get_epsilon(1e-5)
print(f"{rdp:.3f} {pld:.3f}")  # 0.999 0.914
The RDP accountant confirms \(\varepsilon = 0.999\). The privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant, exact for Gaussian noise, gives 0.914, so solving for \(\sigma\) with it gives less noise. To solve, pass a function from \(\sigma\) to this event to dp_accounting.calibrate_dp_mechanism. For many answers the PLD is much slower, so RDP is the fallback. When each query draws a fresh Poisson sample of records, as in Wu et al., wrap each event in a PoissonSampledDpEvent.
crumbs: 49  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning

title: 49  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
49.4 What goes wrong
The guarantee needs each record in exactly one shard. So assign shards by a hash of the record’s or the user’s identifier, never by position in a file, where one inserted record shifts every later shard. Release the label only, and fix \(Q\) in advance.
Noise this large wipes out close votes. With two labels and a gap \(g\) between the counts, the vote returns the plurality with probability \(\Phi(g/(\sqrt2\sigma))\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function.
For example, the noise for 1,000 answers at \(\varepsilon = 4\) is \(\sigma = 51.8\). Then a lopsided vote of 98 to 2 is right with probability 0.9051, but a close vote of 52 to 48 only about half the time. So measure the noiseless vote first, since no budget beats it. Adding teachers widens the gaps, because \(\sigma\) does not depend on their number, until the shards get too small to train on.
Finally, beware of a data-dependent \(\varepsilon\). When teachers agree, a sharper analysis charges less, but that smaller \(\varepsilon\) is computed from the votes and leaks them. Until it is released with noise, it is a measurement, not a guarantee.
Confident-GNMax answers only queries on which a noisy check finds agreement, the cheap and accurate ones.

title: 50  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
50.1 What it is
Gradient descent without momentum adds up its steps. So its weights after each step depend on the sum of all clipped gradients so far, a prefix sum. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with differential privacy (DP), DP-SGD, adds fresh noise at every step. So the noise in the prefix sums grows like a random walk. Matrix mechanisms correlate the noise across steps, so that each step’s noise partly cancels earlier noise in the sums.
Stack the gradient sums of the steps as the rows of a matrix \(x\). The prefix sums are then \(Ax\), where \(A\) has ones on and below the diagonal. The matrix factorization mechanism writes \(A\) as a decoder \(L\) times an encoder \(R\). It adds a matrix of Gaussian noise, written \(z\), to the encoded gradients and decodes the result, \[\hat S = L(Rx + z) = Ax + Lz. \tag{50.1}\] A record enters only through the column of \(R\) for its step, so privacy depends on the longest column of the encoder, its sensitivity. Accuracy depends on the decoder, whose row \(t\) carries the noise into the \(t\)-th prefix sum.
The first such method ran the follow the regularized leader (FTRL) optimizer on sums from a binary tree, and is called DP-FTRL (Kairouz et al. 2021). Today’s usual choice is the square-root factorization, which uses the lower-triangular square root of \(A\) for both factors. At equal privacy over one epoch of 100 steps, it leaves about a quarter of independent noise’s standard deviation in the final sum.

title: 50  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
50.2 When you meet it
You meet matrix mechanisms when your pipeline cannot honestly claim Poisson sampling, the random batches that DP-SGD’s accountant assumes. Examples are fixed batches cut from a shuffled order, data read in arrival order, and phones in federated learning that check in when they can. Accounting them as Poisson understates \(\varepsilon\) (Amplification by subsampling), while a matrix mechanism needs no sampling.
Without sampling, independent noise loses much accuracy, and correlated noise wins most of it back. On the full edition’s synthetic task, trained in a fixed order for ten epochs at \(\varepsilon = 2\), independent noise reaches a test accuracy of 0.8641. The banded square root of Section 50.4 reaches 0.9491, and DP-SGD with Poisson sampling 0.9493. So if you can implement Poisson sampling, use DP-SGD with Opacus. If you cannot, use a banded matrix mechanism, as Google did for its Gboard keyboard models (Xu et al. 2023).

title: 50  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
50.3 How to use it
Google’s JAX Privacy implements banded matrix factorization. The block below was not run, because JAX is not in this book’s environment. It cycles through 100 fixed groups of records, one per step, so each record takes part once every 100 steps.
# jax-privacy==2.0.0 (not run)
from jax_privacy.experimental.execution_plan import BandMFExecutionPlanConfig

config = BandMFExecutionPlanConfig.default(
    num_bands=100,       # at most the 100 steps between a record's turns
    iterations=1000,     # ten epochs of 100 steps
    epsilon=2.0,
    delta=1e-5,
    sampling_prob=1.0,   # all of the step's group joins: no amplification claimed
    l2_clip_norm=1.0,
)
plan = config.plan       # calibrates the noise multiplier with dp_accounting
The training loop draws each batch from plan.batch_selection_strategy, sums its clipped gradients with plan.clipped_grad, and adds the noise with plan.noise_addition_transform. A dp_accounting accountant turns plan.dp_event into the \(\varepsilon\) you report. The module is marked experimental, so pin the version.

title: 50  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
50.4 What goes wrong
The pitfalls come from records that take part more than once. Over \(E\) epochs a record enters through \(E\) columns of the encoder. The square root’s columns for nearby steps are nonzero in the same rows, so they add up and the sensitivity grows faster than \(\sqrt E\). Banding keeps a number \(b\) of the encoder’s diagonals, the main one and those just below it. It needs every two participations of a record to be at least \(b\) steps apart, a condition called \(b\)-min-separation. The record’s columns then share no rows, so the sensitivity is at most \(\sqrt E\) times the longest column, as for independent noise.
So the data order is part of the mechanism. Fix it before training, independently of the data, and keep the same permutation every epoch, because a new shuffle can put a record at the end of one epoch and the start of the next.
The neighbouring relation changes the numbers too. The analysis here leaves a neighbour’s slot empty, so a step moves by at most the clipping norm. If a neighbour replaces the record with another instead, every sensitivity doubles, so state the relation next to every \(\varepsilon\).
dp_accounting 0.6.0 enforces this. Its tree-aggregation event works only in a Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant built with NeighboringRelation.REPLACE_SPECIAL, where a neighbour replaces the record with an empty one. Under add/remove, DP-SGD’s default, it raises UnsupportedEventError, and the privacy loss distribution accountant rejects it too. So DP-FTRL and DP-SGD runs cannot share one add/remove ledger.

title: 50  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
50.5 References

Choquette-Choo et al., “(Amplified) Banded Matrix Factorizations: A Unified Approach to Private Training” (NeurIPS 2023): banding, min-separation and amplification.

title: 51  Disparate impact
text:
51.1 Why this matters
A private model’s test accuracy is an average over everyone, so it cannot show which people lose the accuracy that privacy costs. Bagdasaryan, Poursaeed & Shmatikov (2019) trained networks with differential privacy (DP), using the private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) called DP-SGD. They found that the lost accuracy fell mostly on under-represented groups, and called this the disparate impact of DP.
So a model that is a point worse on average can be ten points worse for one small group, often one that privacy should protect. Before you ship a private model, measure its cost for each group against a non-private baseline, with a confidence interval on every number.

title: 51  Disparate impact
section: 51.2 Evaluating a private model per group
text:
51.2 Evaluating a private model per group
Decide which groups matter before you look at any results, so that the results cannot steer the choice. Then train a non-private baseline with the same data and recipe, because a gap between groups may exist without privacy. DP is responsible only for how far each group’s own accuracy drops when training becomes private.
Write \(\mathrm{acc}_g\) for a model’s accuracy on the test records of group \(g\). Private training is random, so its accuracy is averaged over several training runs, written \(\mathbb E\). The privacy cost \(\pi_g\) is the accuracy the group loses when the same data and hyperparameters are trained privately, \[\pi_g = \mathrm{acc}_g(\text{non-private}) - \mathbb E\big[\mathrm{acc}_g(\text{private})\big]. \tag{51.1}\] DP has disparate impact when groups have different privacy costs.
Every accuracy needs an interval. Each test record is classified correctly or not, so a group’s accuracy is a binomial proportion, and its exact Clopper–Pearson interval contains the true accuracy in at least 95% of test samples (Hypothesis testing).
The gap between two groups needs its own interval. Write \(\hat p_g\) for group \(g\)’s measured accuracy and \(m_g\) for its number of test records. For two groups \(a\) and \(b\) measured on disjoint test records, the variances of the two estimates add. So for large counts an approximate 95% interval for the gap is \[(\hat p_a - \hat p_b) \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_a(1 - \hat p_a)}{m_a} + \frac{\hat p_b(1 - \hat p_b)}{m_b}}. \tag{51.2}\]
These intervals are wider than most people expect. Suppose a test split holds only 100 records of a minority, and 88 of them are classified correctly. The majority gets 1,812 of its 1,900 records right, an accuracy of 0.954, so the measured gap is 0.074. SciPy gives the minority’s interval, and Equation 51.2 gives the gap’s.
from math import sqrt

from scipy.stats import binomtest

minority = binomtest(88, 100).proportion_ci(confidence_level=0.95, method="exact")
print(f"{minority.low:.3f} {minority.high:.3f}")  # 0.800 0.936

gap, se = 0.954 - 0.880, sqrt(0.954 * 0.046 / 1_900 + 0.880 * 0.120 / 100)
print(f"{gap - 1.96 * se:.3f} {gap + 1.96 * se:.3f}")  # 0.010 0.138
So the gap is real, since its interval excludes zero, but it could be anywhere from one point to fourteen. An interval separates a 5-point gap from zero only with a few hundred test records from the group, and a 1-point gap only with thousands.
The privacy cost needs a different interval. Both models are scored on the same test records, so their accuracies are not independent and Equation 51.2 does not apply. Pair them instead. Among group \(g\)’s \(m_g\) test records, write \(u\) for the number only the non-private model gets right, and \(v\) for those only the private one gets right. One run’s cost is then \((u - v)/m_g\), and for large counts an approximate 95% interval is \[\frac{u - v}{m_g} \pm \frac{1.96}{m_g}\sqrt{u + v - \frac{(u - v)^2}{m_g}}. \tag{51.3}\]
Training adds a second source of variation, which no test set removes. A small group’s accuracy varies far more between training runs than a large group’s, so a one-run comparison of two recipes can reverse. So train each recipe with several seeds, and report the mean cost and its spread.
The evaluation can also leak, because per-group accuracies on private test data are statistics of that data. To publish them, add noise to each group’s count of correct predictions and charge it to a budget of its own (Release statistics with a library).

title: 51  Disparate impact
section: 51.4 Why small groups pay: clipping and noise
text:
51.4 Why small groups pay: clipping and noise
DP-SGD loses accuracy through two steps, clipping and noise, and both treat every record alike. Yet the clipping row of Table 51.2, which adds no noise and so gives no privacy, already costs the minority 4.04 points. So clipping by itself treats the groups unequally.
Clipping caps every record’s pull on the update at the clipping norm \(C\), so it cuts back the groups with long gradients hardest. A group’s gradients are long where the model fits it badly, as it does a rare pattern the rest of the data does not teach. So training gives such a group less weight than its share of the records.
The noise is the same for every group, while a group’s signal grows with its size. So a small group’s signal is the weakest against the noise, and its privacy cost grows roughly like one over its share of the training records. The two causes compound, because the noise acts on the weight that clipping has already shrunk. A group whose gradients clipping halves pays like a group half its size.
To see which cause hurts your model, measure per-example gradient norms by group. Opacus’s GradSampleModule, the wrapper DP-SGD training already uses, keeps one gradient per row in each parameter’s grad_sample, so one backward pass gives the norms.
wrapped = GradSampleModule(model)  # adds hooks that keep one gradient per row
wrapped.train()
logits: torch.Tensor = wrapped(split.x)
nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(logits, split.y).backward()  # fills p.grad_sample for every weight p
norms = stacked_norms(wrapped)
Group the norms by each row’s group label, kept beside the batch but not fed to the model. Log each group’s median norm and fraction clipped as training goes on, because the groups can separate late. At initialization on Adult, the median norm is 1.444, so \(C = 1\) clips every row, whatever its group.

title: 51  Disparate impact
text:
51.5 Mitigations and what they cost
At a fixed budget, a change to the training recipe only moves the cost between the groups or between clipping and noise (Table 51.3). Only the last row, which changes the data, the starting model or the budget, reduces it.

Oversampling costs the group’s privacy, because a record’s guarantee depends on its own chance of being sampled (Amplification by subsampling). So run the accountant at the oversampled rate. In the running example, sampling the minority four times as often at \(\varepsilon = 4\) raises the noise multiplier from 1.36 to 4.71. The gap between the groups’ accuracies then narrows from 9.93 points to 3.99, but by levelling down, since the majority loses 8.01 points.
No algorithm avoids some of the cost. Learning a small group’s own rule means estimating it privately from that group’s few records, and private estimation from few records has an error floor that no mechanism beats (Lower bounds).

title: 52  Auditing private training
text:
52.1 Why this matters
When you train with differential privacy (DP), the accountant turns your configuration into a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) at a slack \(\delta\). That number is a proof about an algorithm, but what ships is code. A bug in the noise, the clipping or the sampling makes the model less private but barely changes its accuracy, which is flat across a wide range of noise levels (the training workflow). So the usual tests never notice the bug.
An audit checks the code by attacking it. It plants records called canaries, trains with and without them, and counts how often a membership test guesses right. DP caps how often any test can be right, so a test that is right too often proves that the code is less private than claimed. A test that is rarely right proves nothing, since a weak attack also fails against a leaky model.

title: 52  Auditing private training
section: 52.2 Known bugs, and which audit catches them
text:
52.2 Known bugs, and which audit catches them
These bugs break the private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD.

The variance passed where the standard deviation is expected, or noise scaled for the mean but added to the sum, which adds the batch size times too little noise. A unit test in continuous integration (CI) catches both (Section 52.3).
Clipping applied after averaging, or noise from a weak seed. Nasr et al. (2023) found both in real code with per-step audits like the CI test.
The accountant told the wrong numbers, such as a record count that includes augmented copies, which makes \(\varepsilon\) look smaller than it is. Only an end-to-end audit can catch it, and only if the error is large.
Batches shuffled but accounted as Poisson sampling, which can make the true \(\varepsilon\) several times the reported one (Amplification by subsampling). No audit here exercises the sampling, so check the loader itself.

Audits catch errors only in the unsafe direction, so code that adds too much noise passes them all.

title: 52  Auditing private training
section: 52.3 A CI test for the noise and the clipping
text:
52.3 A CI test for the noise and the clipping
The cheapest strong audit tests one step of the optimizer, many times. A Dirac canary is a per-example gradient that is zero except on one coordinate, where every other record’s gradient is zero. Put it into every step of one run and leave it out of another. The reading \(x_t\) is step \(t\)’s noisy gradient sum on that coordinate, divided by the clipping norm \(C\). The canary is longer than \(C\), so a correct optimizer clips it to length \(C\) and it adds exactly 1 to the reading. The optimizer also adds noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\), where \(\sigma\) is the noise multiplier, so each reading follows \[x_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) \text{ without the canary}, \qquad x_t \sim \mathcal N(1, \sigma^2) \text{ with it}. \tag{52.1}\]
A threshold test says “canary in” whenever a reading exceeds a threshold. Its true positive rate (TPR) is how often it says so when the canary was there, and its false positive rate (FPR) how often when it was not.
For two normal distributions a distance \(\mu\) apart, every threshold gives \(\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{TPR}) - \Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}) = \mu\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function. So measured rates bound the true separation \(\mu\), which a correct optimizer keeps at \(1/\sigma\): \[\mu \ge \Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{TPR}) - \Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}). \tag{52.2}\] The test plugs in the low end of the TPR’s Clopper–Pearson interval and the high end of the FPR’s. Each end is taken at level \(\beta/2\), so the bound holds with probability \(1 - \beta\) (Hypothesis testing). If this bound exceeds \(1/\sigma\), the code adds less noise than it claims.
The script practitioner_audit.py runs the test on Opacus’s own DPOptimizer. It writes per-example gradients into grad_sample by hand, as Opacus’s hooks would, and reads the noisy sum that optimizer.step() leaves in grad.
def canary_coordinate(sigma: float, planted_bug: str, with_canary: bool, steps: int) -> Array:
    """Run the optimizer for `steps` steps; return the canary coordinate of each noisy sum, in units of C."""
    layer = torch.nn.Linear(DIM_CI, 1, bias=False)
    optimizer = make_optimizer(layer, sigma, planted_bug)
    observations = np.empty(steps)
    for t in range(steps):
        setattr(layer.weight, "grad_sample", batch_grad_samples(with_canary))  # as Opacus's hooks would
        optimizer.step()  # clip each row to C, sum, add N(0, σ²C²)
        assert layer.weight.grad is not None
        observations[t] = layer.weight.grad[0, CANARY_COORD].item() / CLIP_CI
        optimizer.zero_grad()
    return observations
The canary’s gradient is ten times \(C\), so the test also exercises clipping. The script chooses the threshold on the first half of the steps and counts the rates on the second half. It also checks that the canary-free readings have a standard deviation within 10% of \(\sigma\), since with no noise every reading is 0. The command uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/practitioner_audit.py tests three optimizers at \(\sigma = 0.7\) and a batch of \(B = 64\) records, the correct one, one with the variance bug and one with no noise. The variance bug removes noise only because \(\sigma^2 < \sigma\) when \(\sigma\) is below 1, and above 1 it would pass.
sigma=0.7  C=1.0  B=64  steps per run=2000  claim mu=1/sigma=1.429
correct: noise std 0.687 (claim 0.7)  FP 206/1000  TP 710/1000
correct: mu_lo=1.201  pass
variance for std: noise std 0.481 (claim 0.7)  FP 206/1000  TP 862/1000
variance for std: mu_lo=1.722  FAIL
no noise: noise std 0.000 (claim 0.7)  FP 0/1000  TP 1000/1000

The correct optimizer’s bound on \(\mu\) is 1.201, below its claimed 1.429, so it passes. The variance bug’s bound is 1.722 and the missing noise’s is 5.360, so both fail. The test takes seconds, so run it on every commit.
Three things go wrong in practice.
First, a correct optimizer still fails with probability \(\beta\), here 5%, so an unseeded test fails one build in twenty. Fix the seed, or use a \(\beta\) of \(10^{-3}\) with more steps. Second, the script builds its own optimizer, so it tests Opacus, not your call to it. To test your code, have your setup function return the optimizer it makes, and drive that one. Third, the test never draws a batch or calls the accountant. So the same suite should assert that the loader is Opacus’s DPDataLoader and that a second library’s \(\varepsilon\) matches yours (Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run).

title: 52  Auditing private training
section: 52.4 From an attack to a lower bound
text:
52.4 From an attack to a lower bound
For a whole training run, the attack is a membership test on a planted canary. A trial is one training run, with or without the canary. Under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, every such test satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta, \qquad 1 - \mathrm{FPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,(1 - \mathrm{TPR}) + \delta. \tag{52.3}\]
Solving these for \(\varepsilon\) turns measured rates into a lower bound on it. Write \(\overline{\mathrm{FPR}}\) for the one-sided Clopper–Pearson upper bound on the FPR at level \(\beta/2\), and \(\underline{\mathrm{TPR}}\) for the TPR’s lower bound. With probability at least \(1 - \beta\), the code is then not \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, at the claimed \(\delta\), for any \(\varepsilon\) below \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}} = \max\Big\{\ln\frac{\underline{\mathrm{TPR}} - \delta}{\overline{\mathrm{FPR}}},\ \ln\frac{1 - \overline{\mathrm{FPR}} - \delta}{1 - \underline{\mathrm{TPR}}}\Big\}. \tag{52.4}\] The bound needs independent trials, and a threshold chosen on other trials than those it counts, because a threshold tuned on them inflates it.
No library installed with this book computes the bound, so the script imports eps_lower_bound from the book’s helper module, practitioner_privacy_tests.py. Suppose an attack catches the canary in 500 of 1,000 runs that include it, and raises one false alarm in 1,000 runs without it.
for false_pos, true_pos in ((1, 500), (0, 1_000)):  # out of 1,000 runs without and with the canary
    eps_lo = eps_lower_bound(false_pos, true_pos, 1_000, DELTA)
    print(f"FP {false_pos}/1000  TP {true_pos}/1000: certified eps lower bound {eps_lo:.2f}")
FP 1/1000  TP 500/1000: certified eps lower bound 4.43
FP 0/1000  TP 1000/1000: certified eps lower bound 5.60
The raw rates alone would suggest 6.21, but the certified bound is only 4.43, and even a perfect attack certifies only 5.60 from 1,000 trials per hypothesis. So do not expect an end-to-end audit to certify all of a large claim.

title: 52  Auditing private training
section: 52.5 A one-run audit of the trained model
text:
52.5 A one-run audit of the trained model
Thousands of runs are out of reach for a real model, so Steinke, Nasr & Jagielski (2023) get many trials from one run. Plant a number \(m\) of canaries, include each one by its own fair coin, train once and score every canary. Then fix a list length \(r\). Guess “in” for the \(r/2\) highest scores and “out” for the \(r/2\) lowest, and make no guess about the rest. Write \(W\) for the number of correct guesses.
Under \(\varepsilon\)-DP, no attack guesses one canary’s coin right with a probability above the limit \(p_\varepsilon\) given below. So the count \(W\) is no more likely to reach any value \(v\) than a binomial count with that success rate is: \[\Pr[W \ge v] \le \Pr\big[\mathrm{Bin}(r, p_\varepsilon) \ge v\big], \qquad p_\varepsilon = \frac{e^\varepsilon}{1 + e^\varepsilon}. \tag{52.5}\] An observed count that this binomial reaches with probability below \(\beta\) rules out that \(\varepsilon\), and the certified bound is the largest \(\varepsilon\) ruled out. Under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, the paper adds at most \(2m\delta\) to that probability. The coins must be independent and fair, and several list lengths need a Bonferroni correction, which runs each test at \(\beta\) divided by their number.
The script runs it on the released pipeline of Train a model with DP-SGD on the Adult census data. It adds only the canaries, 1,000 held-out rows with flipped labels. The coins put 537 of them in the training set, and the release’s noise multiplier gives \(\varepsilon = 3.91\) for this larger set at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). A non-private model uses the release’s baseline recipe, and a memorizing control runs non-private Adam for 60 epochs with small batches. Each canary is scored by minus its loss, and Table 52.1 gives each model’s best of six list lengths from 20 to 1,000.

Both release-recipe models certify nothing, and the reason is the recipe, not privacy. Ten epochs with large batches barely fit the flipped labels, so included canaries have the same loss as excluded ones, with or without noise. Only the memorizing control separates its canaries. Even it certifies just 0.53 for a model with no finite \(\varepsilon\), because each canary is a single trial. A perfect list of all 1,000 guesses would certify at most 5.27.
So use the one-run audit to expose a bug, when a DP model certifies more than its claim, never as evidence of privacy. Report it with its threat model, a black-box attacker who sees only the final model, and with a control that shows the attack can detect leakage on your data.
Stronger black-box attacks, such as the likelihood ratio attack (LiRA) of Pre-release privacy risk assessment, train shadow models. These are copies of the model, trained with its exact recipe on similar data. Run them before release and keep their results with the evidence (Release and governance). LiRA’s TPR at a low FPR shows what a realistic attacker learns. But its (model, record) pairs share models, so they are not independent trials and give no certified bound.

title: 53  Adaptive data analysis
text:
53.1 What it is
When you tune on a held-out validation set, you read the scores and try new settings, so each question depends on earlier answers. Such adaptive reuse overfits the holdout set, whose scores then overstate how the model does on new data.
Each such question is a statistical query, which averages a per-record answer between 0 and 1 over the \(n\) records you hold. A classifier’s accuracy is an example. Its population value is the same average over new data. Suppose the records are drawn independently and a number \(k\) of queries are fixed before any answer is seen. Then the largest gap between the two values is on average at most \[\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2k)}{2n}}. \tag{53.1}\] The number of queries enters through a logarithm, so it hardly matters.
Adaptive queries break this, because a later query can be built to fit the sample’s own noise. For example, Blum & Hardt’s boosting attack runs on a leaderboard whose labels are coin flips, where nothing can beat 0.5 on new data. Yet after 1,000 submissions on as many holdout records, it reports 0.7182.
Differential privacy (DP) is the remedy, because answers that reveal little about any record cannot be used to overfit it. Let a mechanism’s answers be on average within a distance \(\alpha\) of the empirical values. Let the whole exchange be DP at a privacy level \(\varepsilon\), with a small slack \(\delta\), for samples that differ in one replaced record. The transfer theorem then bounds the expected largest error against the population by \[\alpha + e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta, \tag{53.2}\] whatever the analyst does with the answers. For small \(\varepsilon\) the middle term is about \(\varepsilon\), so the bound is useful only well below \(\varepsilon = 1\). It protects the validity of the answers, not the people in the holdout set.

title: 53  Adaptive data analysis
text:
53.2 When you meet it
You meet adaptivity when a validation set, a test set or a leaderboard answers more than one round of questions, as in hyperparameter search. A round is a batch of questions fixed before any of its answers is seen, and the bounds below grow with the number of rounds. Table 53.1 gives the choice for each situation.



Table 53.1: How to reuse a holdout set, by situation.









Situation
What to do




A final evaluation
Keep a test set and use it once


Few adaptive rounds, plenty of data
Give each round its own slice of data


Many adaptive rounds, scarce data
Answer through noise, or use Thresholdout


A search that is private in the holdout set
Nothing more, since the transfer theorem covers the winner


A public leaderboard
Show a new score only when it beats the best by a margin (Blum & Hardt’s Ladder)

title: 53  Adaptive data analysis
text:
53.3 How to use it
The simplest fix is sample splitting, which answers each of \(r\) rounds on its own \(n/r\) records. The expected largest error is then at most \(\sqrt{r\ln(2k)/(2n)}\) for \(k\) queries in all, so the data you need grow in proportion to \(r\). Take 10,000 validation records and a search over 1,000 configurations, each chosen from the earlier scores, so \(r = k = 1{,}000\). Splitting then gives a bound of 0.6165, useless for scores between 0 and 1. A bound of 0.05 would need 1,520,181 records, where fixed queries would need 1,521.
Answering every query with Gaussian noise, under the transfer theorem, needs records that grow only like \(\sqrt k\). But its constants are large, so splitting stays cheaper up to a few hundred adaptive queries.
Thresholdout (Dwork et al. 2015) answers from a training set while the training value agrees with the holdout value. Such answers reveal nothing about the holdout set. When they differ by more than a noisy threshold, it records a detection and returns a noisy holdout value. So its privacy cost grows with the number of detections, not of queries. But its formal \(\varepsilon\) in the full edition’s experiment is about 29, and no mainstream library ships it. So treat it as a brake, not a guarantee.

title: 53  Adaptive data analysis
text:
53.4 What goes wrong
The common failure is not an attack but a long search that picks each setting from earlier validation scores. A fixed grid scored once, as in scikit-learn’s GridSearchCV, is a single round, so Equation 53.1 bounds its winner’s overstatement. So count rounds, and report how many a validation number has been through. Practice is often milder than the worst case, but the risk is real with few records and many rounds.

title: 54  Release and governance
text:
54.1 Why this matters
A model trained with differential privacy (DP) is not finished when training stops. A privacy reviewer or a data protection officer decides whether it may ship. They ask what the guarantee covers, whether its number is right and what it means under the law, and none of them can rerun your training. So the claim must travel with everything needed to check it. This chapter is the book’s home for the privacy statement and for the review of someone else’s claim.
The model is a small network, trained on 30,000 people from Adult with the private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD. It comes from Train a model with DP-SGD, with a target privacy level \(\varepsilon\) of 4. The script practitioner_release.py runs in a few seconds. It reads the run record that the training script writes, passed with --record PATH, or else a built-in copy of the book’s record.

title: 54  Release and governance
text: uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/practitioner_release.py

title: 54  Release and governance
text:
54.2 Assemble the run record
The record must hold what the accountant needs. The accountant is the code that turns a run’s settings into \(\varepsilon\) (Choosing an accountant). It reads four settings, the noise multiplier \(\sigma\), the sampling rate \(q\), the number of steps and the slack \(\delta\). It also takes four things for granted, so the record states those too. They are the privacy unit, here one person, the neighbouring relation and the sampler that drew each batch. The fourth is that no other use of the private data went uncounted.
The record also gives \(n\), the number of units, the seed, Opacus’s secure_mode and the library versions. It says how the hyperparameters were chosen and whether any preprocessing saw private data. In the excerpt, data is the training script’s record and RELEASE_CONTEXT holds the release owner’s additions.
merged = RELEASE_CONTEXT | data  # the training record, plus what the release owner adds
rec = load_record(merged)
for key, value in asdict(rec).items():
    print(f"{key}: {value}")
problems = record_problems(merged)  # missing fields, sampler not Poisson, delta above 1/n^1.1, tuning
limitations = record_limitations(merged)  # stated, so not a problem, but the statement must disclose them
print(f"record problems: {len(problems)}")
for problem in problems:
    print(f"  - {problem}")
print(f"record limitations: {len(limitations)}")
for limitation in limitations:
    print(f"  - {limitation}")

neighbours: add/remove
n: 30000
delta: 1e-05
sigma: 0.972900390625
sample_rate: 0.03333333333333333
sampler: poisson
secure_mode: False
seed: 0
steps: 300
...
record problems: 0
record limitations: 1
  - secure_mode=False: Opacus drew the noise from a seeded, non-cryptographic generator so the numbers reproduce; floating-point attacks on the noise are not excluded. Retrain with secure_mode=True to ship
The record’s \(\delta\) of \(10^{-5}\) follows the book’s rule (How small δ must be). Its values of \(\varepsilon\) come from the cross-check of Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run.
The tuning entry matters most to a reviewer, because the final run’s \(\varepsilon\) leaves out every run that helped choose a hyperparameter. Here non-private runs chose the learning rate on 2,000 held-out Adult rows that play the part of public data, and \(\varepsilon = 4\) was fixed before any private run. So the run’s \(\varepsilon\) is also the \(\varepsilon\) of the whole procedure. Those 2,000 people come from the same survey and get no guarantee, so the statement names them. If you tune on private data, report both values (Hyperparameter tuning).
A record problem stops the release, such as a missing field, a sampler that is not Poisson, a \(\delta\) above the rule or unreported tuning. The one limitation here is secure_mode, left off so that the book’s numbers repeat. The statement discloses it, and a model you ship is retrained with it on.

title: 54  Release and governance
text:
54.3 Recompute the guarantee
The release owner recomputes \(\varepsilon\) from \(\sigma\), \(q\) and the steps alone, with a library other than the one that trained. A recomputation inside the training code would reuse any wrong number. Compare the result only with a budget from the same kind of accountant, because a looser accountant gives a larger \(\varepsilon\) for the same run. The script uses the privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant of dp_accounting, as in the cross-check, and compares it with the looser Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant. It also reads \(\varepsilon\) at a \(\delta\) a hundred times smaller, and the trade-off curve. That curve gives the largest true positive rate (TPR) that any membership test can reach at each false positive rate (FPR) (Choosing ε).
pld = privacy_loss_distribution.from_gaussian_mechanism(sigma, sampling_prob=sample_rate).self_compose(steps)
eps_pld = pld.get_epsilon_for_delta(delta)
eps_pld_small = pld.get_epsilon_for_delta(delta / 100)
eps_rdp = rdp_epsilon(sigma, sample_rate, steps, delta)
eps_rdp_small = rdp_epsilon(sigma, sample_rate, steps, delta / 100)
tpr = {fpr: tpr_bound(pld, fpr) for fpr in FPRS}  # largest TPR of any membership test
eps PLD at delta=1e-05: 3.981
eps RDP at delta=1e-05: 4.503
eps PLD at delta=1e-07: 5.191
eps RDP at delta=1e-07: 5.736
TPR bound at FPR 1e-03: 0.0123 (PLD curve)  0.0536 (pair eps, delta only)
TPR bound at FPR 1e-02: 0.0652 (PLD curve)  0.5355 (pair eps, delta only)
record's PRV eps: reported 3.99, recomputed 3.98: consistent
The PLD value, 3.981, agrees with the reported 3.99. The curve gives a number a non-specialist can use. At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), no membership test can reach a TPR above 0.0123, while the pair \((3.98, 10^{-5})\) on its own would allow 0.0536.
The script flags a reported \(\varepsilon\) more than 0.05 below the recomputation. The subtler failure is a recomputation that agrees on wrong inputs, such as code that shuffles the data into fixed batches while the accountant assumes Poisson sampling (Amplification by subsampling). No number shows that, so the record’s sampler, read from the loader, is what catches it.
